## D245 Vendor GPUs, part 1: write-combining framebuffers (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** Every PC's GPU, Intel, AMD or NVIDIA, leaves the firmware's framebuffer lit (D236),
  and the kernel drew into it as uncached device memory: every pixel a separate bus write, a full
  1920x1080 frame tens of milliseconds. Vendor display drivers (mode setting, several outputs,
  vblank-synced flips) and acceleration are each a large driver of their own.
- **Decision.** The HAL's memory types gain `WriteCombining` (`Attributes::FRAMEBUFFER`): on x86_64
  every CPU programs `IA32_PAT` as Linux does (entry 1 write-combining, so `PWT` alone selects it,
  `PWT | PCD` uncached as before), on AArch64 `MAIR_EL1` gains Normal Non-cacheable at index 2,
  RISC-V encodes no memory types. Device windows remember their memory type, so a framebuffer and
  registers never share one; `devices::window::map_write_combining` maps a framebuffer, and the
  firmware framebuffer (D236) uses it. A flush's full fence drains the CPU's write-combining
  buffers.
- **Order of the vendor drivers** (later parts of M13): Intel's display engine first (taking over
  the pipe the firmware lit: its planes, a second surface in the GTT and flips at vblank, then mode
  setting on eDP, DP and HDMI), then AMD's DCN and NVIDIA's display, each behind the kernel's
  `Scanout`; 3D and compute acceleration after them, under M11's graphics stack. GPUs that need
  vendor firmware at run time (AMD, NVIDIA's GSP) wait for the firmware question D246 records.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; everything in the order above.

## D246 Wi-Fi, part 1: 802.11 frames, WPA2-Personal and CCMP in `eggos-wifi`, SHA-1, PBKDF2, AES key wrap, AES decryption and AES-CCM in `eggos-crypto`; adapters' firmware mirrored by eggspot's component store, outside the repository (D265; M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering; the firmware's distribution is the owner's)

- **Context.** Every Wi-Fi adapter a PC carries (Intel AX2xx/BE2xx, MediaTek, Realtek, Qualcomm)
  runs vendor firmware the operating system loads at start-up; none of it is open source, and
  CLAUDE.md allows only the firmware the machine itself provides outside EggOS, never copied into
  the repository. The part of Wi-Fi that is the same on every adapter is the frames and the
  security, which EggOS writes once.
- **Decision.**
  - **`eggos-crypto`** gains SHA-1, HMAC-SHA1 and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 (`sha1`, for WPA2's key
    derivation and MICs only), AES key wrap (`key_wrap`, RFC 3394), AES block decryption (the
    inverse steps built from the bitsliced forward ones, so no secret-indexed table) and AES-CCM
    with 8-byte tags and 13-byte nonces (`ccm`). Tests: FIPS 180, RFC 2202, RFC 6070, the 802.11
    PSK vector, RFC 3394 4.1, FIPS 197 C.1, RFC 3610 packet vector 1.
  - **`eggos-wifi`** (`wifi/`): beacons and probe responses parsed into networks (SSID, channel,
    BSSID, open, legacy, WPA2-Personal, WPA3-Personal); WPA2-Personal as a supplicant: the PMK from
    the passphrase, the PTK by the 802.11 PRF, EAPOL-Key frames written and parsed, MICs checked in
    constant time, replay counters enforced, the GTK unwrapped from message 3's KDE; CCMP's
    protection of data frames (AAD and nonce from the MAC header, packet numbers out for the
    caller's replay check).
  - **Firmware** (changed by the owner on 2026-11-10, see D265): adapter drivers load their
    firmware from `/usr/lib/firmware/`, filled by the optional `wifi-firmware` component. eggspot
    mirrors the redistributable files (pinned linux-firmware files, with their licence texts and
    `WHENCE` entries) in its own component store, the default source; linux-firmware's release is
    the fallback. Nothing of it enters the repository or the base image. Files whose licence
    forbids redistribution come from the vendor on the user's request only (docs/firmware.md).
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the adapter drivers (Intel's AX200/AX201/AX210 first:
  firmware loading, the command and data queues, scanning, association), the `wifi-firmware`
  component, WPA3-Personal (SAE over P-256, PMF), 802.1X enterprise networks, the Network pane's
  Wi-Fi list and `wifi` CLI and MCP tools (D22), roaming.

## D247 x86_64's clocks without measuring: CPUID's stated TSC frequency and the TSC-deadline timer (D26's follow-ups; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** At boot the HAL asks CPUID for the TSC's frequency before measuring: leaf 15h's
  ratio of the core crystal (its frequency from ECX, or leaf 16h's base frequency when ECX is 0),
  else a hypervisor's timing leaf 40000010h (TSC kHz). When the CPU has the TSC-deadline timer
  (CPUID.01H:ECX[24]) and the frequency is stated, the PIT/PM-timer measurement is skipped
  altogether (about 2 ms less boot) and every CPU's local APIC timer runs in TSC-deadline mode: a
  deadline is written to `IA32_TSC_DEADLINE` as a TSC value (0 disarms), so no APIC count
  conversion and no early expiry to re-arm. With the deadline timer but no stated frequency, the
  TSC is measured as before and the deadline mode is still used; without it, nothing changes.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; checking the TSC is invariant (CPUID 80000007h:EDX[8]) before
  trusting it across idle states; the HPET as another reference.

## D248 x86_64's interrupt stack table: the double fault, NMI, machine check and debug exceptions on stacks of their own (D47's and D49's follow-up for real hardware; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** D47 asked for separate stacks before untrusted programs run on a real CPU: every
  exception ran on the current stack, so a kernel stack overflow ended in a triple fault, and an
  NMI or machine check in the instructions `syscall` and `sysretq` spend in ring 0 on a program's
  stack ran on that stack.
- **Decision.** Each CPU's per-CPU block holds four 16 KiB stacks; its TSS's IST entries 1 to 4
  point at their tops (double fault, NMI, machine check, debug). A second IDT, filled with the first,
  gives those four gates their IST index; each CPU loads it right after `ltr` loads its own TSS, so
  no CPU takes an IST gate before its stacks exist. An IST exception from ring 3 has its seven-word
  frame copied from the IST stack to where `TSS.RSP0` would have put it, then takes the ring-3
  path unchanged.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the paranoid GS check in those four handlers (an NMI between
  `syscall` and its `swapgs` runs the kernel path with the program's GS base); NMIs from ring 3
  handled by the kernel instead of the program (D49); a guard page under each IST stack.

## D249 MDS: CPU buffers cleared with `verw` on every return to user mode, on affected CPUs (D49's speculation follow-up for real Intel CPUs; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** At boot the HAL decides once whether this machine's CPUs need it: CPUID 7's
  `MD_CLEAR` (EDX[10]) present, and `IA32_ARCH_CAPABILITIES` (when CPUID 7 EDX[29] says it exists)
  not reporting both `MDS_NO` and `TAA_NO`. Then both returns to ring 3, `sysretq` and `iretq`, run
  `verw` on a kernel data selector right before `swapgs`, which on those CPUs overwrites the store,
  fill and load-port buffers, so a program cannot sample what the kernel left in them. Elsewhere a
  byte compare skips it.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; buffer clearing before an idle CPU's `hlt` and between
  threads of different programs on SMT siblings; KPTI with PCID for Meltdown-affected CPUs; Retbleed
  and Spectre v2 return and branch mitigations (IBRS, retpolines, return thunks); measurement of
  the cost on a system-call round trip.

## D250 AArch64's `SCTLR_EL1` written whole, not ORed into the firmware's (D47's follow-up for UEFI machines; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Turning translation on now writes the whole `SCTLR_EL1`: its Armv8.0 RES1 bits, the
  MMU and both caches, EL0's cache type and maintenance (`UCT`, `UCI`), `DC ZVA` (`DZE`) and
  untrapped `WFI`/`WFE` (`nTWI`, `nTWE`), as Linux allows EL0; `UMA`, `E0E`, `EE` and the alignment
  checks are 0. A UEFI firmware that left other bits set (D236 keeps EL1's value from the
  firmware) no longer passes them on. Secondary CPUs use the same code.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; `PAN`, `TCO`, `DIT` and `SSBS` (D49).

## D251 x86_64: SMEP and UMIP where the CPU has them (D45's and D47's follow-ups; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Each CPU, as it sets user mode up, also turns on `CR4.SMEP` (CPUID 7 EBX[7]): the
  kernel never executes a user page, so a jump into program memory faults instead of running it;
  and `CR4.UMIP` (CPUID 7 ECX[2]): `SGDT`, `SIDT`, `SLDT`, `SMSW` and `STR` fault in ring 3, so
  programs cannot learn the kernel's table addresses. Neither costs anything on a hot path.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; SMAP, which needs `stac`/`clac` around every user access and
  `clac` on every entry; emulating the five instructions for the rare Windows or Linux program that
  uses one (Linux emulates them).

## D252 The ACPI namespace's static part: devices with a `_HID` from the DSDT join the driver model (M5's ACPI discovery; D237's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** On PCs and Arm servers the devices no bus enumerates (the PS/2 controller, the
  embedded controller, I2C HID touchpads and keyboards, batteries, the lid, GPIO controllers) are
  declared in the ACPI namespace, in AML. Running AML needs an interpreter; most `_HID`s and many
  `_CRS`s are plain data.
- **Decision.** `eggos_hal::aml` walks a definition block's static part: `Scope`, `Device`,
  `Processor`, `PowerResource` and `ThermalZone` bodies are entered; `Name`s with integers,
  strings, buffers and packages are read; methods, conditionals, loops, fields and other known
  terms with a length are stepped over; a term it does not know ends the walk of that scope only,
  so nothing after it there is misread. Each device yields its path, `_HID` (strings, or compressed
  EISA ids decoded to `PNP0303`), `_CID`, `_UID`, `_ADR` and a `_CRS` buffer, whose 32-bit fixed
  memory and DWord/QWord memory descriptors become the node's regions. `Platform::acpi_dsdt`
  (x86_64, AArch64) gives the DSDT; the driver model adds an `Identity::Acpi` node (`_HID`, `_CID`,
  path) per device with a `_HID`, matched by `Match::AcpiHid` on the `_HID` (rank 0) or the `_CID`
  (rank 1), listed as `acpi` in `/proc/driver/devices` with a class from its `_HID`.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; SSDTs; an AML interpreter for `_HID`s, `_CRS`s and `_STA`s that
  methods compute, `_PRT`, `_S5` through it, notifications and the embedded controller; interrupt
  resources; drivers for the ACPI devices (I2C controllers and HID over I2C first, then the
  battery, AC adapter and lid).

## D253 AArch64's GIC and console UART from the device tree too (M5's "the GIC and UART addresses from discovery instead of D12's"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Without ACPI (D237), the HAL reads the GIC from the device tree's first GIC node
  (`arm,gic-v3`: distributor and redistributor range; `arm,cortex-a15-gic`, `arm,gic-400`,
  `arm,cortex-a9-gic`, `arm,cortex-a7-gic`: distributor and CPU interface) and the console from its
  first `arm,pl011` node, before falling back to QEMU `virt`'s fixed addresses (`fdt::gic`,
  `fdt::pl011`). This runs before `kernel_main`, through the boot direct map, like ACPI's.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; `/chosen/stdout-path` naming the console; the UART's and the
  timer's interrupts from the tree; `ranges` translation for nodes under buses.

## D254 USB hubs: keyboards and mice behind hubs (D239's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** Keyboards plugged into a monitor's or a dock's hub, keyboards with a hub of their
  own, and some boards' front ports are behind USB hubs, which D239 did not drive.
- **Decision.** At attach time, a device whose device or first interface class is 09h is set up as
  a hub: its configuration set, its hub descriptor read (USB 2.0's 29h, USB 3.x's 2Ah, with
  `SET_HUB_DEPTH` for the latter), its slot context marked as a hub with its port count (Configure
  Endpoint), every port powered; then each port is polled until a device connects, reset through
  `SET_FEATURE(PORT_RESET)` until the reset change shows, the change cleared, and the device's speed
  read from the port status. A child's slot context carries the route string (four bits a tier,
  up to five tiers), its root port, and, for a low- or full-speed device behind a high-speed hub,
  that hub's slot and port as its transaction translator. Hubs take a device slot and area of
  their own and are never polled.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; hot-plug (the hub's status-change endpoint); multi-TT hubs'
  bit and think time; more than fifteen ports a hub; hubs as their own device class in the list.

## D255 Interrupts for the real machines' drivers: MSI-X or MSI for NVMe, xHCI and e1000 (D238-D240's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `devices::message_interrupts::connect` gives a PCI function MSI-X entry 0, else MSI
  with one vector, turns its legacy INTx off, and connects the message's line to the driver's
  `DeviceEvents`; `waiting_for` makes a driver's wait sleep until those events are raised, or
  poll when there are none, as virtio's does (D220).
  - **NVMe**: the I/O completion queue is created with interrupts on vector 0; each disk's
    transfers sleep instead of spinning.
  - **xHCI**: interrupter 0's `IMAN.IE` and `USBCMD.INTE` turned on; every poll clears `IMAN.IP`
    and `USBSTS.EINT`; the controller is installed as an interrupting input device.
  - **e1000/e1000e**: receive-timer, receive-threshold and link-change causes in `IMS`; reading
    `ICR` at each receive clears them; installed as the stack's interrupting adapter.
  - Where no message interrupt can be had, each stays polled as before.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; AHCI's MSI (HBA and port causes cleared per command), igc's
  extended interrupts and the Realtek chips'; several vectors (one per queue or per CPU);
  interrupt moderation.

## D256 HID report descriptors: USB keyboards, mice, tablets, touch screens and media keys in report protocol (D239's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `eggos_drivers::input::hid_report` parses a HID report descriptor (main, global and
  local items, `Push`/`Pop`, report ids; long items skipped) into the fields of its input reports,
  one field per usage for variable items with several usages, and decodes reports: the keyboard
  page's modifiers and keys (through the boot keyboard's press and release logic), buttons 1 to 3,
  the digitizer's tip switch as the left button, generic desktop X, Y and wheel (relative as
  motion, absolute as positions with the descriptor's logical range), the consumer page's pan as
  the sideways wheel, and a few consumer keys (mute, volume, play/pause, next and previous track,
  brightness). The layout says the device's capabilities (absolute ranges for tablets and touch
  screens). The USB side reads every HID interface, not only boot ones: a non-boot interface's
  report descriptor (its length from the HID descriptor) is fetched and kept per device, and the
  controller's capabilities are the union of its devices'.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; several application collections and several reports per
  device mapped to separate input devices; multi-touch contacts (only the first's position);
  precision touchpads' mode switch and gestures; HID output reports beyond the boot keyboard's
  lights; I2C HID, which needs the ACPI interpreter for its descriptor address (D252).

## D257 Components downloaded on demand: `component install` fetches the release's store over HTTPS when none is attached (M14, part 2; D69; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** D235's store comes from an attached disk or the host share, which a real machine
  installed from a USB stick (D241) has neither of. D69 wants optional components downloaded on
  demand, never in the base.
- **Decision.** When `component install` finds no store, it downloads this version's store from its
  GitHub Release (`https://github.com/eggspot/EggOS/releases/download/v<version>/eggos-<version>-
  <arch>-components.img`, which the release attaches since D235) into `/var/cache/eggos/` with
  `fetch -q -o`, so it shows in the Downloads window like every download, waits for it, then reads
  it as any store (header, index and every file's SHA-256 checked as before) and installs.
  `find_store` looks there after the disks and the share, so a downloaded store serves later
  installs too; `component list --json` names its source `downloaded`. HTTPS from the release is
  the store's authenticity, as the release's own `SHA256SUMS` would be.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; Settings' Components pane downloading too (it uses a store
  already downloaded); a signed store index (needs the owner's key); downloading only the files of
  the component asked for (range requests) instead of the whole store; delta updates applied
  atomically between versions; a background download that does not block the command.

## D258 Editions as component presets: `component edition` and the MCP tool `component_edition` (M16, first part; D18; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `eggos_components::editions` names four editions as lists of components: server
  (the base alone), personal, professional and enterprise (today each with the Windows and Mac
  apps layers, the only components a store offers; the lists grow as the desktop, the built-in
  apps, AI services and server roles become components). `component edition` lists them, with a
  star at the edition the installed components match exactly; `component edition <name>`
  (`--dry-run`) installs every component of it the store offers for this machine and that is not
