  needed (D257). The registry's `COMPONENT_EDITION` and the MCP tool `component_edition` (install
  grant) are its CLI and AI front-ends.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the GUI front-end (D22): an edition choice in Settings'
  Components pane and in first run, which needs a Claude Fable design; editions that also remove
  what they do not include; editions' own settings (updates, policies) for professional and
  enterprise.

## D259 x86_64: SMAP where the CPU has it (D251's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** With CPUID 7 EBX[20], each CPU also turns on `CR4.SMAP`: ring 0 faults on any user
  page except inside `Platform::with_user_access`, which runs its closure between `stac` and
  `clac` (the kernel already reaches program memory only there, D45, and copies otherwise go
  through the direct map, D94). `syscall` already clears `RFLAGS.AC` (`IA32_FMASK`, D47), and the
  kernel's exception entry runs `clac` so an interrupt inside the window does not inherit it; the
  interrupted context's flags come back with `iretq`.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; checking that every user-memory touch sits inside the
  window (a fault in a missed one now reports a kernel page fault).

## D260 x86_64: Spectre v2 basics, enhanced IBRS and IBPB between programs (D49's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Where CPUID 7 EDX[26] reports IBRS and IBPB, each CPU, as it sets user mode up,
  sets `IA32_SPEC_CTRL.IBRS` once if `IA32_ARCH_CAPABILITIES` reports enhanced IBRS (always-on,
  no cost per entry), and every switch to another address space (`switch_address_space`) issues an
  `IBPB`, so one program's branch training cannot steer the next program's indirect branches.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; retpolines or IBRS on every entry for CPUs without enhanced
  IBRS; Retbleed's return thunks; STIBP for SMT siblings; RSB filling on context switch; measuring
  IBPB's cost on a process switch.

## D261 RISC-V: Sstc's `stimecmp` and the device tree's timebase (D26's follow-ups; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The boot hart reads the device tree before arming its timer: when the first hart's
  `riscv,isa-extensions` (or an `_`-separated part of `riscv,isa`) names `sstc`, every deadline is
  written to `stimecmp` (CSR 14Dh) directly instead of through `sbi_set_timer`, a trap to the
  firmware saved per timer arm; and `/cpus/timebase-frequency` replaces QEMU `virt`'s 10 MHz as
  the clock's frequency. The device tree parser now keeps those three properties per node.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; harts that differ in their extensions; Svinval and the
  vector extension's first-use trap (D54).

## D262 AHCI on MSI (D255's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The AHCI controller gets a message interrupt through `message_interrupts::connect`
  (MSI-X or MSI, INTx off); `GHC.IE` is turned on and each disk's port asks for its
  device-to-host register FIS, set-device-bits and task-file-error interrupts. A disk's transfers
  sleep until the controller's events are raised, and after each transfer the port's bit in the
  controller-wide `IS` is cleared, so the next completion sends a new message. All the
  controller's disks share one event, so a completion on one wakes the others to look again.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; one message per port where the controller has several.

## D263 The editions' GUI: the Components pane's Edition band (D22 for D258; design by Claude Fable, docs/ux/editions-v0.4.md; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (the design by Claude Fable)

- **Decision.** As the design's sections 1 and 2: an `Edition` band above the rows (panel, label,
  dropdown named `Edition`, summary; `ROWS_TOP` 196), the dropdown showing the current edition
  (`Custom` added when none matches) and its summary. Choosing another edition builds the plan
  (each missing component the store offers, with what it needs), says `Would install for <Title>:
  ...` and the size in all, and opens the pane's install confirmation; `Install` runs the plan
  through the pane's existing per-component progress. An empty plan answers `<Title> is
  installed: nothing to add.`; with no store the band says the CLI downloads it. The capability
  now records the chosen edition (`/var/lib/eggos/edition`) after `component edition <name>` and
  after the pane's plan, and `editions::current_preferring` prefers it while its list still
  matches, so Personal, Professional and Enterprise (the same components today) are told apart;
  Server's summary is shortened to fit a label.
- **Deviations from the design, for the next GUI pass.** The confirmation opens under the plan's
  first row with the install note's lines, not under the band with one line per component; the
  pane does not download the store itself (the design's section 4) or show the band's messages
  under it (they go in the summary line); the phone, tablet and TV layouts of section 7 are not
  done. These need the pane's note to sit under the band, and a store-download request (D257).

## D264 USB flash drives as disks (D239, D238; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session

- **Decision.** The xHCI driver attaches a device whose interface is mass storage (class 08h,
  subclass 06h SCSI, protocol 50h bulk-only) by configuring its bulk IN and OUT endpoints, then
  speaks the bulk-only transport (31-byte `USBC` command block, data, 13-byte `USBS` status) with
  SCSI TEST UNIT READY (up to 20 tries), READ CAPACITY(10), READ(10), WRITE(10) and SYNCHRONIZE
  CACHE(10). Data moves through one 64 KiB bounce buffer at the end of the controller's DMA block,
  which the buddy allocator aligns to its size, so no transfer TRB crosses a 64 KiB boundary.
  Sectors are 512 bytes to the kernel whatever the drive's block size (512 to 4096); partial
  blocks are read, patched and written back. Disks past 2 TiB (READ(16)) are refused.
- **Sharing.** The kernel puts the controller behind one `SleepLock` shared by the input device
  and one `UsbDisk` per drive. The input thread only `try_lock`s it, so a disk transfer never
  blocks input; HID reports seen while a disk transfer waits are kept (up to 64) and handed out at
  the next poll instead of dropped.
- **Left out.** USB Attached SCSI (UAS), more than one LUN, hot-plug, and stall recovery on the
  bulk endpoints (a stalled drive fails its transfers until the next boot).

## D265 Vendor firmware in eggspot's component store: pinned linux-firmware files as optional components, linux-firmware as the fallback (D246's firmware, the owner's answer; M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the owner (2026-11-10, through Main Chat); the engineering by the code-only session

- **Context.** D246 left with the owner whether EggOS's own store may redistribute the vendors'
  firmware. The owner's answer (2026-11-10): "yes eggos store ship those file itself", refined to
  "we could store our self and still allow the user to download".
- **Decision.**
  - eggspot hosts the redistributable firmware as a mirror in its component store (D235's store,
    attached to each release and downloaded on demand, D257): optional components the user
    installs on request, never built into the EggOS image. Our store is the default source;
    linux-firmware's tagged release is the fallback.
  - Only files linux-firmware carries, whose licence allows redistribution, are mirrored, from one
    tagged release (`20261019`) and each pinned by SHA-256 in `eggos_components::firmware`, the one
    table the store build (`cargo xtask`, fetching into `target/firmware/<tag>/`) and the
    on-device fallback share. The binaries are never committed to the repository.
  - Each component installs one folder under `/usr/lib/firmware/` (which the base image links into
    the component, as it links the Windows and Mac layers) holding the firmware, its licence text
    and a `WHENCE` file with the files' entries from linux-firmware's `WHENCE` (the driver's
    header and licence lines, and only our files' entries). docs/firmware.md lists every file.
  - Two components to start: `wifi-firmware` (Intel AX200, AX201, AX210, AX211:
    `LICENCE.iwlwifi_firmware`) and `display-firmware` (Intel DMC for Tiger Lake to Meteor Lake:
    `LICENSE.i915`), both for x86_64. The store index allows `usr/lib/firmware/` beside
    `usr/lib/eggos/`, and firmware files are installed with mode 644.
  - When `component install <firmware>` finds no store, or one without that component, it
    downloads each pinned file from linux-firmware with `fetch` into `/var/cache/eggos/`, checks it,
    assembles a one-component store there (`eggos-<version>-<arch>-<name>.img`, source
    `linux-firmware`) and installs from it through the usual atomic install.
  - Firmware whose licence forbids redistribution is never mirrored: a driver needing it downloads
    it from the vendor on the user's request only, listed in docs/firmware.md with the reason
    (none needed yet; Broadcom's `b43` firmware is the known case).
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the drivers that load these files (the Intel Wi-Fi adapter and
  display drivers); AMD and NVIDIA GSP firmware components when their drivers come; the Components
  pane saying a firmware component came from linux-firmware; a signed store index.

## D266 The device tree's chosen console: `/chosen`'s `stdout-path` picks the PL011 on AArch64 (D253's follow-up; M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** D253 took the first PL011 a device tree lists. Boards with several UARTs (and QEMU
  `virt` with a second `-serial`) name the console in `/chosen`'s `stdout-path`, which may be a
  path (`/pl011@9000000`) or an alias (`serial0`), with options after a `:` (`115200n8`).
- **Decision.** `Fdt::property_at` reads one property of the node at a path (a part without a
  unit address names the first node of that name); `Fdt::stdout_path` reads `stdout-path` (or the
  older `linux,stdout-path`), drops the options and resolves an alias through `/aliases`;
  `fdt::stdout_node` finds that node. `fdt::pl011` uses it when it is a PL011, else the first
  PL011 as before. The ACPI path (the `SPCR`, D236) is unchanged.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; RISC-V's console still assumes QEMU `virt`'s UART0 (an
  NS16550 found through `stdout-path` also needs its `reg-shift` and a check that it lies in the
  boot direct map); other UARTs (the 8250 family on Arm boards, `snps,dw-apb-uart`).

## D267 x86_64: IBRS on every kernel entry for Intel CPUs without enhanced IBRS, against Spectre v2 and Retbleed (D260's follow-up; M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** D260 set IBRS once on CPUs with enhanced IBRS. Older Intel CPUs (Skylake to Comet
  Lake) have IBRS but not its enhanced form, and on them a program can train the predictions the
  kernel's indirect branches use, and, when the return stack underflows, its returns too
  (Retbleed, CVE-2022-29901). The fix Intel documents for them is IBRS while the kernel runs.
- **Decision.** On an Intel CPU with IBRS and IBPB (CPUID 7 EDX[26]) but without enhanced IBRS,
  `IA32_SPEC_CTRL.IBRS` is set at boot, set again by the entry code on every entry from user mode
  (after the registers are saved, with `wrmsr`), and cleared right before every return to user
  mode (both the `iretq` and the `sysretq` paths), so the kernel always runs with it and programs
  never pay for it. Enhanced IBRS keeps D260's single write; CPUs with neither are unchanged.
  Labels in the entry code are named (`.Lx86_64_entry_predictions_set`), as the global assembly
  already reuses its numbered ones.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; measuring the two `wrmsr`s per system call; AMD's Retbleed
  mitigations (an IBPB on entry or the untrained return thunk, CVE-2022-29900) and SRSO; filling
  the return stack buffer on context switch; STIBP for SMT siblings; KPTI for CPUs Meltdown
  affects (separate user page tables, D47).

## D268 Intel's integrated display engine: the firmware's mode taken over, tear-free flips between two GTT-mapped buffers and the cursor plane (M13's vendor GPU drivers, part 1; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** On a real PC the display was the firmware's framebuffer (D236): drawn in place, so
  the screen can show a frame half drawn, every read of it is a slow uncached one, and the
  pointer is drawn into the frame. Most PCs EggOS targets have Intel integrated graphics.
- **Decision.**
  - `eggos_drivers::gpu::intel` drives display versions 9 to 14 (Skylake to Meteor Lake,
    integrated only, by the device id's high byte; discrete cards keep their surfaces in their
    own memory and are left to the firmware framebuffer). It finds the pipe whose primary plane
    the firmware lit (`PLANE_CTL` enabled, linear, 32-bit XRGB in BGRX order), reads its size,
    stride and surface, writes global-GTT entries (BAR 0's second half, 8-byte entries, each a
    4 KiB page, flushed through `GFX_FLSH_CNTL`), flips by writing `PLANE_STRIDE` then
    `PLANE_SURF` (latched at the next vertical blank), checks `PLANE_SURFLIVE`, and drives the
    64x64 ARGB cursor (`CUR_CTL`, `CUR_POS` with sign bits, `CUR_BASE` arming the change).
  - The kernel's `intel_display` scanout (x86_64, feature `intel-display`, on by default) keeps
    the kernel's framebuffer in cached memory, so drawing and reading it is fast, and two scanout
    buffers in DMA memory (4 MiB chunks, as the frame allocator gives no more at once) mapped at
    the top of the global GTT, below the cursor, clear of the firmware's surface. A flush waits
    for the previous flip to show, copies this flush's damage and what that buffer missed since
    it was last shown into the hidden buffer, writes those lines back with `clflush` (the display
    engine does not snoop the caches) and flips. The pointer moves without redrawing anything.
  - Mode setting stays the firmware's: no display PLLs, link training or hot-plug yet, and the
    mode the firmware picked is the one EggOS shows. The DMC firmware (D265's
    `display-firmware`) is not loaded yet, so the deepest display power states stay off.
- **Not yet.** Building and running on Intel hardware; loading the DMC; mode setting and a second
  display; waiting for flips on the vertical-blank interrupt instead of polling; AMD's display
  engine (DCN) and NVIDIA's; the Wi-Fi adapter driver.

## D269 Device-tree `ranges` translated: devices behind a translating bus get CPU addresses (M5's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** The node walker treated only identity (`ranges;`) buses as giving CPU addresses, so
  devices behind a bus that remaps its children (an SoC's `simple-bus` with `ranges = <0 0x0
  0x10000000 ...>`, common on real Arm and RISC-V boards) had no usable `reg`.
- **Decision.** Each node now carries the translating `ranges` of its ancestors (up to
  `MAX_TRANSLATIONS`, 4), with the cell counts each needs: the bus's own `#address-cells` and
  `#size-cells` and its parent's `#address-cells`. `Node::reg_entries` translates every address
  through them, nearest bus first, and skips a pair no range covers; `untranslated_reg_entries`
  keeps the bus's own addresses. A bus with no `ranges` still makes its children's addresses
  private (I2C, SPI), and a PCI host's three-cell addresses are not translated (PCI devices are
  enumerated through its configuration space instead). Address and size cells above two are not
  translated.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; `dma-ranges` for devices whose DMA addresses differ from the
  CPU's; PCI hosts' `ranges` for their windows from the device tree.

## D270 Set-user-id and set-group-id programs: `execve` takes the program file's owner and group as the effective ids (M7's last item, issue #94's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from execve(2) and credentials(7))

- **Decision.** When `execve` runs a program file whose mode has `S_ISUID`, the process's
  effective (and file system) user id becomes the file's owner; with `S_ISGID` and the group's
  execute bit, its effective group id becomes the file's group (`S_ISGID` without group execute
  marks mandatory locking, not a set-group-id program). Then exec's usual step saves the effective
  ids as the saved ones, so the program may later drop back to its real ids and return.
  `AT_SECURE` is then 1, as the effective ids differ from the real ones. The bits of a `#!`
  script are ignored, as on Linux: only the program file finally run counts, which for a script
  is its interpreter. Programs the kernel starts from bytes (`exec::load`) take no ids.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; `nosuid` mounts; dropping the bits on a write by someone
  other than root, and on `chown`; refusing them while the process is traced; capabilities.

## D271 Components downloaded alone: `fetch --range` and `component install` fetching only the store's index and the files it installs (M14, D257's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from RFC 9110 section 14)

- **Context.** D257 downloads this version's whole component store to install one component; the
  store holds every optional component (the Windows and Mac layers, the firmware), so installing
  the Wi-Fi firmware meant downloading the layers too.
- **Decision.**
  - `eggos_net::http` writes a `Range: bytes=<first>-<last>` header (`ByteRange`,
    `write_ranged_request`); `fetch --range <first>-<last>` sends it, follows redirects with it,
    and fails unless the answer is `206 Partial Content`, so a server that ignores ranges never
    leaves a whole file where a piece was asked for.
  - `component install <name>` with no store attached first asks the release's store for its
    header and the largest index there may be (bytes 0 to 66,047), reads the index, plans the
    install (the component and what it needs), downloads each planned file's bytes alone into
    `/var/cache/eggos/` (`…-components-<piece>.part`), checks each against the index's length and
    SHA-256, assembles a store of just those components (`…-components-for-<name>.img`) and
    installs from it as from any store. When any step fails it falls back to D257's whole-store
    download. `component edition`, which may install several components, still downloads the
    whole store.
  - The MCP tool `fetch` keeps its arguments; `--range` is for programs and the CLI.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; reusing pieces across installs; a signed index (needs the
  owner's key); a download that runs in the background without blocking the command.

## D272 The Intel Wi-Fi driver, written from OpenBSD's `iwx(4)`: an owner-approved exception to the clean-room rule, and part 1, the adapters and the firmware file (M13's Wi-Fi; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the owner (2026-11-10, through Main Chat: "yes do it openbsd"); the engineering by the code-only session

- **Context.** Intel publishes no programming specification for its Wi-Fi adapters. The only
  descriptions are Linux's `iwlwifi` (dual GPL-2.0/BSD-3-Clause) and OpenBSD's `iwx(4)` (ISC),
  and `iwx(4)` says it is "Based on BSD-licensed source modules in the Linux iwlwifi driver",
  carrying Intel's dual BSD/GPLv2 notice beside its own. CLAUDE.md forbids copying or translating
  code from copyleft projects, the Linux kernel included.
- **Decision (the owner's).** The Intel Wi-Fi driver is written with OpenBSD's `iwx(4)`
  (`if_iwx.c`, `if_iwxreg.h`, `if_iwxvar.h`) as its reference. This is an owner-approved exception
  to the clean-room rule for Intel's BSD-licensed iwlwifi-derived code, by way of OpenBSD: EggOS
  uses that code under its BSD terms only, never under the GPL. Linux's own `iwlwifi` files are
  never opened. `drivers/src/wifi/iwx/NOTICE.md` reproduces OpenBSD's ISC notices and Intel's
  BSD-3-Clause notice (without the GPL summary), and the base image carries it at
  `/usr/share/licenses/eggos/iwx-NOTICE.md`, as the BSD licence asks of binary distributions. The
  exception covers this driver only.
- **Part 1.** `eggos_drivers::wifi::iwx`:
  - `devices::identify` maps a PCI function (device and subsystem ids, `CSR_HW_REV`) to the
    adapter and its firmware: AX200 (`cc-a0`), AX201 (`QuZ-a0-hr-b0`, `Qu-c0-hr-b0` or
    `Qu-b0-hr-b0` by the chipset's revision; the chipset-only ids 02F0h and 06F0h only as QuZ),
    AX210 (`ty-a0-gf-a0` with its PNVM) and AX211 (`so-a0-gf-a0` with its PNVM), with the
    reference's latency tolerance delays, crystal latencies and 6 GHz flags. Killer AX1690s and
    AX1690i (the `gf4` radio) and the Jf/Hr radios on AX211 chipsets are left out: the component
    carries no firmware for them, and telling Jf/Hr apart needs the radio's id register, which
    part 2 reads.
  - `firmware::Firmware::parse` reads the firmware file: the header's magic and version, every
    record, the four images' sections (each section's device offset and its bytes, as offsets
    into the file), the image loader, the platform NVM, the API and capability bits, the command
    versions, the scan channel limit; `split` divides an image at its separators into the LMAC,
    UMAC and paging sections. Unlike the reference, unknown records are skipped, not refused, so a
    newer file still loads.
  - D265's `wifi-firmware` now pins the API 77 files the reference runs (the AX210 and AX211 files
    were API 89) and adds the Qu-b0 and Qu-c0 AX201 files.
- **Next.** Part 2: the host interface (`CSR` registers, the NIC lock, power-up), the command
  queue and receive ring the context info names, handing the firmware over (context info for the
  AX200 family; context info, scratch area and image loader for the AX210 family) and waiting for
  its alive notification; then the PNVM, NVM, scanning, association with `eggos-wifi`'s WPA2, and
  data frames.

## D273 The Intel Wi-Fi driver, part 2: the host interface, power-up, the rings and the firmware handover up to its alive notification (D272's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from OpenBSD's `iwx(4)` under D272's exception)

- **Decision.** `eggos_drivers::wifi::iwx::transport::Transport`, polled throughout:
  - Register access: the CSR block, `PRPH` registers through the HBUS window (a 20-bit address on
    the AX200 family, 24-bit on the AX210 family), and the nesting NIC lock that requests MAC
    access in `CSR_GP_CNTRL` and waits for the clock.
  - `start_hardware`: the ready handshake (`NIC_READY`, then `PREPARE` and retries), clearing the
    persistence bit on the AX200 family, a software reset, power gating forced and a second reset
    on integrated AX201s, and power-up (L0s off, the HPET threshold, `INIT_DONE`, waiting for the
    MAC clock). `radio_killed` reads the hardware switch.
  - The rings, in one 128 KiB DMA block: the default receive queue's free and used descriptors
    and status (512 buffers of 4 KiB in a 2 MiB block), and the command queue's 256 long-format
    descriptors; the prph scratch area and prph info page for the AX210 family.
  - `load_firmware`: the regular image's sections, split into LMAC, UMAC and paging, are each
    copied into DMA memory from a `DmaAllocator` (a new trait in `eggos_drivers::dma`). The AX200
    family gets one context info (rings, command queue, every section's address) at
    `CSR_CTXT_INFO_BA`; the AX210 family gets a prph scratch area (control flags, free ring,
    sections), a gen3 context info (prph info and scratch, the rings and their index arrays) at
    `CSR_CTXT_INFO_ADDR`, and the image loader at `CSR_IML_DATA_ADDR`, with auto-boot set. Both
    then set the boot latency tolerance and start the CPU (`UREG_CPU_INIT_RUN`).
  - Waiting for alive: the `ALIVE` bit in `CSR_INT`, then the receive descriptors are filled
    again and 8 buffers handed over (`RFH_Q0_FRBDCB_WIDX_TRG`), and the first `ALIVE` packet in
    the ring is read: status `CAFE`h means running, anything else is the failure's status.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the kernel's probe, which must wait for the root file system
  before it can read the firmware from `/usr/lib/firmware`; the PNVM for the AX210 family; the
  receive ring's used-descriptor order on the AX210 family (read in order here); interrupts and
  MSI-X; then commands, the NVM, scanning and association.

## D274 The Intel Wi-Fi driver, part 3: the kernel's probe, and the firmware started once the file systems are mounted (D273's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** Probes run before any disk is mounted, and the adapters' firmware comes from the
  optional `wifi-firmware` component under `/usr/lib/firmware/intel/iwlwifi/` (D265), which a
  user may install long after boot.
- **Decision.** The kernel's `intel_wifi` driver (feature `intel-wifi`, on by default) matches
  PCI class 02h subclass 80h from Intel, reads the subsystem id and `CSR_HW_REV`, and keeps the
  mapped registers and the adapter `devices::identify` named, refusing ones it does not run.
  After the file systems are mounted, `devices::start_wifi` starts a kernel thread that reads the
  adapter's firmware file (at most 4 MiB), retrying every 10 seconds until the component is
  installed, parses it, allocates the rings, powers the adapter up and loads the firmware,
  each section in DMA memory of its own. Waits between register polls spin for whole
  milliseconds, the clock's smallest deadline. `/proc/driver/wifi` says what the adapter reached:
  waiting for the file systems or the component, starting, `firmware running` (with whether the
  radio's switch is off), or why it stopped.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; microsecond pauses; the AX210 family's PNVM and every host
  command (part 4); restarting the adapter after a firmware error.

## D275 The Intel Wi-Fi driver, part 4: the command queue, the firmware's packets, the init sequence, the NVM and the MAC address (D274's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from OpenBSD's `iwx(4)` under D272's exception)

- **Decision.**
  - The receive ring is read as the reference reads it: every closed buffer, each packet in it
    (several per buffer on the AX200 family, aligned to 64 bytes; one on the AX210 family) until
    an empty or invalid header; a packet whose queue byte lacks bit 7 and names the command
    queue is the response to the command in that slot, the rest are notifications, kept (at
    most 32) until something waits for them. The buffers go back to the firmware by the write
    index, rounded down to 8.
  - `send_command` writes the command's wide header (code, group, slot, queue, length) and
    payload into a 4 KiB command buffer, a long-format descriptor with the first 20 bytes in one
    buffer and the rest in a second, moves the queue's write pointer, and waits for the
    response; a response with the failure bit is an error. Group 0's commands go as group 1's,
    as the reference does for firmware API 50 and later. One command is in flight at a time.
  - After alive: the AX210 family is told to go on without a platform NVM (the PNVM doorbell)
    and waits for `PNVM_INIT_COMPLETE`; then `INIT_EXTENDED_CFG` asks for the NVM,
    `NVM_ACCESS_COMPLETE` and the `INIT_COMPLETE` notification end the init, and `NVM_GET_INFO`
    (version 3 or 4 by the firmware's API bit 48) gives the NVM's version, the bands and
    standards, the antennas, location-aware regulatory, and the 2.4 and 5 GHz channels' flags
    (valid, active scan, radar). The MAC address is the strapped one in the CSR block, else the
    OTP one, checked as the reference checks it.
  - The kernel's bring-up thread runs it after the firmware, and `/proc/driver/wifi` then says
    `ready`, the address and the number of channels.
  - Fixes part 2: `iwx/mod.rs` now declares `transport` (and `nvm`); the edit that should have
    added it in part 2 did not apply.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the PNVM's data itself (the platform's tuning) and 6 GHz
  channels; more than one command in flight; then scanning, association and data (part 5).

## D276 The Intel Wi-Fi driver, part 5: readying the firmware and scanning; `/proc/driver/wifi` lists the networks heard (D275's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from OpenBSD's `iwx(4)` under D272's exception)

- **Decision.**
  - `scan::configure` sends what the reference sends after the NVM: the valid transmit antennas
    (the firmware's PHY chains masked by the NVM's), Bluetooth coexistence as Wi-Fi only, the
    SoC configuration (discrete, or the crystal's low-latency flag and latency on integrated
    adapters; the reference's latency-tolerance delay bits mask to nothing, so none are sent),
    the dedicated command queue where the firmware supports DQA, power saving off, the world
    regulatory domain (`ZZ`) when the firmware chooses the domain itself, the reduced scan
    configuration (required: API bit 56), and beacon filtering off.
  - `scan::scan` sends `SCAN_REQ_UMAC` version 14: passive on every channel the NVM allows (at
    most the firmware's scan channel limit), adaptive dwell, all beacons and probe responses
    passed up, with the probe request (broadcast, the adapter's address, the 2.4 and 5 GHz
    rates) the request carries. It collects `REPLY_RX_MPDU` packets, unwrapping each frame from
    its descriptor (48 bytes on the AX200 family, 64 on the AX210 family; CRC and overrun checked,
    the firmware's 2-byte pad after the header removed) with its channel and signal, until
    `SCAN_COMPLETE_UMAC` or 15 seconds. The firmware's notification list now holds 256 packets.
  - The kernel's bring-up thread configures the firmware, then scans every 30 seconds (not while
    the radio's switch is off), parses each frame with `eggos_wifi::frames::network`, keeps one
    entry per BSSID at its strongest signal, and `/proc/driver/wifi` lists them under its status
    line: BSSID, channel, signal, security and SSID. The kernel depends on `eggos-wifi` for it.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; scan request version 17 (firmware that asks for it);
  active and directed scans; 6 GHz; then association: the MAC, PHY and binding contexts, the
  station, authentication and association frames, WPA2's handshake through `eggos-wifi`, keys,
  and the data path (part 6); the `wifi` CLI, MCP tools and the Network pane (D22).

## D277 The Intel Wi-Fi driver, part 6: joining a network, the management queue and frames sent through it (D276's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from OpenBSD's `iwx(4)` under D272's exception)

- **Decision.** `eggos_drivers::wifi::iwx::station::join` sends what the reference's
  authentication step sends: the PHY context on the network's channel at 20 MHz (version 3 or 4,
  the wide channel layout when the firmware has ultra-high-band channels; the receive chains in
  the RLC configuration instead when that command is at version 2), the MAC context for a client
  station (the adapter's address, the BSSID, group frames and, until associated, beacons let in),
  the binding of MAC to PHY on the right LMAC, the station entry for the access point (station
  0, a link station), the management transmit queue (queue 1, TID 15, through `TX_QUEUE_CFG` or
  `SCD_QUEUE_CONFIG` version 3, checked against the queue the firmware answers with) in a DMA
  block of its own (256 descriptors, the byte-count table, a command and a 2 KiB payload slot
  per descriptor), and session protection for nine beacon intervals. `Link::send` writes the
  transmit command (version 7 layout on the AX200 family, 8 on the AX210 family) with the frame's
  header, the body in its slot, the descriptor (first 20 bytes, the rest of the command, the
  body), the byte count, and moves the queue's write pointer; the firmware picks the rate, as the
  reference leaves it. `associated` gives the MAC context the association id and the station its
  update. Rate scaling, aggregation and the data queues are left out: every frame goes through
  the one queue, as the reference sends non-aggregated traffic.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; reclaiming slots from the firmware's transmit responses;
  removing the contexts on disconnect; HT, VHT and HE rates and widths.

## D278 Connecting to a WPA2-Personal or open network: the client station's frames in `eggos-wifi`, the four-way handshake, and the network chosen by `/var/lib/eggos/wifi.conf` (M13 Wi-Fi; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from IEEE 802.11-2020)

- **Decision.**
  - `eggos_wifi::client` (written from the standard) builds the open-system authentication
    request and the association request (ESS, short slot, privacy when protected, listen interval
    10, SSID, the 2.4 GHz rates, WPA2-Personal's RSN element), reads the access point's
    authentication status and association answer (only from its BSSID), reads a beacon's
    interval, and wraps and unwraps data frames: to the distribution system with LLC/SNAP and the
    ethertype, and back as Ethernet's destination, source, ethertype and payload.
  - The kernel's Wi-Fi thread reads `/var/lib/eggos/wifi.conf` (`ssid=` and `passphrase=` lines)
    after each scan; when it heard that network, it joins it (D277), authenticates, associates,
    and for WPA2-Personal runs `eggos_wifi::handshake::Supplicant` with the PMK from the
    passphrase and a nonce from the kernel's generator, sending messages 2 and 4 as EAPOL data
    frames, until message 3 gives the keys. `/proc/driver/wifi` then names the network.
  - Encryption stays in software: frames go to the firmware with its encryption off, and CCMP
    (`eggos_wifi::protection`) will protect and check data frames on the host, so no key is
    installed in the firmware. That keeps the data path one piece of code for every adapter.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the data path (Ethernet frames to and from the kernel's
  network stack through CCMP, part 7); group-key rekeying; WPA3-Personal (SAE); the `wifi` CLI and
  MCP tools that write the settings file and the Network pane's list (D22); roaming and
  reconnecting after a disconnect.

## D279 The Wi-Fi link as the network stack's adapter: Ethernet frames over 802.11 data frames, CCMP on the host, attached after boot (M13 Wi-Fi, part 7; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - `net::attach_late` lends the stack an adapter after boot, when none is in use, and starts the
    network's thread as boot does: a Wi-Fi link comes up only once its network is joined, long
    after the boot-time `net::start`. It is the stack's one adapter and keeps the name `eth0`.
  - Once connected, the Wi-Fi thread hands the transport, the link and the keys to a
    `WifiDevice` (a `NetDevice`) and ends. Sending wraps the Ethernet frame's payload in a data
    frame to the access point (D278) and, on a WPA2 network, protects it with CCMP and the
    pairwise key on the host (`eggos_wifi::protection`, packet numbers counting up from 1),
    then sends it through the management queue with the firmware's encryption off. Receiving
    takes the firmware's received frames, decrypts protected data frames (group-addressed ones
    with the group key the key id names, the rest with the pairwise key), drops replays (packet
    numbers that do not increase, per key) and unprotected frames on a protected network, and
    hands the rest up as Ethernet frames; EAPOL frames are not passed up.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; a name of its own (`wlan0`) and Wi-Fi and Ethernet together;
  the firmware's hardware CCMP; group-key rekeying (EAPOL group messages); power saving;
  reconnecting after the access point drops the station.

## D280 `wifi list`, `wifi connect` and `wifi forget`, with the MCP tools `wifi_list`, `wifi_connect` and `wifi_forget` (D22 for the Wi-Fi driver; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `wifi` is a noun whose verbs are the core `list` and, added here, `connect` and
  `forget`. `wifi list` (also plain `wifi`) prints `/proc/driver/wifi`: the driver's state, its
  address and channels, the joined network, and the networks the last scan heard. `wifi connect
  <ssid> [<passphrase>]` checks the name (1 to 32 bytes) and passphrase (8 to 63 characters, or
  none for an open network) and writes `/var/lib/eggos/wifi.conf` with mode 600, which the
  driver reads after its next scan (D278); `wifi forget` removes it. Each has its MCP twin;
  `wifi_connect` and `wifi_forget` need the run grant, `wifi_connect` asks the user first. They
  live in coreutils, and the image links `/bin/wifi` to it.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the Network pane's Wi-Fi list and join dialog (a Claude
  Fable design); the passphrase kept out of the command line (programs could read it from
  standard input); forgetting while connected disconnecting at once.

## D281 `nosuid` mounts: the memory file systems, `/dev`, the work folder and the host share ignore set-id bits (D270's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from mount(2))

- **Decision.** A mount may ignore its programs' set-user-id and set-group-id bits
  (`vfs::mount_without_set_ids`, Linux's `MS_NOSUID`), and `execve` then runs them with the
  caller's ids. The tmpfs mounts (`/tmp`, `/home`, `/var`, `/run`, `/dev/shm`), `/dev`, the work
  folder and the host share are mounted so, as a desktop Linux mounts them: those are where a
  user or another machine can put files. The root and the EggFS folders the system installs
  from keep their bits. `vfs::ignores_set_ids_at` tells `/proc/mounts` which.
  `/proc/mounts` lists them with `rw,nosuid` (or `ro,nosuid`).
- **Not yet.** Building and running; a `mount` system call for programs.

## D282 The kernel's generator reseeded from virtio-rng every five minutes after boot (M8; D220's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Where a virtio entropy device answered at boot, a kernel thread reseeds the
  generator from it every 300 seconds through the same `seed_random` boot uses (D220's credit
  rules), so a long-running machine keeps mixing fresh device entropy in, as Linux's periodic
  reseed does.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; reseeding from the CPU's instruction (RDSEED, `RNDR`) on the
  same schedule.

## D283 The Network pane's Wi-Fi section, and masked text fields in the toolkit (D280's GUI; design by Claude Fable, docs/ux/wifi-v0.4.md; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (the design by Claude Fable)

- **Decision.** As the design's sections 1 to 6:
  - Settings > Network gains a Wi-Fi section under the wired one (`wifi_section`, 37 widgets),
    always shown: the driver's state as a value and a hint (every first line of
    `/proc/driver/wifi` has its row; a failure is the driver's own sentence, kept as
    `Trying again...` until the state is connected or the chosen network changes), `Open
    Components` while the firmware component is missing, and the networks heard, one row a name,
    six a page with `More`/`Strongest`: name, `<security> · <signal>` in words, and `Join`,
    `Forget` or a disabled `Cannot join` with one sentence why. The chosen network (`wifi.conf`'s
    `ssid=`) is row 0; connected, the list is the joined row alone with the accent mark.
  - `Join` on an open network writes `wifi.conf` at once; on a WPA2 network it opens a note under
    the row with a masked passphrase field, `Show`, `Cancel` and `Join` (the window's default
    button while open), checked against `wifi connect`'s 8-to-63 rule. `Forget` removes the file.
    The program writes and removes the file as `wifi connect` and `wifi forget` do (mode 600).
  - The wired section's first row reads `Wi-Fi` while the joined network is the adapter, and its
    hints point at the Wi-Fi section when there is an adapter and no cable.
  - The toolkit's `Field` gains `masked` (`Kind::masked_text_field`): one `*` a character, the
    caret and selection measured on the stars, and copy and cut refused; the passphrase field is
    also person-only, so agents see no value. Settings' widget capacity grows by 37, and the
    installer dialog's with it.
- **Deviations from the design, for the next GUI pass.** The rows are not reordered by focus
  after a scan (the focus stays on the same slot), and Up/Down between row buttons and Esc
  emptying the field before closing the note follow the toolkit's defaults; accessible names do
  not carry the network's name yet. The design's backend asks (joining as soon as the file
  changes, scanning while connected, failure codes) are left for the driver's next part.

## D284 The Wi-Fi driver acts on `wifi.conf` at once, scans while joined, leaves and rejoins, and names its failures (D283's backend asks 1 to 5; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the design's section 8)

- **Decision.** The Wi-Fi thread keeps the adapter for good and the network stack gets a device
  that only moves frames through two queues the thread serves (`TRAFFIC`, a leaf lock, 64 frames
  each way), so one thread can scan, leave and join while the stack keeps its interface:
  - It reads `wifi.conf` every second. A changed file scans at once and joins the chosen network
    after that scan; a removed or changed file while joined sends a deauthentication frame
    (reason 3) and undoes the firmware's contexts (`station::leave`: session protection, the
    management queue, the station, binding, MAC and PHY contexts), so leaving or changing network
    needs no restart.
  - It scans every 30 seconds, joined or not (the firmware's UMAC scan works while associated),
    and refreshes the joined network's signal from the scan.
  - A disassociation or deauthentication from the access point ends the link (`dropped`) and the
    thread joins again at once. A failed join is tried again after the next scan.
  - While joined it moves frames every 2 ms, or at once when the stack queues one (its own
    `DeviceEvents`), and raises the stack's events when frames arrive. The device is attached to
    the stack at the first join and stays; its link is down while nothing is joined, so DHCP runs
    again on each join.
  - `/proc/driver/wifi`'s first line gains `joining <name>` while the chosen network is not
    joined, `signal <n> dBm` after `network <name>`, and `failed <code>: <words>` for the last
    failure until the next try ends. Codes: `not-in-range`, `no-answer`, `wrong-passphrase`
    (message 2 of the handshake went unanswered, or the access point sent the station away during
    the handshake, which is how a wrong passphrase shows from the station's side), `refused`,
    `unsupported-security`, `dropped`, `ethernet-in-use` (a wired adapter is already the stack's),
    `channel` and `adapter` (the firmware or the adapter failed). A failed join leaves the
    firmware's contexts before the next try.
  - The Network pane reads the new segments: the failure's sentence (`The network did not accept
    this passphrase.` for `wrong-passphrase`), the joined row's signal, and the other networks
    listed under the joined row instead of the joined row alone.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the note reopening by itself on `wrong-passphrase`;
  `/proc/net/interfaces` naming the adapter's kind (ask 6); the radio switch's kind (ask 7);
  hidden networks and names as escaped bytes (asks 8 and 9); group-key rekeying.

## D285 WPA3-Personal: SAE on P-256, the SHA-256 handshake and protected management frames (D284's ask 8; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from IEEE 802.11-2020 12.4, 12.7 and RFC 4493)

- **Decision.** A network whose RSN element offers SAE and no PSK is joined as WPA3-Personal
  (`Security::Wpa3Personal`); a transition-mode network offering both stays WPA2-Personal, which
  it accepts.
  - `eggos_crypto::p256` gains the group operations SAE needs, all on the existing constant-time
    Montgomery field and complete addition formulas: points multiplied (the same ladder as the base
    point's), added and negated, a point found from its x-coordinate (square root as
    `a^((p+1)/4)`, the Legendre symbol as `a^((p-1)/2)`, by a constant-time exponentiation), the
    curve equation checked, and scalars added modulo the order. `eggos_crypto::cmac` is AES-CMAC
    (RFC 4493's vectors as tests).
  - `eggos_wifi::sae` runs SAE on group 19 with hunting-and-pecking: all 40 rounds whatever the
    password, the password element from `max(addresses) || min(addresses)`, a commit of
    `(rand + mask) mod r` and `-(mask · PWE)`, the peer's commit checked (range, curve, not our own
    reflected), the shared x-coordinate through HMAC-SHA-256 and KDF-SHA-256 to the KCK and PMK,
    and confirms over both commits. Anti-clogging tokens are sent back as asked, up to three
    commits. Hash-to-element (needed for 6 GHz) is not written: hunting-and-pecking is what every
    WPA3-Personal access point takes on 2.4 and 5 GHz.
  - `eggos_wifi::kdf` is IEEE 802.11's KDF over HMAC-SHA-256. The handshake takes an `Akm`: for
    SAE the PTK comes from KDF-SHA-256, EAPOL-Key frames carry key descriptor version 0 with
    AES-CMAC MICs, message 2 carries WPA3's RSN element (SAE, management frame protection capable
    and required, BIP-CMAC-128), and message 3 must hold the IGTK KDE, kept in `Keys::igtk`.
  - The station sends SAE authentication frames (algorithm 3) instead of open-system ones, and a
    wrong password shows as `wrong-passphrase`: the access point never confirms. With management
    frames protected, CCMP covers unicast management frames too (nonce flag bit 4), and only a
    protected disassociation or deauthentication addressed to the station, decrypted and newer
    than the last, ends the link; unprotected ones are ignored.
  - The Network pane offers `Join` with the passphrase note on WPA3 networks.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; hash-to-element and 6 GHz; checking BIP on group management
  frames (they are ignored instead) and noticing a silent access point by lost beacons; answering
  SA Query requests, which an access point sends when the station joins again while it still
  holds the old association; PMKSA caching.

## D286 Wi-Fi and Ethernet together: `eth0` and `wlan0`, routes by network then wired first (D279's and D284's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Linux's routing and NetworkManager's default metrics)

- **Decision.** The kernel's network keeps a list of adapters instead of one: the wired adapter a
  driver installs at boot is `eth0`, and the Wi-Fi station attaches as `wlan0` at its first join
  (`net::attach_wireless`), whether or not there is a wired one. Each has its own interface: its
  own DHCP lease, ARP table and counters. The network's thread polls all of them and starts once,
  with whichever comes first.
  - A packet leaves through the adapter whose network holds its destination; otherwise through
    the first adapter whose link is up and whose lease names a router, wired before Wi-Fi (Linux
    distributions' network managers give wired routes metric 100 and Wi-Fi 600); otherwise the
    first adapter up. A UDP datagram sent from an interface's address leaves through that
    interface. `source_for` picks the address of the adapter the route leaves through, so a TCP
    connection's address and its route agree.
  - Every interface's address is local; a datagram to any interface's broadcast address is a
    broadcast. DNS servers come from the default adapter's lease, else the first lease naming any.
  - `/proc/net/interfaces` lists `lo`, `eth0` and `wlan0`; the name says the kind (the design's
    ask 6). `/proc/net/route` gives each route its interface's metric (100 wired, 600 Wi-Fi), and
    `/proc/net/arp` lists every interface's neighbours.
  - The desktop's indicator shows the first adapter that is up with an address, else the first up,
    else the first.
  - D284's `ethernet-in-use` failure is gone: Wi-Fi joins beside a cable.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; moving open TCP connections when the default adapter
  changes (they keep their address and break if its adapter goes down, as on Linux); a Wi-Fi
  glyph on the bar; per-interface DNS.

## D287 The display's size chosen in settings, applied at boot; virtio GPU mode changes (M8, M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from virtio 1.2 5.7)

- **Decision.** A display mode changes at boot, before the desktop starts, as `display.scale`
  does (D195): the desktop and every window are laid out for one screen size, and changing it
  live would mean laying all of them out again, which waits for a desktop that can.
  - `display.resolution` is settable: `auto` (the default, the display's own size) or one of
    twelve common sizes from 1024x768 to 3840x2160 (`eggos_settings_file::RESOLUTIONS`), saved in
    the settings file and applied by the kernel's `load_saved_settings` before `display.scale`.
    `display.size` (read-only) is the size now and `display.resolution_changeable` (read-only)
    whether the display can change; `/proc/driver/display` says the device's size, its scale and
    `changeable yes|no`. `settings set` and the `settings_set` MCP tool take it, as every key.
  - The virtio GPU driver shows a new framebuffer as a second resource (ids 1 and 3 in turn):
    create, attach backing, set the scanout, then detach the old one's backing and destroy it
    and hand its memory back (`replace_framebuffer`); flushes name the shown resource. It also
    reads the device's display-changed event and asks for the preferred mode again
    (`preferred_mode`), which `auto` uses.
  - `Scanout` gains `can_change_mode`, `preferred_mode` and `change_mode`; the virtio GPU and the
    offscreen display change, a firmware's framebuffer (UEFI GOP, D236) and the Intel display at
    the firmware's mode (D268) do not. `Display::change_mode` refuses sizes below 1024x768 or above
    3840x2160's bytes, keeps scale 2 only where the desktop fits at half the size, and draws the
    boot screen again when it showed.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the Display pane's control (a Claude Fable design,
  docs/ux/display-resolution-v0.4.md, then its Rust); a live change without a restart; acting on a
  host window's resize while the desktop runs; Intel modesetting to other modes (needs the
  display engine's PLLs and link training).

## D288 The Display pane's resolution control (D287's GUI; design by Claude Fable, docs/ux/display-resolution-v0.4.md; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (the design by Claude Fable)

- **Decision.** As the design's sections 1 to 4: the `Resolution` row gains the toolkit's
  dropdown (`Automatic`, then the sizes smallest first, written `1920 × 1080`) at the row's right,
  the size in force moves before it, and a resolution line sits under the row; `Scale`, its line
  and `Pointer` move down 40 px. Choosing writes `display.resolution` at once
  (`Request::SetDisplayResolution`, the same write as `settings set`), with no Apply button. At
  saved scale 2x the sizes that do not fit the desktop's 640x400 minimum at half size are left out
  of the list (a second static option list, swapped into the dropdown); at 1x with such a size
  chosen the `Scale` group is disabled with the design's sentence. On a display that cannot change
  size the dropdown is hidden and the line says so; without a disk it is disabled. Search finds
  the pane by `screen size`, `mode`, `1080p`, `1440p`, `4K`, `Full HD` and `Automatic`. Settings'
  widget capacity grows by 2, and the app dialog's with it (317).
- **Deviations, for the next GUI pass.** The desktop minimum is a constant in the pane, not a
  fact from the kernel (ask 3); `Automatic`'s pending line (the display's own size, ask 2) is not
  shown, since the kernel does not report the preferred size yet; the phone, tablet and TV layouts
  and the dropdown's digit keys (`2` to `2560 × 1440`) follow the toolkit's defaults.

## D289 The return stack buffer filled at every thread switch on CPUs without enhanced IBRS (D49's speculation follow-ups; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Intel's and AMD's Spectre v2 guidance)

- **Decision.** Where the CPU has IBRS and IBPB but not enhanced IBRS (D260, D267), the x86_64
  thread switch, once on the new thread's stack, calls 32 times in pairs to `pause; lfence` traps
  and drops the 32 return addresses, so the returns that follow the switch predict only those
  traps: never an entry the previous thread or a program trained, and never an empty buffer that
  older Intel cores answer from the indirect predictor. It costs about 32 calls a switch on those
  CPUs and nothing elsewhere (one byte compared).
- **Moved to the end of the code-only queue** (written last, then built and tested first in the
  build pass): KPTI and AMD's SRSO mitigation. KPTI changes every x86_64 entry and exit (a
  trampoline stack in the entry area, the CR3 switch before any kernel memory is touched, a
  user view of PML4 511 holding only the entry text, the IDT and the per-CPU tables, and roots
  allocated as 8 KiB pairs); written blind, an error there stops every x86_64 boot, and only
  pre-2019 Intel cores (no `RDCL_NO`) need it.

## D290 LoongArch64, part 1: boot, translation, timer, CPUs, exceptions, user mode and the Linux ABI (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the LoongArch Reference Manual volume 1, Linux's LoongArch boot protocol and QEMU's `virt` board)

- **Decision.** LoongArch64 is M9's first new architecture: QEMU emulates it well (`virt`,
  LA464), Rust has its kernel (`loongarch64-unknown-none-softfloat`) and Linux
  (`loongarch64-unknown-linux-musl`) targets, and its Linux ABI is the generic one AArch64 and
  RISC-V already use. Part 1 is everything a kernel binary for it needs:
  - **Boot.** QEMU loads the image at 2 MiB and enters `_start` in direct address mode with the
    command line and the EFI system table it builds in the first megabyte; the entry turns on
    `DMW0` (uncached, `0x8000...`) and `DMW1` (cached, `0x9000...`), moves to its cached alias,
    turns translation on, finds the device tree in the system table's configuration tables
    (`DEVICE_TREE_GUID`), copies the command line, then zeroes physical page 0 and builds boot
    tables (a 512 GiB direct map of 1 GiB pages and the kernel's gigabyte) before jumping to the
    top 2 GiB. The first 2 MiB stay out of the frame allocator. `DMW1` is turned off once the
    kernel's own tables load; `DMW0` stays for the console's UART, which is reached uncached
    from the first instruction on.
  - **Translation.** Four levels of 512 entries (48-bit addresses), `PGDL` for programs and
    `PGDH` for the kernel (two roots, as AArch64), 4 KiB pages and 2 MiB and 1 GiB huge pages
    (`paging::loongarch64`, with host tests). The TLB refill handler walks them with `lddir` and
    `ldpte` in direct address mode. The walk does not check directory entries, so an empty one
    (0) leads it to physical page 0, which stays zeroed: the walk ends at an invalid leaf and the
    access raises a page-invalid exception, a page fault that may be stale. Kernel pages are
    global, programs' are not: a switch drops non-global translations only (`invtlb 3`).
  - **Timer and CPUs.** The stable counter (`rdtime.d`) at the frequency `CPUCFG` words 4 and 5
    give, each core's one-shot `TCFG` timer (interrupt 11), wake-ups as IPIs through the IOCSR
    block (interrupt 12), and secondary CPUs started through QEMU's boot code: their entry's
    physical address in mailbox 0 and their `CpuStart` in mailbox 1, then an IPI. Power-off and
    reset write QEMU's generic event device.
  - **Exceptions and user mode.** One entry for every exception and interrupt (`ECFG.VS` 0),
    which `EENTRY` points at; while a program runs `EENTRY` points at the user entry instead,
    which saves its registers into its `UserContext` (`SAVE0` holds it), as RISC-V's `stvec`
    does. The per-CPU block lives in `$r21`, which the psABI reserves; the user entry puts the
    kernel's back. The FP unit is off until a program's first FP instruction (`EUEN.FPE`, the
    FP-disabled exception reported as an illegal instruction for the kernel's lazy start); LSX
    and LASX stay off and are not in `AT_HWCAP`. Every test program of the self-tests is
    translated.
  - **Linux ABI.** `kernel/src/linux/abi/loongarch64.rs`: the generic table, `uname` machine
    `loongarch64`, ELF machine 258, the generic `stat`, no `sa_restorer` (the kernel's
    trampoline), signal frames of 880 bytes whose `uc_mcontext` holds `sc_pc`, `sc_regs` and
    `sc_flags` and then the FPU context record (`f0`-`f31`, the condition flags, `fcsr0`) and the
    end record; faults as RISC-V's, FP exceptions `SIGFPE`.
  - **Programs and the build.** The user runtime's `_start`, system calls and `clone`, the
    programs' signal actions and thread pointer, the kernel and Linux targets in
    `rust-toolchain.toml` and `.cargo/config.toml`, xtask's architecture table (`-machine virt
    -cpu la464`, PCI virtio devices) and the CI boot job.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the interrupt controllers (EIOINTC, PCH-PIC, PCH-MSI), so
  console input, device interrupts and MSI wait; PCI discovery from the device tree on
  LoongArch, so the virtio devices are not found yet; LSX and LASX for programs; `RDCL`-style
  speculation controls; QEMU 9.0 or later is needed for the device tree in the system table.

## D291 PCI hosts from the device tree with BARs the kernel assigns, and LoongArch's interrupt controllers (M5, M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the device-tree PCI binding, the PCI Local Bus specification and Loongson's 7A and 3A5000 manuals)

- **Decision.**
  - **PCI from the device tree.** Where no ACPI `MCFG` gave a configuration space, the kernel
    looks for a `pci-host-ecam-generic` node (QEMU's `virt` boards on AArch64, RISC-V and
    LoongArch): its ECAM window from `reg`, its buses from `bus-range`, its 32-bit and 64-bit
    memory windows from `ranges`. It enumerates the functions as on x86_64, and every memory BAR
    left at 0 (no firmware ran: QEMU's direct kernel boot) gets an address from a window, aligned
    to its size, 64-bit BARs from a 64-bit window first (`pci::assign`); a BAR firmware assigned
    keeps its address, translated from the bus's addresses to the CPU's. The device table holds
    CPU addresses, so drivers do not change. The device tree parser keeps a node's own `ranges`
    and `bus-range` for this.
  - **LoongArch's interrupts.** EIOINTC (through IOCSR) routes all 256 vectors to the boot CPU's
    hardware interrupt 1 and enables them; its pending words are read, cleared and handed to the
    kernel vector by vector. PCH-PIC lines are made level, active-high and routed to the vector
    of the same number (the UART's line 2 is the console's input); PCH-MSI's doorbell turns a
    device's write of vectors 32 to 255 into those vectors, which `message_interrupt` hands out,
    so virtio-pci's MSI-X works. Device-tree specifiers name PCH-PIC lines.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; bridges below the host bus (no bus numbers are assigned);
  I/O BARs; prefetchable windows kept apart; vectors spread over CPUs; the same PCI discovery
  tried on the AArch64 and RISC-V boots (it runs there too now, untested).

## D292 Apps' own actions: `app.actions`, `app actions`, `app do` and one MCP tool per action (M14 part 70, CLAUDE.md note 6; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** An installed app declares what it offers besides opening in `app.actions` in its
  folder (`eggos_app_manifest::actions`): `eggos-actions 1`, then blocks starting `action=<name>`
  with `title`, `description`, `run` (the program, absolute or relative to the app's folder, and
  its words), `effect` (`read`, `change` or `destroy`) and up to eight
  `argument=<name>:<text|number|boolean>:<required|optional>:<description>` lines. In `run`, a
  word's `{argument}` is replaced by the argument's value inside that word, and the word is left
  out when an optional argument has none; values are type-checked and never split or passed to a
  shell, so a value cannot add words. A separate file keeps `app.manifest` within its 1 KiB and the
  kernel's launcher, which reads manifests, unchanged; uninstalling removes the folder and with it
  the actions.
  - **CLI.** `app actions [--json] [<name>]` lists them; `app do <name> <action>
    [<argument>=<value>]... [--values <json>]` runs one in the app's folder with `PATH=/bin`,
    passing its output, errors and exit status through. An action whose effect is `destroy`
    needs `--confirmed`, given once the user agreed (`needs_confirmation` otherwise). New error
    `no_such_action`.
  - **MCP.** `app_actions` (reading), `app_do` (install grant) and `app_do_confirmed` (install
    grant, always asks the user) are static tools; on top, `tools/list` lists each installed
    action as its own tool `app_<app>_<action>` (lower case, other bytes as `-`, at most 64
    bytes) with its arguments as the input schema and its effect as the annotations, read from
    the files at each list, so installing or uninstalling changes the list at once. Calling one
    becomes a call of `app_do`, or of `app_do_confirmed` for a `destroy` action, with the
    arguments as `values`, so grants, the user's yes and the audit log are the generic tools'.
    The server reads `/Applications` through a new `System::folder_entries`.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the GUI front-end (the launcher's app menu listing an app's
  actions, a Claude Fable design); actions of Windows and macOS apps from their own automation
  interfaces (COM, AppleScript, App Intents), which D21 names; `notifications/tools/list_changed`
  when an app is installed or removed.

## D293 Component updates: only changed files fetched, each component staged whole and swapped in (M14 part 64, D69; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `component update [--dry-run] [--json] [<name>]` and the MCP tool
  `component_update` (install grant) bring the installed components to the copies in the
  component store for this EggOS:
  - **What changes** (`manager::plan_update`): a file whose path, mode and SHA-256 match the
    installed record is kept; the others are changed; installed files the new copy lacks are
    dropped; a component whose files and description are the same is up to date.
  - **Delta download.** With no store on a disk, the command fetches the release store's index
    with one range request, then each changed file's bytes with one range request each, checks
    them against the index's digests and packs them into a small local store
    (`update_store`). Unchanged files are never downloaded: they are copied from the installed
    folder, each checked against its digest again.
  - **Atomic swap.** Each component is staged whole in `.staging-<name>` (its record last); then
    the installed folder is renamed to `.replaced-<name>`, the staged one into its place, and
    the old one removed. `tidy`, which runs before every install, update and remove, finishes a
    swap a crash cut short: the new copy when its record is there, else the old one back. A
    separate prefix keeps an interrupted remove from ever being brought back.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; updating in the background on a schedule with the
  Components pane's update button and progress (a Claude Fable design) and the bar's notice;
  binary deltas inside a file (whole changed files are fetched); verifying a release store's
  signature beyond its digests (D257's limit).

## D294 Wi-Fi group-key rekeying: the group key handshake answered while joined (D279's follow-up; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from IEEE 802.11-2020 12.7.7)

- **Decision.** Access points change the group key on a timer (often hourly) and when a station
  leaves; a station that misses it stops hearing broadcasts and multicasts, ARP and DHCP
  renewals among them. The station keeps its four-way handshake's supplicant while joined; an
  EAPOL frame from the access point (decrypted with the pairwise key, as every frame then is) goes
  to `Supplicant::receive_group`, which checks the MIC with the handshake's KCK and the replay
  counter, unwraps the new GTK (and IGTK on WPA3) with the KEK and writes message 2. The answer
  goes back protected like any data frame, the new group key replaces the old one and its replay
  counter starts again. A message that does not check out is dropped.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; keeping the old group key for frames still in flight under
  it (one key index at a time); pairwise rekeying (a new four-way handshake while joined).

## D295 A process's exit and signals interrupt only the CPUs that have its address space loaded (M6's follow-up of D95; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `exit`, `end_for_exec` and `record_signal_sent` interrupted every other CPU so a
  thread running the program somewhere came back to the kernel. Only a CPU whose active address
  space is the process's can be running its program, so only those are asked to reschedule and
  woken; a CPU that switches the address space in afterwards still looks for sent signals and
  the end before it runs the program (`after_look`, D95), so nothing is missed. On a machine
  with many CPUs a signal no longer costs an interrupt on each of them.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; a measured cost on a many-CPU machine.

## D296 Touch screens drive the pointer: the first finger moves it and presses its left button (M12's first backend piece; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Linux's multi-touch protocol B)

- **Decision.** A virtio-input device that reports multi-touch positions (`ABS_MT_POSITION_X`
  and `_Y`) but no plain `ABS_X`/`ABS_Y` takes the multi-touch ranges as its absolute ranges,
  so QEMU's `virtio-multitouch` is a pointer device. The input layer follows the protocol's
  slots: the first slot's positions move the pointer, and `BTN_TOUCH` presses and releases the
  left button, as a single-touch screen behaves, so the desktop, its menus and every app work by
  touch today. `input::has_touch_screen` says a touch screen was used, for the shell's form
  (docs/ux/adaptive-shell-v0.5.md, being designed).
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the other fingers (gestures, pinch), touch events of their
  own for apps, and the touch shell itself.

## D297 M9's remaining architectures: which the pinned stable toolchain can build, and in what order (code-only session; research from Rust's platform-support tiers) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **The constraint.** EggOS builds on one pinned stable Rust (`rust-toolchain.toml`) with no
  third-party crates, so a kernel target needs a prebuilt `core` from rustup: tier 2. Bare-metal
  tier-2 targets exist for AArch64, RISC-V, x86_64 and LoongArch64 (done or in progress, D290),
  32-bit Arm (`armv7a-none-eabi`) and RV32 (`riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf`). PowerPC64 and
  s390x have only Linux targets at tier 2 (`powerpc64le-unknown-linux-gnu`,
  `powerpc64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `s390x-unknown-linux-gnu`), whose prebuilt `core` a `no_std`
  kernel can link against with its own linker script, as the user programs already do with
  `*-linux-musl`; MIPS64 and SPARC64 are tier 3 only, so no `core` is shipped and building them
  needs a nightly toolchain's `build-std`.
- **Decision.** The order: (1) ppc64le, on QEMU `powernv` (bare metal, OPAL firmware) with the
  POWER9 radix MMU, through `powerpc64le-unknown-linux-gnu`; (2) s390x on QEMU `s390-ccw-virtio`,
  the first big-endian one, which brings an endian-aware ELF loader and Linux ABI (`elf.rs`
  notes it); (3) the 32-bit ones, Arm and RV32, after the kernel's 64-bit assumptions
  (`usize` as `u64`, 64-bit page tables, a 3 GiB/1 GiB split) are taken out behind the HAL, which
  is a refactor of its own; (4) MIPS64 and SPARC64 wait: a nightly toolchain goes against the
  pinned-stable rule, which only the owner can change, so they wait until Rust ships tier-2
  targets for them or the owner allows `build-std` for those two.
- **Revised (Main Chat for the owner, 2026-11-11).** Code-only mode builds nothing, so the
  toolchain does not hold the code back: the MIPS64 and SPARC64 HALs are written now, in this
  order, like every other port. They need a nightly toolchain's `build-std`, which the
  pinned-stable rule does not allow today. At test-and-fix time the owner decides whether to
  allow nightly for those two or to wait for tier-2 targets. Until then they stay out of CI and
  the release matrix.
- **Not yet.** Every one of the ports; the owner's call on nightly for MIPS64 and SPARC64.

## D298 Hidden Wi-Fi networks and network names that read back exactly (the Wi-Fi design's asks 8 and 9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Linux iwlwifi's scan request layout and iwx(4))

- **Decision.**
  - `wifi connect --hidden <name> [<passphrase>]` adds `hidden=yes` to `wifi.conf`. While not
    joined, the driver's scans for such a network are active: the scan request names it in its
    first directed SSID (after the probe template and its counts) and every channel probes for it,
    so the access point answers with a probe response that carries the name, which the join uses
    as any other. A network not marked hidden is scanned passively as before.
  - `/proc/driver/wifi` writes network names with printable ASCII as it is, `\\` for a backslash
    and `\xHH` for any other byte and for a space at either end; the Network pane reads them back
    (`wifi_section::unescaped`), so a name with spaces at its ends, line breaks or other bytes is
    the same in the pane, the CLI and the driver.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the pane's `Join another network` row (the design's ask 8
  GUI); several hidden networks at once; `wifi connect` naming a network by escaped bytes.

## D299 The Components design's backend: a stored update check, the daily check, job progress and `component cancel` (docs/ux/components-v0.5.md section 12, asks 1 to 3 and 6; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `eggos_components::state` keeps small text files every front-end reads:
  - `/var/lib/eggos/updates`: the last full `component update --dry-run` (when, from `release`
    or `disk`, and each component's bytes to fetch and files changed). `component list --json`
    gives it back: `updates_checked`, `updates_source` and `updates_daily` on the store line,
    `update` (or `null`) and the running job's `percent` and `phase` on each row, whose state is
    `updating` while one runs.
  - `/var/lib/eggos/updates-daily`: `component update --daily on|off` (and `daily` on
    `component_update`); on unless turned off. init starts an update checker that runs the dry run
    ten minutes after the network has an address, then every 24 hours, while it is on; nothing
    is installed by it.
  - `/run/eggos/component-job`: the running job's kind, component, phase and bytes, written as
    it copies; `/run/eggos/component-cancel`: `component cancel` asks it to stop, and the
    update's progress callback stops at its next piece (the installed copy stays). The progress
    callbacks now get the file system, so they can write and look.
  - `component list --download` fetches the release's store into the cache when no store is
    attached, recorded as a `downloading` job.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the pane's rework, the bar's `Updates` chip
  (`Desktop::set_updates`) and the per-install cancel through the same file (ask 1 for install
  and remove); download progress in bytes (the fetch runs as a separate program); `download` on
  the `component_list` tool.

## D304 M9: 64-bit little-endian PowerPC (POWER9, QEMU `powernv9`), part 1: boot, radix page tables, timer, CPUs, exceptions, user mode and the Linux ABI (D297's first port; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Target.** The kernel builds for `powerpc64le-unknown-linux-gnu` (tier 2, D297) with a
    static relocation model, soft float, `rust-lld` and the HAL's linker script. Programs build
    for `powerpc64le-unknown-linux-musl`. Rust names the architecture `powerpc64`, so the HAL
    folder, the paging format and the Linux ABI file use that name; `uname` says `ppc64le`.
  - **Boot.** skiboot enters `_start` big-endian in hypervisor real mode with the device tree,
    OPAL's base and its entry in `r3`, `r8` and `r9`. The entry code:
    - turns the CPU little-endian (Linux's `FIXUP_ENDIAN` words);
    - moves the image to its linked physical address `0x2001_0000` if skiboot put it
      elsewhere;
    - zeroes `.bss`;
    - copies the interrupt vectors to physical `0x4000`;
    - builds a boot radix tree (512 GiB of 1 GiB pages at `0xc000...`) with the partition and
      process tables;
    - sets `PTCR`, `LPCR` (host radix, process tables, `AIL` 3) and `PIDR`, and `rfid`s into
      translation.

    Kernel and direct map share quadrant 3 (`0xc000...`), as on Linux:
    `KERNEL_VIRTUAL_OFFSET` is `0xc000_0000_0000_0000`.
  - **Page tables.** POWER9 walks only 52-bit trees, so the format has five levels: a root
    whose process table entry says 4 index bits (16 entries), then four levels of 512.
    Entries are stored byte-swapped, because the hardware reads them big-endian. Root 0 is a
    program's tree, quadrant 0, through process table entry `1 + PIR`; root 1 is the kernel's,
    entry 0. Address-space switches rewrite the CPU's own entry and invalidate by PID.
  - **Interrupts.** The interrupts relocate to `0xc000...4000` plus the vector. Each vector
    keeps `r13` in `HSPRG1`, takes the CPU's scratch area from `HSPRG0` and jumps to one
    common entry. From problem state, the entry saves the program's registers into its
    `UserContext` and returns from `run_user` (D47); from the kernel, it saves a frame below the
    288-byte red zone and returns with `hrfid`. The per-CPU block is `r13`.
  - **Timer and wake-ups.** The decrementer, over the 512 MHz time base, is the timer.
    Wake-ups are hypervisor doorbells (`msgsnd`). Idle is `stop` with `PSSCR` 0.
  - **Firmware calls.** The console, power-off, reset and secondary CPUs (`OPAL_START_CPU`)
    are OPAL calls made in big-endian real mode; their buffers are in the kernel image, whose
    physical addresses are known.
  - **FP.** The FP, vector and VSX registers are lazy as elsewhere (D54): all 64 VSX
    registers, `FPSCR`, `VSCR` and `VRSAVE`, with the facilities turned on for programs by a
    per-CPU flag the way into user mode reads.
  - **Linux ABI.** The table is PowerPC's own: legacy calls and `renameat`, no `arch_prctl`.
    A failed call sets `CR0.SO` with the error number positive, and the HAL converts it.
    `struct stat` is x86_64's layout. `O_DIRECTORY` and `O_NOFOLLOW` are Arm's. The terminal
    `ioctl` numbers are PowerPC's, so the kernel's request numbers moved into the ABI files
    (`abi::tty`) and userland's into `eggos_runtime::syscall::tty`. Signal frames are
    PowerPC's `rt_sigframe`: `gp_regs`, `fp_regs` and the vector and VSX areas, the
    `li r0, 172; sc` trampoline, and the handler's frame 128 below with its back chain. The
    user test programs are written in PowerPC assembly.
  - **CI.** It joins the CI boot matrix as LoongArch did.
- **Known gaps for the build pass.**
  - The prebuilt `core` of the Linux target is hard-float, and the kernel provides `memcpy`
    and its siblings itself.
  - The kernel's `termios` and userland's raw-mode code use the generic layout, which
    PowerPC orders differently (`c_cc` before `c_line`, other `VMIN`/`VTIME` indices).
  - std-selftest and the Windows and macOS layers keep the generic tty numbers (those layers
    do not run here).
  - Whether skiboot loads the image as one blob (the relocation copy assumes it may) is
    checked at the first boot.
- **Not yet (part 2).** XIVE for device interrupts, console input through OPAL events and
  wake-ups between cores beyond what doorbells reach; PCI host bridges (PHB4) from the device
  tree; building and running.
