  - **Keys.** OK opens; Menu opens the tile menu (`Open`, then `Close` or `Uninstall...`);
    `Power` opens `Power off` and `Restart`. The remote's `Home` (key 172, new) shows the
    home screen from anywhere with every scroll at 0; `Back` over an app follows the phone's
    rules, including `HANDLES_BACK`. `wm home` and `wm back` work in this form.
- **Deviations.** Pointer mode and its menu for apps without `FOCUS_NAVIGABLE`, keys mode,
  centred dialogs with chrome, the toolkit's (48, 28) padding, the network glyph and `Agent`
  chip in the strip, the notice's TV place, a boot option that sets `input::pretend_remote`,
  and an attached pointer's clicks on the home screen are not built yet.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the deviations above.

## D308 M12: the phone's bars act on release, and the gestures of section 2.8 with the pointer as the finger (docs/ux/adaptive-shell-v0.5.md section 2.8; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The status bar and the navigation bar act when the finger (the pointer's
  button, until the touch path) lifts, not when it touches, so a press can become a swipe:
  - a swipe down of 48 px from the status bar opens the shade, as a tap does;
  - a swipe up of 64 px from the navigation bar is `Home`, whichever zone it started on;
  - a swipe right of 48 px from the left 16 px of the work area is `Back`, and that edge
    belongs to the shell.

  A tap on a zone acts only when the finger lifts inside the same zone.
- **Deviations.** The hold that turns the upward swipe into `Apps`, the swipe up on the shade
  and dragging a switcher card away wait for the touch path's timing.
- **Not yet.** Building and running.

## D309 M12: the TV's pointer mode for apps not driven by focus (docs/ux/adaptive-shell-tv-v0.5.md sections 5.3 and 5.4; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Toolkit windows are created with the new `FOCUS_NAVIGABLE` flag, which the
  console terminal counts as having. On a TV, a shown window without it is driven in pointer
  mode:
  - the arrows move a pointer 8 px a press (the window gets each move), and OK clicks the
    primary button there;
  - `Back` sends Esc;
  - Menu opens the pointer menu: `Right click`, `Scroll up` and `Scroll down` (three notches,
    the menu staying open), `Send arrows to the app` (keys mode, whose row then reads
    `Move the pointer with arrows`) and `Close app`.

  Keys mode is per window.
- **Deviations.** The pointer does not accelerate when the key is held (no key repeat
  timing in the shell yet); the first-show notice, the pointer drawn while hidden in keys
  mode, and holding OK to drag are not built.
- **Not yet.** Building and running.

## D310 virtio-console input as the console: a virtio console whose port is not the agent channel is the machine's console, as `hvc0` is Linux's (M8; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A virtio console whose port is not named `org.eggos.mcp` (one with no name
  included, QEMU's plain `virtconsole`) is no longer refused: the first such device becomes the
  host console.
  - Everything `console::write` writes (programs' output and the input's echo) is written to
    it too (`console::mirror_output`).
  - A kernel thread passes what the host types into it to the console's input, through the line
    discipline, as a keyboard's typing goes (`receive_from_keyboard`). The thread waits on the
    device's interrupts where the machine routes them, else reads every 20 ms.

  This gives machines without a UART the kernel reads (POWER's OPAL console without XIVE
  events, D304) and hosts that prefer virtio a full console.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; several host consoles; the kernel's own messages
  (`PlatformConsole`) on it.

## D311 The display follows the host window's size: virtio-gpu's display event changes the mode and the desktop is laid out again (M11's display events; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Twice a second at most, the drawing path asks the display whether its device
  raised a display event (QEMU's window resized). It does so only while no size is chosen in
  Settings (`display.resolution` `auto`; a chosen size keeps the display at that size). On an
  event:
  - the device's preferred mode becomes the display's (D287's `change_mode`);
  - the desktop is laid out for the new logical size: the wallpaper for that size, the panels
    of the profile and form, maximised windows filling the new work area, the others moved into
    it, chromeless windows refitted in the touch and TV forms
    (`Desktop::resize`, `Desktop::new` now sharing its wallpaper code);
  - everything is drawn again.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the QMP check that resizes QEMU's window; a size that does
  not fit the terminal's window, which is left as it was; the GPU's interrupt for the event
  instead of the half-second look.

## D312 ppc64le part 2: XIVE in exploitation mode and the PHB4's PCI through OPAL, DMA by the bypass window (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** POWER9's devices are reached through OPAL, as Linux's powernv platform does,
  with the smallest set of calls that gives virtio-pci and NVMe their configuration space, DMA
  and MSI-X:
  - **XIVE** (`hal/src/arch/powerpc64/xive.rs`):
    - At boot, `OPAL_XIVE_RESET` puts XIVE in exploitation mode. The boot CPU gets one 4 KiB
      event queue at priority 7 (`OPAL_XIVE_SET_QUEUE_INFO`, enabled and always notifying).
    - The TIMA's hypervisor window (second `reg` of `ibm,opal-xive-pe`) and the ESB pages of
      the first 32 MSIs of the first PHB (`OPAL_XIVE_GET_IRQ_INFO`) are early device regions,
      mapped in the direct map.
    - `message_interrupt` takes the next prepared MSI:
      - OPAL gives its address and data (`OPAL_PCI_SET_XIVE_PE`, `OPAL_GET_MSI_64`);
      - `OPAL_XIVE_SET_IRQ_CONFIG` routes it to the boot CPU's queue with its source number as
        the data;
      - a load at the ESB's `SET_PQ_00` offset unmasks it.
    - `LPCR.HVICE` is set, so physical interrupts come at 0xea0 (and 0x500 is handled the same).
      The handler acknowledges at the TIMA (`ACK_HV_REG`) and drains the queue by its
      generation bit. It hands each source's line to the kernel and EOIs the source by an ESB
      load, or a store when OPAL says `STORE_EOI`.
  - **PCI** (`hal/src/arch/powerpc64/pci.rs`):
    - Configuration space is `OPAL_PCI_CONFIG_READ_WORD` and `WRITE_WORD` on the first
      `ibm,ioda3-phb` (or `ioda2`) node's `ibm,opal-phbid`.
    - Every function joins PE 1 (`OPAL_PCI_SET_PE`, all RIDs), with its MSI validation entry
      enabled.
    - PE 1's second DMA window bypasses translation from bus address `1 << 59`
      (`OPAL_PCI_MAP_PE_DMA_WINDOW_REAL`, 1 TiB).
  - **Platform trait.** `firmware_pci()` (the configuration space, `None` by default) and
    `dma_device_offset()` (0 by default, `1 << 59` here).
  - **Kernel.** `pci_bus::discover_firmware` enumerates a firmware-served host with the same
    BAR assignment as D291's ECAM host (now `add_host_functions`, shared), using the PHB node's
    `ranges`. `DmaRegion::dma_addr` adds the platform's device offset.
  - The device tree walker keeps a node's `ibm,opal-phbid` and `ibm,opal-msi-ranges`.
  - `ppc64_opal_call` passes up to seven arguments (r3–r9); its return address moved to r12.
- **Why.** QEMU's `powernv9` has no ECAM and no emulated interrupt controller simpler than
  XIVE, and OPAL already knows the PHB4 and XIVE register layouts. Calling it keeps the
  register-level drivers (and their unverifiable details) out of EggOS. The bypass window
  avoids programming a TCE table for coherent DMA.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time; written from memory of the OPAL API, unverified).**
  - The tokens (15, 18, 31, 33, 34, 37, 40, 45, 128, 129, 131, 133) and argument orders.
  - The TIMA register offsets (0x830, 0x31).
  - The bypass window's base and the window number (`pe << 1 | 1`).
  - Whether QEMU's PHB4 model implements `MAP_PE_DMA_WINDOW_REAL`; if not, a TCE table is
    needed.
  - Only the first PHB and the boot CPU's queue are used, and only 32 MSIs.
  - The OPAL console's input stays polled; OPAL events through XIVE are not wired.
- **Not yet.** Building and running on `powernv9` with virtio-pci; secondary CPUs' queues;
  LSIs; other PHBs.

## D313 MIPS64 part 1: the HAL on QEMU `loongson3-virt`, with a device tree the HAL writes and a software TLB refill (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode; nightly `build-std` per D297) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Order (changes D297's).** MIPS64 comes before s390x. It is little-endian, and its TLB is
  filled by software, so the generic page tables fit it as they are. s390x needs two refactors
  of its own first: big-endian ELF and Linux ABI, and DAT tables whose levels are not 512
  entries of 9 bits each. SPARC64 shares the first refactor. The order is now MIPS64 (parts 1
  and 2), the big-endian groundwork, s390x, then SPARC64.
- **Decision.** The machine:
  - **Target and build.** QEMU `loongson3-virt` with a `Loongson-3A4000` (MIPS64 Release 2,
    little-endian). The kernel is built for `mips64el-unknown-linux-gnuabi64` as a static,
    non-`abicalls`, soft-float image with nightly `build-std`. xtask's `NIGHTLY_ARCHES` holds
    it, named only with `--arch mips64el`; `all`, CI and the release matrix leave it out.
  - **Boot.** QEMU enters `_start` in `CKSEG0` with Linux's `a0`/`a1` argument table (the
    command line) and the Loongson boot parameters in `a2` (`lefi.rs`: the RAM map, the CPU
    count and the clock).
  - **Device tree.** The board gives none, so the HAL writes one into a 4 KiB buffer in its
    image. `fdt::writer` is a new allocation-free device-tree writer with tests. The tree holds
    the RAM, the CPUs, the NS16550 UART and the generic ECAM PCI host with QEMU's windows.
    Memory, CPU and device discovery read it like any firmware's.
  - **Translation.**
    - The image runs in `CKSEG0` and the direct map is the cached `XKPHYS` window, both
      unmapped.
    - Programs (`XUSEG`) and the device window go through the TLB. The device window is one
      root entry of `XKSEG` at `0xc000_ff00_0000_0000`; the new `Platform::device_window` hook
      overrides the generic place, which would be an address error here.
    - `paging::mips64` keeps four levels of 512 entries. Directory entries are cached-window
      pointers, and leaves are `EntryLo` words with two software bits (user, kept) in the bits
      the hardware drops. Only 4 KiB leaves.
    - The refill handler walks the tables with `k0`/`k1`: a program's root comes from
      `KScratch1`, the kernel's from a static. Where nothing is mapped it writes an invalid
      pair, so the kernel sees a TLB-invalid fault.
    - Every address-space switch takes a new ASID, and the whole TLB is flushed when the ASIDs
      wrap. A long `drop_user_translations` takes a new ASID; a short one probes and
      invalidates each pair.
  - **Exceptions.**
    - The general vector saves the registers on the kernel stack. It clears `EXL`, so the
      handler can take refills, and restores everything on the way out.
    - From user mode, the registers go to the `UserContext` that `KScratch2` names, as on the
      other ports (D47). `UserLocal` is the thread pointer, and `syscall_a3` keeps the
      program's fourth argument for restarts.
    - n64 system calls: `v0` holds the number, `a0`–`a5` the arguments. An error sets `a3` to
      1 and leaves the error number positive in `v0`.
  - **Timer and CPUs.**
    - The 32-bit `Count` and `Compare` are extended to one 64-bit clock shared by all CPUs.
      With no deadline, `Compare` stays half a wrap ahead.
    - Wake-ups are IPIs through the Loongson IPI block. Secondary CPUs start through its
      mailboxes, which QEMU's boot code polls.
  - **Lazy FP.** `Status.CU1`, with 32 64-bit FP registers (`FR`) and `FCSR`.
  - **Per-CPU block.** `$gp`, which a static, non-`abicalls` kernel leaves alone; the switch
    does not save it.
  - **Fixes on the way.**
    - The device self-test's machine match lacked LoongArch's `virt` and did not cover every
      machine; it now covers it and `loongson3-virt` (the NS16550 must be found).
    - PowerPC's `rt_sigreturn` trampoline passed two words to the three-word `code_bytes`; a
      `nop` fills it.
- **Part 2 (next).** MIPS's Linux ABI differs from every other port's in values, not only
  numbers. The error numbers (`ENOSYS` is 89), the signal numbers, `sigset_t` (128 signals,
  16 bytes) and `struct sigaction` (flags first, no restorer) all differ. So do the `open`,
  `mmap`, `fcntl` and socket constants, `struct stat` and the terminal `ioctl` numbers. The
  Linux layer gains per-architecture tables for each, then `abi/mips64.rs`, the user runtime
  and the Linux test programs. Until then, `TestProgram`'s Linux programs beyond `linux_hello`
  exit with 1, and the kernel's `compile_error!` for an architecture without a Linux ABI
  still fires for MIPS64. Device interrupts (Loongson's `liointc` and PCI MSIs) also come in
  part 2.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time; written from memory of QEMU's board and Loongson's
  boot parameters, unverified).**
  - The board's addresses: the UART, the PCI windows, the power-management block (writing
    `0xff` powers off, `0x00` resets), the IPI block and its mailbox protocol.
  - The `boot_params` offsets.
  - Whether the `Loongson-3A4000` model has `KScratch1`/`KScratch2`, `UserLocal`, `RI`/`XI`
    and 48 `SEGBITS`.
  - That the counter runs at half the CPU clock.
  - That `EntryLo` drops the software bits, and that LLVM never uses `$gp` with
    `+noabicalls` and the static relocation model.
  - The page tables still map the direct map and the image although nothing walks them there
    (2 MiB of tables per GiB of RAM).

## D314 The on-screen keyboard, slice 1: a server-drawn panel whose keys go through the kernel's typist (docs/ux/on-screen-keyboard-v0.5.md; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The design brief (Fable, committed with this change) is built in two slices.
  Slice 1:
  - **The panel** (`drivers/src/desktop/osk.rs`). It sits at the bottom of the work area in
    the phone (portrait 260, landscape 176), tablet (300) and TV (204) forms.
    - While it shows, the work area ends at its top, and every shown window is fitted again
      (one `Resize`). A layout recomputed by a form or size change gets the panel back on the
      next frame.
    - The zones come from one function per form, following the brief's rules (4.1 to 4.4, 8):
      the phone's pitch from the widest row, the tablet's and landscape phone's unit, and the
      TV's 12 by 4 grid. Host tests pin the brief's numbers for `us` and `de`.
  - **Pages.** `Letters` is read from `LAYOUTS` (the new `Layout::plain_letter`): letter keys
    with a Latin-1 capital from codes 16–27, 30–40 and 86, 44–53, 43, plus `ß`. `Numbers` and
    `Symbols` are the same for every layout. The seven accent keys come from `DEAD_ACCENTS`.
    Email and URL fields change key 18, and number fields open on `Numbers`.
  - **Keys.**
    - Character keys type on release, the key under the finger. Backspace and the arrows act
      on the press and repeat at `keyboard.repeat_delay_ms` and `keyboard.repeat_rate`.
    - Shift cycles `off`, `once`, `locked`; Ctrl and Alt latch for one key.
    - A key held 500 ms (or right-clicked) opens its Latin-1 alternates; the strip stays open
      when the finger lifts without choosing. The phone's portrait preview is drawn too.
    - The layout key cycles the chosen layouts (`Action::ChooseKeyboardLayout`).
    - Hide keyboard, `Back` (navigation bar, key or `wm back`), Home, the shade, the switcher,
      and the field losing the focus all hide the panel.
  - **Typing.** The panel queues `ScreenKey`s (a key code with modifiers, a character, or an
    accent). Each frame the kernel takes them (`Desktop::take_screen_keys`) and feeds them to
    `InputState::screen_key` under the input lock:
    - a key goes through the `Typist` as a USB key would;
    - a character becomes a key-less character event;
    - an accent becomes pending through the new `Typist::set_pending_accent`, whatever the
      layout, with the dead key's event.

    Their events reach the window like a keyboard's. Bytes meant for the console wait in
    `SCREEN_BYTES` until the next input poll, so the desktop's lock is never held while the
    console takes them. Shifted letters are sent with Shift, else Caps Lock, else as the
    capital character, so `ü` gives `Ü` on `ch` (the brief's 3.3).
  - **TV.** On the TV, the arrows walk the grid without wrapping, OK types, Menu (Compose)
    opens the alternates, Back closes or hides, and Enter hides except in multi-line and
    terminal fields. The panel's own keys coming back through `key_typing` are not taken as
    remote presses (`own_keys`), and the toolkit's `activate` that the panel's own Enter causes
    does not show the keyboard again.
  - **Window protocol.**
    - `SET_TEXT_FOCUS` (48) carries the window, the field kind (none, text, multiline, masked,
      number, email, url, search, terminal), the Enter word (six) and the cause (tap, activate,
      other).
    - `ON_SCREEN_KEYBOARD` (49) takes 0 status, 1 show, 2 hide, or 3 + the mode to set
      `keyboard.on_screen`, and replies whether the keyboard shows and its panel.
    - The toolkit sends the text focus after every event that changes it, and on each tap or
      Enter while a field has it (`View::text_focus`: text, masked and multi-line fields).
  - **Setting.** `keyboard.on_screen` (`auto`, `always`, `never`) is in the settings file, the
    `settings` keys (`ALL` 38) and the kernel (read at boot, set at once).
  - **Agents (D22).**
    - `wm keyboard` prints `shown x y w h` or `hidden`; `wm keyboard show` and
      `wm keyboard hide` act. `show` is refused with `not_applied` (the server's `Unsupported`)
      with no focused field or in `never`.
    - MCP has `wm_keyboard`, `wm_keyboard_show` and `wm_keyboard_hide`.
    - Typing stays `wm type` and `wm press`, shown or hidden.
- **Deviations from the brief (slice 2 or later).**
  - The caret and selection handles (section 7, toolkit asks 6–7).
  - The second contact (5.1, ask 3): the touch path still gives one contact, so a second
    finger is not tracked.
  - Settings' Keyboard pane row: the setting has its CLI and MCP twins, and the row comes with
    slice 2.
  - The Terminal's `terminal` kind: the console window is the server's own and sends no text
    focus yet.
  - The layout key's long-press menu sheet: a tap cycles.
  - `wm show shell`'s keyboard group: the shell has no element tree yet;
    `Desktop::on_screen_keyboard_key_names` lists the keys for when it does.
  - Space remembering its column on the TV.
  - The landscape phone's panel spans the full width: the navigation bar stays at the bottom
    in this build (D303), not on the right.
  - Drawn caps have square corners, not the push button's corner table.
  - Scale 2 is not doubled: the shell's layout runs at scale 1 throughout (D303).
- **Build-pass notes.**
  - Counts: `COMMANDS` 116, registry `TOOLS` 86, MCP `TOOLS` 83, settings `ALL` 38; update
    `docs/mcp.md` and `docs/coreutils.md`.
  - The desktop's `colour` module gains the toolkit's existing button tokens (`BUTTON`,
    `BUTTON_PRESSED`, `BUTTON_PRIMARY`, `BUTTON_PRIMARY_HOVER`), the same values.
  - `Canvas::character_doubled` draws any Egg Mono character at 2x.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the acceptance list of the brief's section 13.

## D315 MIPS64 part 2: n64's Linux ABI, its values translated at the boundary (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** MIPS's Linux ABI differs from every other port's in values, not only call
  numbers. The kernel keeps working in the generic values and translates at the edges:
  - **Numbers.** `kernel/src/linux/abi/mips64.rs` holds n64's table (5000 on). `time` and
    `vfork`, which n64 lacks, get numbers past `LAST`, which answers `ENOSYS` before any
    lookup.
  - **Errors.** The HAL's `set_syscall_result` gives an error its MIPS number (`MIPS_ERRORS`,
    generic 35–133 to MIPS's; `ENOSYS` 89), sets `a3` and leaves the number positive in `v0`.
  - **Arguments in, results out.** A new HAL call, `UserContext::set_syscall_arguments`
    (every architecture), lets the dispatcher rewrite arguments before it dispatches, when the
    ABI's `REWRITES_ARGUMENTS` is set (only MIPS; the check compiles away elsewhere).
    `abi::arguments_in` rewrites:
    - `open`/`openat` and `F_SETFL` flags, and `mmap` flags;
    - `fcntl`'s `F_GETLK`, `F_SETOWN` and `F_GETOWN`;
    - the `O_NONBLOCK` of `pipe2`, `dup3`, `inotify_init1`, `eventfd2`, `timerfd_create`,
      `signalfd4` and `accept4`;
    - socket types (`SOCK_STREAM` and `SOCK_DGRAM` swapped);
    - `SOL_SOCKET` (`0xffff`) and its options.

    `abi::result_out` gives `F_GETFL`'s flags back.
  - **Signals.** The numbers are now the ABI's (`abi::signal`, the generic module elsewhere,
    MIPS's own here, `SIGEMT` standing in for `SIGSTKFLT`), so masks, default actions and wait
    statuses follow.
  - **Signal structures.**
    - `sigset_t` is 16 bytes (`SIGSET_SIZE`): the kernel reads the first 8 and writes zeros
      after them.
    - `struct sigaction` is flags first, no restorer (`SIGACTION_FLAGS_FIRST`), with
      `SA_SIGINFO` and `SA_NOCLDWAIT` translated.
    - `stack_t` puts the size before the flags (`STACK_T_SIZE_BEFORE_FLAGS`).
    - The signal frame is n64's `rt_sigframe`: `sigcontext` with the 32 registers, the FP
      registers, `hi`/`lo`, the PC and `FCSR`; the handler gets `a0`–`a2`, `t9` and `ra`.
  - **`struct stat`.** n64's 104 bytes (`StatLayout::Mips64`: a 32-bit device, 32-bit times).
  - **Terminal `ioctl` numbers.** MIPS's.
  - **`set_thread_area`.** It sets `UserLocal` (a new want, `SET_THREAD_AREA`).
  - **The user runtime.**
    - n64 numbers, and a `syscall` stub that translates its arguments out and its errors and
      `F_GETFL` back (`mips_abi.rs`, the same tables), so EggOS's programs keep the generic
      values.
    - `_start` finds `$gp` from `t9` and the load bias from the unrelocated GOT; the
      relocation applies the `DT_REL` table of `R_MIPS_REL32`/`R_MIPS_64` and the local GOT
      entries.
    - `clone`, the terminal numbers, and per-architecture signal numbers in
      `eggos_runtime::signal`, which `kill`, init, the coreutils and eggway now use.
    - init's and eggsh's `struct sigaction` for MIPS, and the `st_mode` offset (24).
- **Part 3 (left, so MIPS64 programs beyond the basics work).**
  - The other programs' `struct sigaction` and 8-byte signal sets (coreutils, eggway, the
    runtime's own, selftest, mcp): on MIPS the kernel wants 16-byte sets, so those calls fail
    with `EINVAL`.
  - `termios` (MIPS's `c_cc` order, 23 entries and `c_lflag` bits).
  - `siginfo_t`'s `si_code` and `si_errno` swapped on MIPS.
  - `poll`'s `POLLWRNORM`/`POLLWRBAND`, and `getsockopt` values coming back (`SO_TYPE`,
    `SO_ERROR`).
  - `pipe`'s two results in `v0`/`v1`.
  - The Linux test programs past `linux_hello`, and Loongson's `liointc` for device
    interrupts.
- **Known gaps (unverified, from memory of `asm/errno.h`, `asm/signal.h`, `asm/stat.h`,
  `asm/ioctls.h`, `asm/fcntl.h`, `asm/mman.h`, `asm/socket.h` and the n64 table).** Every
  value table above; LLVM's MIPS assembler accepting the runtime's `%gp_rel`/`%got_disp`
  `_start`.

## D316 MIPS64 part 3: EggOS's own programs use the architecture's signal-set size and `struct sigaction` (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `eggos_runtime::signal` gains `SET_BYTES` (8, or MIPS's 16), `IGNORE` and
  `action(handler)`, a `struct sigaction` in the architecture's layout (handler first, or MIPS's
  flags first). Every program that sets a signal's action or mask uses them instead of its
  own 8 and `[handler, 0, 0, 0]`: init, eggsh, the coreutils, eggway, mcp, selftest and the
  runtime's `spawn`.
  - init, eggsh, the coreutils and selftest gain a MIPS `SignalAction` (flags, handler, a
    16-byte mask).
  - selftest's `SA_SIGINFO` is MIPS's 8 there, and its `SIGCHLD` comes from the runtime.
  - No program passes an old-set pointer to an 8-byte buffer, which the kernel's 16-byte
    writes on MIPS would overrun.
- **Why the rest waits.** `termios`, `siginfo_t`'s field order, `poll`'s write bits and
  `getsockopt`'s values stay generic between the kernel and EggOS's own programs, which agree
  on them. Only a foreign MIPS program would read them wrongly; translating them is part 4,
  with Loongson's `liointc` (the UART's and PCI's interrupts) and the HAL's Linux test
  programs past `linux_hello`.
- **Not yet.** Building and running.

## D317 The on-screen keyboard, slice 2: the Keyboard pane's row, the Terminal's focus, the layout menu and the touch handles (docs/ux/on-screen-keyboard-v0.5.md 1.1, 5.5, 5.6, 7; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Settings > Keyboard.** The pane gains `On-screen keyboard`, a dropdown of `Automatic`,
    `Always` and `Never` below `Switch key` (label at (16, 318), control (16, 336, 208, 28)).
    It saves `keyboard.on_screen` and applies it through `ON_SCREEN_KEYBOARD` (3 + mode),
    which completes D314's D22 twins: GUI, `settings set` and MCP's `settings_set`.
  - **The Terminal.** A tap in the console terminal's content, the server's own window, which
    sends no text focus, counts as a field of kind `terminal` (`Desktop::terminal_tapped`), so
    the keyboard shows there too.
  - **The layout key.** A long press (500 ms) or a right click opens the keyboard-layout menu
    the bar's indicator opens (`open_keyboard_layout_menu`); a tap still cycles.
  - **Touch handles** (`toolkit/src/tree/handles.rs`), in the touch form factor (`Phone`):
    - A tap in a text field shows the caret handle (a 6-row point on a 12x8 block in
      `accent`, its point at the caret's bottom), grabbed within a 44x44 square and dragged by
      the offset it was grabbed at.
    - A press resting 500 ms within 8 px selects the word under it and shows a handle at each
      end; each one drags its end. A masked field shows the caret handle and selects no word.
    - A key or a tap elsewhere hides them, and they draw only while their field has the
      focus. The long press is one more deadline of `next_deadline`, so idle costs nothing.
- **Deviations from the brief.**
  - Text areas get no handles yet: only single-line fields do.
  - Dragging a handle past the field's edge does not scroll its text further than the caret
    placement already does.
  - The handles' ends do not swap when dragged across each other: the caret and the anchor
    stay what they are, which selects backwards.
  - The layout menu opens where the indicator's opens, not as a bottom sheet over the panel.
  - The second contact (brief 5.1, ask 3) still waits for a touch path that reports more than
    one.
- **Build-pass notes.** Settings' widget `CAPACITY` grows by 2 (the label and the dropdown);
  the Keyboard pane's tests that count widgets or read positions.
- **Not yet.** Building and running.

## D318 Big-endian groundwork, step 1: device registers are little-endian whatever the CPU (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `Mmio`'s 16- and 32-bit accesses and ECAM configuration space convert with
  `from_le`/`to_le`: PCI and virtio registers are little-endian, so a big-endian CPU (SPARC64)
  reads them right. On every little-endian port the conversions are no-ops.
- **Step 2.**
  - **Virtio rings.** Every field of a split virtqueue's rings (descriptors, the available
    and used rings, their flags and indices) is written `to_le` and read `from_le`, on both
    the driver's side and the stand-in device's.
  - **ELF.** The loader takes images in the kernel's own byte order (`EI_DATA` 1 or 2 by
    `target_endian`) and reads their fields in native order.
  - **Code bytes.** `abi::code_bytes` lays instructions out in native order.
- **Next.** Virtio devices' in-memory request structures (block, net, GPU and input headers)
  where they are built as native words; then s390x (channel I/O, the DAT geometry) and
  SPARC64.
- **Not yet.** Building and running.

## D319 Settings > Network: joining a hidden Wi-Fi network (docs/ux/wifi-join-hidden-v0.5.md; M14; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The design brief (Fable, committed with this change) is built in the Wi-Fi
  section (`wifi_section.rs`):
  - **The row.** `Join another network` (`Hidden or not listed`, `Join`) is the last row on
    every page whenever the list shows. It is hidden, not disabled, while the list cannot
    show.
  - **The form.** `Join` opens an inline note, 180 tall, under the row: the lead line, a
    `Network name` field with a live byte count, a `Security` radio pair (`Open`,
    `WPA2 or WPA3`), and the passphrase note's own field, `Show`, message, `Cancel` and
    `Join` at their new places.
    - `Open` disables the passphrase.
    - The resting message follows the brief: a space at an end, else the open-network line,
      else the length rule.
    - A name of 0 or over 32 bytes, or a short passphrase, is refused in `text`, with the
      focus on the failing field.
  - **Heard nameless rows.** A heard nameless network that is open, WPA2 or WPA3 now has
    `Join`, which opens the same form under it, with the security it was heard with.
  - **Saving.** It writes `hidden=yes` (`Request::WifiJoin.hidden`) unless the last scan heard
    the name.
  - **The `Hidden` mark.** The chosen network's detail starts with `Hidden` while `wifi.conf`
    says `hidden=yes` (`Status.chosen_hidden`, read by the program; `chosen_hidden_in`).
  - **Failures.** `not-in-range` for it reads `No network here answers to this name. Check its
    spelling.`
  - **Retry.** The form opens with a not-yet-connected hidden network's name filled in.
  - **MCP.** `wifi_connect` gains `hidden` (backend ask 1), mapped to `wifi connect
    --hidden`, and names WPA3.
- **Deviations.**
  - A refused field's text is not selected (focus only).
  - Forgetting a hidden network leaves the focus where the forget left it, not on the row's
    `Join`.
  - Settings' search words for the pane are unchanged.
  - The touch-form metrics wait for the Wi-Fi section's own phone layout (brief section 5).
  - Backend asks 2 to 5 (the driver holding to the file's security, `; hidden` in
    `/proc/driver/wifi`, escaped names in `wifi connect`, counting the passphrase in bytes)
    are not done.
- **Build-pass notes.**
  - `wifi_section::WIDGETS` is 46, which raises Settings' `CAPACITY` and the installer's with it.
  - `Request::WifiJoin` has a new field, and its tests construct it.
  - The fake driver's tests gain `chosen_hidden`.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; the acceptance list of the brief's section 8.

## D320 s390x part 1: page tables of each format's own geometry, and z/Architecture's DAT format (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Per-format geometry.** The page-table code no longer assumes 512-entry tables of 9 bits
    a level. `Format` gains provided methods with the old values as defaults: `index_shift`,
    `entries`, `table_order` (the frames a table takes, as a power of two), and the
    `leaf_bytes` and `index` built from them.
    - `kernel/src/paging.rs` walks, allocates (`new_table::<F>(frames, level)`, contiguous
      frames above order 0), frees (`free_table`) and scans tables through them, and the
      device window aligns with `leaf_bytes`.
    - The free functions `paging::index`/`leaf_size` stay for the boot code of the 512-entry
      formats.
  - **`paging::s390x`.** A region-second root (53-bit addresses), region-third and segment
    tables of 2048 entries (16 KiB, order 2), and page tables of 256 entries (2 KiB in a 4 KiB
    frame).
    - Leaves are 4 KiB pages and EDAT-1 1 MiB segments (kernel-only).
    - Page entries keep three software bits in the low byte, which the hardware ignores:
      user, kept and writable.
    - No memory type: s390x memory is coherent, and I/O is not memory-mapped.
  - **Keeping programs out of the kernel half (for the HAL, part 2).** DAT has no privilege
    bit, so the HAL will:
    - run the kernel in the home space, through the process's whole root (the generic code's
      single root, kernel half shared);
    - run programs in the primary space, through a per-CPU root that holds the user half's
      root entries alone, sharing the process's lower tables. It is copied on each switch,
      and refreshed when a program's region-translation exception finds an entry the whole
      root has gained since.

    The kernel then reaches user memory directly in the home space, as on every other port.
- **Next (part 2).** The HAL on QEMU `s390-ccw-virtio`: the IPL entry and the lowcore's PSWs,
  the SCLP console, the CPU timer and clock comparator, external, program, SVC and I/O
  interrupts, problem state, the floating-point registers, SIGP for CPUs, and the spaces
  above. Then virtio-ccw (channel I/O), and s390x's Linux ABI and runtime, big-endian.
- **Not yet.** Building and running.

## D321 s390x part 2: the HAL on QEMU `s390-ccw-virtio` (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Empty entries.** `Format::empty(level)` is the entry that translates nothing: 0 for
    every format but s390x's, whose hardware takes 0 as valid and needs the invalid bit. The
    page-table code fills new tables with it, clears entries to it, and compares against it.
  - **Boot.** QEMU starts `_start` in real mode at its physical address (`_start_physical`,
    1 MiB). In real mode, `_start`:
    - zeroes `.bss`;
    - builds a region-second root, region-third tables and one segment table of 1 MiB leaves
      mapping the first 2 GiB, at the direct map (`1 << 52`) and at the image's virtual
      address (`0x001f_ffff_8000_0000` above its physical one);
    - sets CR0 (EDAT-1, and the clock comparator's, emergency signals' and service signal's
      subclasses);
    - loads CR1 and CR13;
    - fills the lowcore's new PSWs and the HAL's continuation PSWs;

    then it enters the kernel in the home space.
  - **Interruptions** (`exception.rs`).
    - Every class's new PSW enters a real-mode stub. It saves the registers and the old PSW in
      the lowcore (`0x200`/`0x280`, the class, code and TEID after them), then either:
      - loads the kernel continuation PSW, which copies them to a frame on the kernel stack,
        calls `s390x_exception` and returns through the real-mode `s390x_kernel_return_real`;
      - or, from problem state, copies them into the `UserContext` (its real address in the
        lowcore) and loads the PSW that returns from `run_user`.
    - Programs are entered through real mode too (`s390x_to_user_real`: access registers,
      then `lmg`, then `lpswe`).
    - A wait PSW's wait bit and interruption masks are cleared in the old PSW, so the kernel
      goes on with interruptions off.
  - **Spaces (D320's design).** The kernel runs in the home space through the process's whole
    root (CR13). Programs run in the primary space through a per-CPU program root (CR1)
    holding the user half's root entries. It is copied on each switch, purging the TLB, and
    refreshed when a program's region-translation exception finds an entry the whole root
    gained since.
  - **Console and memory.** The SCLP: write and read event data for the ASCII console, `READ
    SCP INFO` for the RAM's size. `servc` completes in QEMU before it returns, so the response
    code is polled.
  - **Timer and wake-ups.** The TOD clock (4.096 GHz) and the clock comparator; wake-ups are
    SIGP emergency signals.
  - **Other pieces.**
    - Lazy FP through CR0's AFP control: `f0`, `f2`, `f4` and `f6` stay usable without it, so
      the kernel's load of a fresh state before a program without FP state is what keeps them
      from leaking.
    - The per-CPU block's address is in the lowcore, which the prefix makes each CPU's own.
    - Exit and halt stop the CPU with `sigp stop` (QEMU ends when every CPU is stopped).
    - The thread switch keeps r6–r14 below the ABI's 160-byte save area.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time; written from memory of the Principles of Operation
  and QEMU's s390x machine, unverified).**
  - The lowcore offsets and the stubs' real-mode reach.
  - The SCLP SCCB layouts and `READ SCP INFO`'s fields.
  - Where QEMU leaves the command line for an ELF kernel (`0x10480` assumed).
  - The PSW mask bits and the entries' bit values.
  - Secondary CPUs are not started (`start_cpu` refuses).
  - `restart` stops instead of re-IPLing.
  - The breakpoint is delivered without a trap.
  - The program-check PC is the old PSW's (after the instruction for suppressing
    exceptions).
  - The user test programs past the basic ones exit with 1.
- **Next (part 3).** The channel subsystem and virtio-ccw (block, network, GPU, input,
  console). Then s390x's Linux ABI (its own table, big-endian structures, `struct stat`) and
  the user runtime, and secondary CPUs through SIGP set-prefix and restart.
- **Not yet.** Building and running; xtask and CI entries (s390x has a tier-2 Linux target,
  `s390x-unknown-linux-gnu`, as ppc64le's).

## D322 s390x part 3a: the channel subsystem and virtio-ccw (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **The channel subsystem in the drivers crate** (`drivers/src/channel.rs`): the
    subchannel identification word, the SCHIB, ORB, IRB and SCSW, and format-1 CCWs, all
    built big-endian with explicit byte orders, so they are tested on little-endian hosts.
    - The `ChannelSubsystem` trait carries the I/O instructions (`stsch`, `msch`, `ssch`,
      `tsch`) and virtio-ccw's notification hypercall (`DIAGNOSE 0x500`, function 3). The
      HAL implements it with inline assembly (`hal/src/arch/s390x/channel.rs`) and hands it
      out through `Platform::channel_subsystem`, `None` on every other architecture.
    - `ChannelBuffer` holds one command and its data in one DMA block below 2 GiB (a
      format-1 CCW's data address has 31 bits), and runs single-command programs to their end.
      `enable` turns a subchannel on, and `sense_id` reads its control unit.
  - **Polled, in interruption subclass 3.** Subchannels are enabled in ISC 3 and control
    register 6 leaves every subclass disabled, so a program's status waits for
    `TEST SUBCHANNEL`, which the buffer polls. This matches the polled virtio core (D111).
    Interruptions through virtio-ccw's indicators come later; until then
    `connect_interrupt` refuses virtio-ccw devices, and their drivers poll.
  - **The bus** (`kernel/src/devices/channel_bus.rs`). Discovery walks subchannel set 0 from
    subchannel 0 and stops at the first one that is not there, since QEMU numbers them without
    gaps. Each I/O subchannel with a device is enabled and asked `SENSE ID`, and becomes an
    `Identity::Channel` node (subchannel, device number, control unit type and model).
    `Match::ControlUnit` matches it, and `/proc/driver/devices` lists it on the `ccw` bus.
  - **virtio-ccw** (`drivers/src/virtio/ccw.rs`, the `virtio-ccw` bus driver): control unit
    `0x3832`, whose model is the virtio device type.
    - It sets revision 1, and refuses a device that turns it down as legacy.
    - It reads and writes the status and the 64 feature bits as two little-endian words.
    - It reads the queue sizes, sets the queues up with `SET_VQ`'s revision-1 block (three
      big-endian addresses), and reads the configuration from offset 0 up to the field.
      Writes rewrite that prefix.
    - Every virtio driver (block, network, console, input, GPU, entropy) runs on it through
      `AnyTransport::Ccw` unchanged.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).**
  - The SCHIB field offsets, the ORB's bits and QEMU's reading of the `READ_FEAT` index were
    written from memory of the Principles of Operation and virtio 1.2, 4.3.
  - A machine with more than 2 GiB can give the channel buffers memory above 2 GiB. Such
    devices are refused until the DMA allocator can ask for low memory.
  - A gap in the subchannel numbers ends discovery early.
- **Next (part 3b and 3c).** s390x's Linux ABI and user runtime; then secondary CPUs through
  SIGP, and the xtask, toolchain and CI entries.

## D323 s390x part 3b: its Linux ABI and the user runtime (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **`kernel/src/linux/abi/s390x.rs`.**
    - **System calls.** s390x's own table, the 64-bit entries, with the legacy calls and
      `renameat`. `time` and `accept` exist only for 31-bit programs or through
      `socketcall`, so their names get numbers past `LAST`, which answer `ENOSYS`.
    - **Structures.** The generic terminal numbers, `open` flags and signal numbers.
      `struct sigaction` has `sa_restorer`. `struct stat` is a new `StatLayout::S390x`: 144
      bytes, x86_64's first fields, then the three times before `st_blksize` and
      `st_blocks`.
    - **Calls that differ.**
      - `mmap` takes one pointer to its six arguments (Linux's `old_mmap`):
        `MMAP_ARGUMENTS_IN_MEMORY`, read in `memory_call`.
      - `clone` takes the stack before the flags (`CLONE_BACKWARDS2`): `CLONE_STACK_FIRST`,
        read in `clone`'s `Arguments::of`.

      Both are `false` on every other architecture (defaults in `abi/mod.rs`), so their
      paths fold away there.
    - **Signal frames.** `rt_sigframe`: the 160-byte save area with the back chain, the
      `svc 173` halfword, `siginfo_t`, then the `ucontext`. That holds `_sigregs` (PSW, `r0`
      to `r15`, `a0` to `a15`, the FP control word and `f0` to `f15`) and `uc_sigmask`, then
      a zero vector extension. Handlers get `r2` the signal, `r3` the info, `r4` the context,
      `r14` the restorer (the kernel's `svc 173` trampoline without `SA_RESTORER`) and `r15`
      the frame.
    - **ELF machine** 22 (`EM_S390`).
  - **The user runtime.**
    - `svc 0` with the number in `r1` and the arguments in `r2` to `r7`. `call` passes
      `mmap`'s six arguments in a block on its stack and swaps `clone`'s first two, so its
      callers stay the same on every architecture.
    - `_start` hands `start` the stack and `_DYNAMIC`, with a 160-byte save area and a zero
      back chain. `R_390_RELATIVE` is 12.
    - `clone_onto_stack` keeps the child's save area.
    - The self-test reads and sets the thread pointer in `a0:a1`. The signal actions and the
      `stat` mode offset of init, eggsh, coreutils and the self-test take s390x's.
  - **Fix on the way.** The PowerPC runtime's `readlinkat`, `symlinkat`, `linkat`, `openat2`,
    `fchmodat`, `fchmodat2`, `statfs`, `fstatfs`, `lseek` and `faccessat` carried MIPS's
    numbers. They now carry PowerPC's.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).**
  - Every syscall number and frame offset is written from memory of Linux's s390x headers
    and table.
  - The kernel's own self-tests that make `mmap` calls pass registers. On s390x they need
    the block.
  - The vector registers are not saved: programs get no vector facility (CR0's AFP only).
- **Next (part 3c).** Secondary CPUs through SIGP (set prefix, initial CPU reset, restart),
  and the xtask, toolchain and CI entries.

## D324 s390x part 3c: secondary CPUs and the build entries (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Rust's platform-support tiers)

- **Decision.**
  - **Secondary CPUs** (`hal/src/arch/s390x/smp.rs`).
    - `cpus` lists the boot CPU and every address up to 16 that answers `SIGP SENSE`.
    - **Preparing a CPU.** `start_cpu` gives the CPU an 8 KiB lowcore of its own (its prefix
      area, one of 16 in `.bss`). The lowcore gets:
      - a copy of the boot CPU's new PSWs and continuation PSWs (`lowcore::COPIED`);
      - a restart PSW into `s390x_secondary_real`;
      - in `lowcore::CPU_START`, the absolute address of a start block holding CR0 (with
        the AFP control off), the root's ASCE, the stack and the kernel entry PSW.
    - **Starting it.** Then `SIGP` does an initial CPU reset, sets the prefix and restarts
      the CPU.
    - **On the new CPU.** In real mode it loads CR0, CR1 and CR13 from the block, takes the
      stack and enters the kernel in the home space. There `secondary_started` sets the home
      and program roots, purges the TLB, disarms the clock comparator and calls the entry.
  - **Build entries: s390x joins MIPS64 under D297's nightly rule.**
    - The kernel builds on the pinned stable toolchain for `s390x-unknown-linux-gnu` (tier 2,
      added to `rust-toolchain.toml`), with the vector facility off and soft float.
    - Rust has no tier-2 user target for s390x: `s390x-unknown-linux-musl` is tier 3. So
      the user programs need a nightly toolchain's `build-std`.
    - **What changes in xtask.** s390x is a `NIGHTLY_ARCHES` entry (QEMU `s390-ccw-virtio`,
      `-cpu max`, the `-ccw` virtio devices). `nightly_build_std` now goes by a list of
      tier-3 targets, so s390x's kernel still builds on stable.
    - **What waits for the owner.** As for MIPS64 (D297 revised), the owner decides at
      test-and-fix time whether to allow nightly for it. Until then s390x stays out of CI
      and the release matrix; it is built with `--arch s390x` only.
    - This replaces D321's plan of a CI entry like ppc64le's: that needed a tier-2 user
      target, which s390x does not have.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).**
  - The SIGP orders' codes, the prefix's 2 GiB limit, and whether QEMU's restarted CPU
    loads the restart PSW from its new prefix area were written from memory.
  - Whether `+soft-float` is a valid s390x target feature on the pinned toolchain.
- **M9 s390x: written.** Parts 1 to 3c (D320 to D324) are the whole port. What is left is
  building it, running it, and interrupts for the channel subsystem.

## D325 MIPS64 part 4: Loongson's `liointc`, and the structures foreign MIPS programs read (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **`liointc`** (`hal/src/arch/mips64/liointc.rs`). QEMU `loongson3-virt`'s legacy I/O
    interrupt controller at `0x3ff01400`: 32 level-triggered inputs, the UART on input 0.
    - A routed input's route byte names the boot core and `IP2`, and its enable bit is set.
      The interrupt entry reads the core's pending register when `Cause.IP2` is set and
      hands each input to the kernel: the console's input, or the routed device's line.
    - An input nobody asked for is turned off.
    - `enable_console_input` now works, and `route_device_interrupt` takes a `liointc`
      specifier (its input).
    - `message_interrupt` stays refused: the board's PCI Express has no MSI controller, so
      its devices need INTx (inputs 2 to 5), which the kernel's PCI layer does not route yet
      (M8's INTx item).
  - **What foreign MIPS programs read** (D316 left these generic, which EggOS's own programs
    agree on). New hooks in `abi/mod.rs` are no-ops on every other architecture.
    - `reorder_siginfo`: MIPS's `siginfo_t` has `si_code` before `si_errno`. It is
      applied to every `siginfo_t` the kernel writes (`Info::to_bytes`, `fault_info`) and
      reads (`rt_sigqueueinfo`).
    - `poll_events_in` and `poll_events_out`: MIPS's `POLLWRNORM` is `POLLOUT` and its
      `POLLWRBAND` 0x100; the generic ones are 0x100 and 0x200.
    - `socket_option_out`: `SO_TYPE` answers MIPS's socket types and `SO_ERROR` MIPS's
      error numbers. The HAL's `mips_errno` is now public for it.
    - `termios::to_program` and `from_program`: MIPS's `struct termios` has 23 control
      characters in its own order (`VMIN` 4, `VEOF` 16, `VEOL` 17, `VEOL2` 6), and
      `IEXTEN`, `TOSTOP` and `FLUSHO` at its own bits. `TCGETS`, `TCGETS2` and `TCSETS*`
      go through them.
- **Moved.** The HAL's MIPS64 Linux test programs past `linux_hello` move to one later batch,
  with s390x's (D321 left those exiting with 1). Both are hand-written assembly translations
  of the PowerPC programs, and they test rather than add what users get.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).** `liointc`'s register offsets and route-byte
  format, and MIPS's `termbits.h` values, are from memory of QEMU's and Linux's sources.

## D326 SPARC64 part 1: the HAL on QEMU `sun4u` (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Machine and boot.** QEMU `sun4u` (UltraSPARC IIi, one CPU) with OpenBIOS.
    - `_start` runs at the image's physical address, 4 MiB, on OpenBIOS's identity mapping.
      It locks two 4 MiB TLB entries (instruction and data) that map the image at the top
      2 GiB (`KERNEL_VIRTUAL_OFFSET`), and jumps there.
    - `sparc64_boot` asks Open Firmware's client interface for `/memory`'s `available`
      ranges, the CPU node's `clock-frequency` and `/chosen`'s `bootargs` (`firmware.rs`).
    - Then the HAL takes the traps over (`%tba`, its window registers, empty roots) and enters
      `kernel_main`.
    - The HAL writes a device tree (memory, the CPU, the EBus 16550 at `0x1fe020003f8`),
      as for MIPS64.
  - **Console.** The 16550 through physical loads and stores (`ASI_PHYS_BYPASS_EC_E`), which
    need no mapping.
  - **Translation** (`paging/sparc64.rs`, `exception.rs`).
    - The MMU's TLBs are loaded by software, on the MMU globals (`%g6` the program's root,
      `%g7` the kernel's).
    - The direct map (2 TiB from `0xffff_f800_0000_0000`, the 44-bit high half) gets 4 MiB
      entries computed from the address. The device window is walked through the kernel's
      root.
    - Leaves are 4 KiB in the TTE's own layout, with software bits for user, executable and
      kept. The MMU's smallest page is 8 KiB, so an aligned pair of 4 KiB leaves that are both
      present, physically contiguous and alike becomes one 8 KiB entry. Any other miss is a
      fault.
    - Kernel pages are global and privileged. Programs get a fresh context (1 to 8191) at
      every switch, with the TLB flushed when the contexts wrap.
  - **Traps.** A 32 KiB table with the kernel's and programs' spill, fill and clean-window
    handlers (`%wstate` 0 and 1, programs' through `ASI_AS_IF_USER_PRIMARY`) and the TLB
    misses, at both trap levels.
    - **From the kernel** (where it opens interrupts, or a fault): the trap saves the state on
      a new kernel window, drops to TL 0 and calls `sparc64_kernel_exception`. It returns with
      `retry`, or `done` after a trap instruction.
    - **From a program:** the trap flushes the program's windows to its stack, saves its
      current window, globals, `%pc`, `%npc`, `TSTATE` and `%y` into the context, and returns
      from `sparc64_enter_user` on the kernel stack.
    - System calls are `ta 0x6d`. Errors return positive with the carry bits set, as SPARC's
      Linux does, and `%g7` is the thread pointer.
  - **Other pieces.**
    - The timer is `%tick` and `TICK_COMPARE` (level 14).
    - Lazy FP through `%fprs.FEF`: `fp_disabled` is reported as an illegal instruction (D54).
    - The thread switch flushes the windows and keeps `%sp` and `%i7`. A new thread's two
      initial frames take 320 bytes, so `INITIAL_FRAME_MAX` grows to 320.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time; written from memory of the UltraSPARC IIi manual,
  QEMU's board and OpenBIOS, unverified).**
  - **4 KiB pages on an MMU with 8 KiB pages.** User memory works only where the kernel maps
    4 KiB pages in aligned, contiguous pairs. The kernel does not do that yet; that is part 3.
    Until then, a miss on half a pair loops between the fault and the stale-entry retry.
  - Whether OpenBIOS enters an ELF image at its physical address with an identity mapping.
  - The TTE bit positions and the MMU register addresses.
  - LLVM's acceptance of `%hh`/`%hm` in `sethi`, and of `clobber_abi("C")` on SPARC64.
  - A fault while spilling or filling a program's window, at trap level 2, stops the CPU.
  - OpenBIOS's own locked entries stay in the TLB.
  - No device interrupts (the PCI bridge's interrupt mapping), no PCI bus, so no virtio
    devices. Console input is polled.
  - The Linux test programs past `linux_hello`, and `checks` and `fp_registers`, exit with 1.
  - The kernel's `compile_error!` for an architecture without a Linux ABI still fires: that
    ABI is part 2.
- **Next.** Part 2: SPARC64's Linux ABI (its table, its error numbers, which differ from 35
  on, its `stat`, signal frames with the register windows) and the user runtime, with the
  build entries. Part 3: the kernel's user memory in 8 KiB granules where the format asks for
  it.

## D327 SPARC64 part 2: its Linux ABI, the user runtime and the build entries (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Rust's platform-support tiers)

- **Decision.**
  - **`kernel/src/linux/abi/sparc64.rs`.**
    - **System calls.** SPARC64's table (the 64-bit entries) with the legacy calls and
      `renameat`; `time`, 32-bit only, gets a number past `LAST`.
    - **Values that differ, as on MIPS (D315).** SPARC's values differ from the generic ones
      in:
      - the signal numbers (SunOS's: `SIGUSR1` 30, `SIGCHLD` 20, `SIGSTOP` 17);
      - `sa_flags`;
      - `open`'s flags, `mmap`'s `MAP_NORESERVE`, `MAP_LOCKED` and `MAP_GROWSDOWN`, and
        `fcntl`'s lock and owner commands;
      - `O_NONBLOCK` and `O_CLOEXEC` wherever they are taken;
      - `SOL_SOCKET` (0xffff) and its options;
      - `poll`'s write bits (as MIPS's);
      - `SO_ERROR`'s error number;
      - `struct termios`: 17 control characters, with `VMIN`/`VTIME` sharing `VEOF`/`VEOL`'s
        places by `ICANON`, and `FLUSHO` at its own bit;
      - its `ioctl` numbers (PowerPC's `_IOC`);
      - the error numbers from 35 on. The HAL's `sparc_errno` gives them, positive with the
        carry set.

      `arguments_in` and `result_out` translate at the boundary, and the kernel stays
      generic. `rt_sigaction`'s fourth argument, a restorer, gives way to the set size.
      Handlers return through the kernel's trampoline (`mov 101, %g1; ta 0x6d`), what
      glibc's restorer does too.
    - **Shared helpers.** MIPS's and SPARC's flag translation now share
      `abi/translate.rs` (`flags_to_generic`, `flags_to_architecture`, `value_to_generic`,
      `value_to_architecture`).
    - **Structures.** `struct stat` is `StatLayout::Sparc64`: 104 bytes, a 32-bit `st_dev`
      and `st_rdev`, a 16-bit `st_nlink`, whole-second times. ELF machine 43
      (`EM_SPARCV9`).
    - **Signal frames.** `rt_signal_frame`: the handler's window save area, `siginfo_t`,
      `pt_regs` (globals, outs, `TSTATE`, `%pc`, `%npc`, `%y`, the magic word),
      `fpu_save`, `stack_t` and the mask, then the FP state.
      - The handler gets `%o0` the signal, `%o1` and `%o2` the `siginfo_t`, `%o7` the
        restorer less 8, and `%sp` the frame less the bias.
      - The interrupted window's locals and ins go to its stack's save area, where a spill
        would put them, and are read back from there on `rt_sigreturn`.
  - **The HAL hides the stack bias.** `UserContext`'s stack pointer is the real address; `%o6`
    holds it less 2047.
  - **The user runtime.**
    - `ta 0x6d` with `%g1`, the carry giving the error.
    - `sparc_abi` translates the flags, options and errors as `mips_abi` does.
    - `_start` hands `start` `argc`'s address (above the 128-byte save area) and `_DYNAMIC`.
      `R_SPARC_RELATIVE` is 22.
    - `clone_onto_stack` keeps the 192-byte frame.
    - The signal numbers, `SA_SIGINFO` 0x200, `%g7` as the self-test's thread pointer, and
      init's, eggsh's and the coreutils' signal actions.
  - **Build entries.** Rust has two tier-2 targets for this, so no nightly is needed.
    - The kernel builds for `sparcv9-sun-solaris` (target arch `sparc64`, `no_std` with
      `rust-lld`, the medium code model, soft float, `eggos_kernel`).
    - The user programs build for `sparc64-unknown-linux-gnu` (`eggos_user`, static PIE).
    - This corrects D297, which counted SPARC64 as tier 3 only. It stays out of `all`, CI and
      the release matrix, with MIPS64 and s390x, until the owner's call at test time:
      `NIGHTLY_ARCHES` becomes `NAMED_ONLY_ARCHES`, and only `TIER_3_TARGETS` take
      nightly's `build-std`.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).**
  - The table, the constants and the frame layout are written from memory of Linux's SPARC
    headers.
  - A Linux `clone` child gets `%o1` 1 and the parent `%o1` 0. The kernel returns the
    generic 0 and pid only, which EggOS's runtime reads but glibc does not.
  - A program's `clone` stack is taken as a real address, not biased.
- **Next (part 3).** The kernel's user memory in 8 KiB granules, so that every program page
  has its pair (D326).

## D328 SPARC64 part 3: a program's pages in 8 KiB pairs (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **The problem (D326).** The UltraSPARC's smallest page is 8 KiB, and the kernel's frames
  and pages are 4 KiB. The TLB loads map an aligned pair of 4 KiB pages only when both are
  present, alike and in one physically contiguous, 8 KiB-aligned block.
- **Decision.**
  - **Pairs in the format.** `Format::PAIRED_PAGES` (default `false`; `true` for SPARC64)
    says the MMU maps a program's pages in pairs. The rest of the kernel keeps its 4 KiB
    pages; only the page-fault path knows about pairs.
  - **Resolving a fault.** With pairs, `Process::resolve_page_fault` takes the fault as one on
    the pair. It resolves each page as before (demand paging, files, copy on write), and
    succeeds when either could be resolved. Then `join_pair` gives the two pages one block:
    - when both are mapped alike and their frames are not already a block, it allocates an
      aligned 8 KiB block (order 1, the user's reserve applied);
    - copies both pages into it and maps it;
    - lets the old frames go as copy on write does (freed, or released from their sharers).

    The pair's translations are dropped, and the retried access finds a pair the TLB loads
    can map.
  - **Nothing changes on other architectures.** The new path is behind a constant that is
    `false` everywhere else, out of line and cold.
- **Known gaps.**
  - A page of a `MAP_SHARED` mapping that another process or the page cache shares becomes
    a private copy when it is paired. Writes to it are then not seen by the others: shared
    writable mappings are not coherent on SPARC64 until frames are allocated in pairs from
    the start.
  - A pair whose pages differ in protection, or that is half outside any mapping, cannot be
    mapped, and an access to it faults again. So SPARC64 tells programs its pages are 8 KiB
    (`AT_PAGESZ`, `abi::REPORTED_PAGE_SIZE`), as SPARC64's Linux does, and programs that
    align their mappings to it never split a pair. The kernel itself still takes 4 KiB
    `mmap` and `mprotect` ranges there.

## D329 The on-screen keyboard, slice 3: two-finger typing and the touch handles in text areas (docs/ux/on-screen-keyboard-v0.5.md; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Two-finger typing.**
    - **Input layer.** It follows multi-touch slot 1, the second finger: its positions and
      its tracking id (down at an id, lifted at -1). It sends `InputEvent::SecondTouch { x,
      y, down }` when that finger goes down or lifts, at the screen position scaled as the
      first finger's.
    - **Desktop** (`Desktop::second_touch`). The second finger going down on the panel
      commits the key the first finger holds, as its lift would, and holds the key under the
      second finger.
      - So `Shift` held and a letter tapped types a capital, and fast typists' overlapping
        taps are not lost.
      - Lifting types the held key: a character key wherever on the panel, a function key
        only in its own zone, as a lift by the first finger does.
      - Elsewhere the second finger does nothing (gestures come later).
    - The first finger's own release then finds nothing held and types nothing twice.
  - **Handles in text areas** (`toolkit/src/tree/handles.rs`). A tap that places the caret
    in a text area (one click, no Shift) shows the caret handle under it, on its line. A
    press resting 500 ms selects the word under it, with the same word rule as a double
    click (`text_areas::word_around`, now shared), and shows both handles. A drag moves an
    end across lines too: handles now keep the grab's vertical offset as well.
- **Not yet.** The second finger's key is not drawn pressed. The orientation of the screen
  (`display.rotation`) is the next slice.

## D330 The screen turns: `display.rotation` (docs/ux/adaptive-shell-v0.5.md 1.4 and 2.10; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **The display turns the picture** (`kernel/src/display.rs`).
    - `Rotation`: upright, a quarter, a half, three quarters, clockwise.
    - When the display turns, the desktop draws upright into the display's own buffer, at
      the device's size with width and height swapped for a quarter turn. `flush_turned`
      copies each damaged rectangle onto the device, turned, at the scale in force, and
      flushes the turned rectangles.
    - The pointer's position on the device is turned too.
    - The scale and the turn share one buffer (`reallocate_logical`), given only when either
      changes the picture.
  - **Input follows** (`kernel/src/input.rs`). An absolute device's axes are the device's, so
    the first and second fingers are scaled to the device's size and turned back into the
    upright picture. A mouse's movement is turned back as well. The rotation sits in an
    atomic the input layer reads without the display's lock.
  - **The setting** `display.rotation`: `auto` (the default: an orientation sensor, or
    upright without one, as no driver reports orientation yet), `0`, `90`, `180`, `270`
    (`eggos_settings_file::DISPLAY_ROTATIONS`).
    - **At boot.** The kernel applies it before the desktop starts.
    - **Set later.** The window server's new `SET_ROTATION` request (50, one word) turns the
      screen at once and resizes the desktop to the new size. The settings program sends it
      after saving, as for `keyboard.on_screen`.
    - **Three front-ends (D22).** `settings set display.rotation 90` (CLI), `settings_set`
      (MCP), and the phone shade's `Rotation` tile (GUI), which switches between `auto` and
      the rotation in force (`Automatic`/`Locked`), as the design says.
- **Not yet.**
  - **Sensors.** No orientation sensor driver, so `auto` stays upright.
  - **The pointer sprite.** The pointer's sprite does not turn.
  - **Holding an orientation.** An app cannot hold the screen in one orientation (the
    design leaves that for later).
  - **The desktop's Display pane.** It has no rotation row; the design gives the shade
    tile only.
  - **Build-pass notes.** Settings' `Key::ALL` is 39. Protocol request 50 is taken.

## D332 AMD's Speculative Return Stack Overflow (SRSO): a prediction barrier on every entry from user mode (code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from AMD's SRSO whitepaper and Linux's `srso=ibpb` mode)

- **Decision.** On AMD Zen 1 to 4 (families 0x17 and 0x19) without `SRSO_NO` (CPUID
  0x80000021 EAX bit 29), a program can train the return predictions the kernel's `ret`s use.
  Every entry from user mode (exceptions, interrupts and `syscall`, all through
  `user_exception_save`) then writes `IA32_PRED_CMD.IBPB`, which flushes them:
  - always on Zen 1 and 2;
  - on Zen 3 and 4 only with `IBPB_BRTYPE` (CPUID 0x80000008 EBX bit 28), the microcode that
    makes IBPB flush return predictions too.

  Like `IBRS_ON_ENTRY` (D267), it is one flag the entry code reads (`IBPB_ON_ENTRY`), set once
  at start-up (`set_up_return_predictions`), and nothing on other CPUs.
- **Why IBPB and not "safe RET".** Linux's default rewrites every `ret` into a return thunk.
  That needs the compiler's `-Zfunction-return=thunk-extern`, which the pinned stable toolchain
  does not have. IBPB on entry is Linux's `srso=ibpb`: costlier per entry, but complete without
  compiler support.
- **Left.** Zen 3 and 4 without the `IBPB_BRTYPE` microcode stay exposed, as under Linux's
  `ibpb` mode, with no other option on stable Rust. KPTI is the one item still at the end of
  the queue (D289).
- **Cost.** One `wrmsr` per entry on affected AMD CPUs, measured by the weekly performance pass
  (D122).

## D333 Settings > Display gains a Rotation row (docs/ux/display-rotation-v0.5.md by Claude Fable; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, design by Fable)

- **Decision.** The desktop's GUI front-end of `display.rotation` (D330; D22's third face beside

    `Pointer` and `Layout` move down 80. The Display pane is 428 tall
