## D334 Windows menus: `MFT_RADIOCHECK` and `CheckMenuRadioItem` (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the Win32 documentation of `MENUITEMINFO` and `CheckMenuRadioItem`)

- **Decision.**
  - **The dot.** A menu item with `MFT_RADIOCHECK` (0x200, kept with its flags as given to
    `AppendMenuW`) that is checked shows a dot where a checked item shows its tick. It is the
    radio button's 6 px dot (`controls::button::dot`) in the item's text colour, at the tick's
    place. `MenuLabel` gains `radio` for it.
  - **`CheckMenuRadioItem(menu, first, last, check, flags)`** (now exported by user32). Of the
    items `first` to `last` (commands, or positions with `MF_BYPOSITION`), it checks `check`
    with `MFT_RADIOCHECK` and unchecks the others.
    - Items of the range that do not exist are skipped.
    - It answers `FALSE` with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` when `check` is outside the range or
      not in the menu.
    - Unlike Windows, it does not take the radio flag off the others: they are unchecked, so
      they show nothing.
- **Left of part 10's rest:** scroll bars on windows, multi-line edits, editable combo boxes,
  submenus, menu keys, menus from templates, word selection.

## D335 Windows menus: menu keys (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' menu keyboard behaviour)

- **Decision.** A Windows program's menu bar answers the keyboard as on Windows:
  - **With no drop-down open**, Alt and a letter or digit (`WM_SYSKEYDOWN`) that is a bar
    entry's mnemonic (`&File`'s `F`, a doubled `&&` being no mnemonic) opens that entry's
    drop-down, or sends its command when the entry has no drop-down. Keys that are no
    mnemonic stay the program's.
  - **With a bar drop-down open:**
    - Down and Up move the highlight over the items that can be chosen (enabled, not
      separators, not submenus), wrapping.
    - Right and Left close it and open the next or previous bar entry, wrapping.
    - Enter chooses the highlighted item.
    - An item's mnemonic chooses it, with or without Alt.
    - Escape closes it, as before.
  - Context menus keep their keys (Escape and Enter).
- **Left of part 10's rest:**
  - Alt alone and F10 to select the bar, and the underlines shown only after Alt (they are
    always drawn).
  - Submenus.
  - Menus from templates.
  - Scroll bars on windows, multi-line edits, editable combo boxes and word selection.

## D336 Windows menus from templates: `LoadMenuW` (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the documented `MENUITEMTEMPLATEHEADER` and `MENUITEMTEMPLATE` layouts)

- **Decision.** `LoadMenuW(module, name)` finds the program's `RT_MENU` resource (type 4) and
  builds the menu its standard template describes, through the same `CreatePopupMenu` and
  `AppendMenuW` work a program would do:
  - **The template.** A header of two words: version 0, and the offset of the items after it.
    Then the items, each a flags word, a command word unless it opens a drop-down
    (`MF_POPUP`), and a NUL-terminated UTF-16 label (cut at 127 units).
  - **Nesting.** A drop-down's items follow it. `MF_END` (0x80) marks each level's last item,
    and the level closes; it is not kept in the item's flags. Up to 8 levels nest.
  - **What it answers.** The menu handle, ready for `SetMenu` or the window class.
    `ERROR_RESOURCE_NAME_NOT_FOUND` when there is no such resource.
    `ERROR_RESOURCE_DATA_NOT_FOUND` for a malformed template, or an extended (`MENUEX`,
    version 1) one, which is not read yet.
- **Not yet.** Extended templates (`MENUEX`, `LoadMenuIndirectW`), and submenus inside a
  drop-down: they load, and show grayed as before.

## D337 Windows menus: submenus in the bar's drop-downs (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' cascading menu behaviour)

- **Decision.** An item of a bar drop-down that opens a menu (`MF_POPUP`, from `AppendMenuW`
  or a template, D336) is no longer grayed. It shows an arrow at its right and opens its
  submenu:
  - **Where.** Beside the drop-down: at its right edge, overlapping by 2, or flipped to its
    left when that would leave the window. The submenu's first item is level with the parent
    item (`layout::cascade_rect`).
  - **With the pointer.** Hovering opens it. Hovering in it highlights its items, and
    releasing on one sends that item's command. Hovering another drop-down item closes it.
    Releasing on the parent item sends nothing.
  - **With the keys.** Right or Enter on the highlighted parent opens it with its first item
    that can be chosen highlighted. In it, Up and Down move and Enter or a mnemonic chooses.
    Left or Escape close it alone.
  - `Tracking` gains `cascade: Option<Cascade>`. Closing the drop-down also leaves the
    submenu's area for the program to repaint.
- **Limits.** One level: a submenu's own submenu items stay grayed. Context menus
  (`TrackPopupMenuEx`) open no submenus yet.

## D338 Windows menus: F10 opens the menu bar (batch part 10's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** F10 (`WM_SYSKEYDOWN` `VK_F10`) in a window with a menu bar and no drop-down
  open opens the first enabled bar entry that has a drop-down. From there, D335's keys move
  (arrows, Enter, mnemonics, Escape). A window without a menu bar leaves F10 to the program.
- **Not yet.** Alt pressed and released alone, which on Windows selects the bar without
  opening it, and mnemonic underlines shown only once Alt is pressed (they are always drawn).

## D339 Windows menus: Alt pressed and released alone opens the menu bar (batch part 10's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** In a window with a menu bar and no drop-down open:
  - Alt going down (`WM_SYSKEYDOWN` `VK_MENU`) is remembered for that window (`Gui::alt_alone`),
    and still reaches the program.
  - Any other key or a button press in between forgets it, so Alt+letter (D335) and Alt+F4
    stay what they were.
  - Alt coming back up alone opens the first enabled bar entry with a drop-down, as F10 does
    (D338), and D335's keys go on from there.
- **Deviation.** Windows selects the bar without opening a drop-down, and opens one only on
  Down or Enter. Here the drop-down opens at once, since the bar has no selected-but-closed
  look. The mnemonic underlines stay always drawn.

## D340 Windows controls: editable combo boxes (`CBS_DROPDOWN`) (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' combo box behaviour; the look reuses the design's edit field and drop-down button, docs/ux/windows-controls-v0.3.md)

- **Decision.** A `COMBOBOX` with `CBS_DROPDOWN` is made with an edit field
  (`ComboBox::editable`, `edit: Some(Edit)`).
  - **The closed box.** It is the edit field, painted as an `EDIT` (caret and selection when
    focused), beside the drop-down button with the chevron.
  - **The pointer.** A click in the field places the caret, closing the list if it is open. A
    click on the button opens or closes the list.
  - **Typing.** Characters, Backspace, Delete and the caret keys go to the field. Up, Down
    and the page keys move the selection, and F4 or Alt+Up/Down toggle the list. Each change
    of text sends `CBN_EDITUPDATE` then `CBN_EDITCHANGE`.
  - **Choosing.** Choosing a row in the list, or moving the selection with the keys, puts the
    item's text in the field, selected whole.
  - **Messages.** `WM_SETTEXT` sets the field, and `WM_GETTEXT` and `WM_GETTEXTLENGTH` read it.
    `CB_SETEDITSEL` sets its selection.
  - Drop-down lists (`CBS_DROPDOWNLIST`) are unchanged.
- **Not yet.**
  - `CBS_SIMPLE`'s always-shown list.
  - `CB_GETEDITSEL` and `CB_LIMITTEXT`.
  - Auto-completing the field from the list.
  - Selecting the item that matches typed text when the list opens.

## D341 Windows controls: multi-line edits (`ES_MULTILINE`) (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' edit control behaviour; the look is the design's edit field, docs/ux/windows-controls-v0.3.md, with one text row per line)

- **Decision.** An `EDIT` with `ES_MULTILINE` keeps lines in the same model (`Edit::multiline`),
  broken at `\r\n` as Windows stores them (a lone `\n` breaks a line too). The caret never stands
  between the `\r` and the `\n`: moves, deletes and `EM_SETSEL` step over the pair.
  - **Typing.** Enter (`\r`) and Ctrl+Enter (`\n`) insert `\r\n`, Tab a tab. In a dialog, Enter
    goes to the edit only with `ES_WANTRETURN` (otherwise it is the default button) and
    Ctrl+Enter always does, as on Windows.
  - **Keys.** Up and Down move one line and Page Up and Page Down a window's lines, keeping the
    column within the shorter line; Home and End go to the line's ends, Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End to
    the text's.
  - **The view.** The edit shows whole rows of `CELL_HEIGHT` from 4 pixels in and scrolls by
    whole lines and cells to keep the caret shown (`edit::View`, cells across and rows down; a
    bare cell count is the single-line view, so callers of single-line edits are unchanged).
    Clicks, drags and double-clicks take the row from the pointer's `y`.
  - **Messages.** `EM_GETLINECOUNT`, `EM_LINEINDEX`, `EM_LINELENGTH` (with -1, the unselected
    characters of the selection's lines), `EM_LINEFROMCHAR`, `EM_GETLINE` (narrowed to UTF-8 for
    `SendMessageA`), `EM_GETFIRSTVISIBLELINE`, `EM_LINESCROLL` and `EM_SCROLLCARET`. A
    single-line edit answers them as one line.
  - `ES_PASSWORD` is ignored on a multi-line edit, as on Windows.
- **Not yet.**
  - Word wrap (a multi-line edit without `ES_AUTOHSCROLL`): lines run past the right edge and
    the view scrolls sideways.
  - The edit's own scroll bars (`WS_VSCROLL`, `WS_HSCROLL`), which wait for window scroll bars.
  - Windows' larger default limit (30,000 characters): the edit still holds `EDIT_CAPACITY`
    (1,024) units.
  - `EM_SETRECT`, `EM_SETTABSTOPS` and `EM_FMTLINES`.

## D342 Windows: a window's own scroll bars (`WS_VSCROLL`, `WS_HSCROLL`) (batch part 10's rest, D228's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' standard scroll bar behaviour; the look is the design's scroll bar, docs/ux/windows-controls-v0.3.md section 14)

- **Decision.** A program's window (top-level or child) with `WS_VSCROLL` or `WS_HSCROLL` has
  its own bars, `SB_VERT` and `SB_HORZ`, kept in its window entry (`Window::bars`).
  - **Where.** The vertical bar takes a `scroll_bar::WIDTH` (16 pixel) strip right of the client
    area and the horizontal one a strip under it; with both, the corner square is the track's
    colour. `Window::fit_client` sets the client area to the window's size less its menu bar
    and its bars whenever the size, the menu or the style changes, so `GetClientRect`,
    painting, clipping and `WM_SIZE` all see the smaller area. The system's controls keep
    drawing their own bars inside themselves (a list box's, a combo box's list).
  - **Painting.** The bars are painted on the top-level buffer each time it is shown
    (`paint::show_pending`, under any open drop-down) and when the program changes one.
  - **The pointer.** A press on a bar is the bar's, before the program sees it: arrows, the
    track and the thumb behave as the `SCROLLBAR` control does, and the bar keeps the pointer
    until the release. Each step posts `WM_VSCROLL` or `WM_HSCROLL` to the window itself with
    a `lParam` of 0, thumb drags as `SB_THUMBTRACK` and `SB_THUMBPOSITION`, then
    `SB_ENDSCROLL`.
  - **Functions.** `SetScrollInfo`, `GetScrollInfo` (with `SIF_TRACKPOS` while dragging),
    `SetScrollPos`, `GetScrollPos`, `SetScrollRange` and `GetScrollRange` take `SB_HORZ` and
    `SB_VERT` as well as `SB_CTL`. A new range or page that makes a bar needed shows it, and
    one that makes it unneeded hides it unless `SIF_DISABLENOSCROLL` is given, as on Windows.
    `ShowScrollBar` shows or hides `SB_HORZ`, `SB_VERT` and `SB_BOTH` (and a scroll bar
    control, as a window). A bar shown or hidden refits the client area and sends `WM_SIZE`.
- **Not yet.**
  - The arrows' repeat while held (the control's repeat timer is per control window).
  - `EnableScrollBar`, `ScrollWindowEx` and `ScrollWindow`, and the bars' own window menu.
  - An `EDIT`'s and a `LISTBOX`'s bars as non-client bars (they draw inside themselves).
  - `WM_NCHITTEST` answering `HTVSCROLL` and `HTHSCROLL`.

## D343 Windows controls: simple combo boxes (`CBS_SIMPLE`) (batch part 10's rest, D340's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' combo box behaviour; the look reuses the design's edit field and drop-down list, docs/ux/windows-controls-v0.3.md section 10)

- **Decision.** A `COMBOBOX` with `CBS_SIMPLE` is made with an edit field and a list that is
  always shown (`ComboBox::simple`). The window keeps the whole height the program gave it
  (drop-down combo boxes still shrink to the 24 pixel box): the edit field fills the top
  24 pixels across the whole width (no button), and the list fills the rest, 2 pixels below,
  drawn inside the control rather than over the window's content.
  - **The list.** Its rows are as many as its height holds; it highlights the selection and
    scrolls to keep it shown. A press on a row selects its item at once, puts its text in the
    field selected whole and sends `CBN_SELENDOK` then `CBN_SELCHANGE`; a press on its scroll
    bar scrolls it.
  - **Keys.** The field takes typing as in `CBS_DROPDOWN` (D340); Up, Down and the page keys
    move the selection. F4, Alt+Up/Down and `CB_SHOWDROPDOWN` open nothing.
  - Fixed on the way: the control-state path (`controls::new_state`) called
    `combo_box::new_state` without the style D340 added.
- **Not yet.** The list's own scroll repeat while the pointer holds an arrow, and the mouse
  wheel over the list.

## D344 Windows: function tables registered at run time (`RtlAddFunctionTable`, growable tables and table callbacks) (batch part 12's rest, D230's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented behaviour)

- **Context.** Programs that generate code (JavaScript engines, .NET, LuaJIT, emulators) tell
  Windows how to unwind it with run-time function tables. Without them an exception thrown
  through generated code ends the walk, and the program's `__try` and C++ handlers above it
  never run.
- **Decision.**
  - kernel32 and ntdll export `RtlAddFunctionTable` and `RtlDeleteFunctionTable`, and
    `RtlInstallFunctionTableCallback`; ntdll also `RtlAddGrowableFunctionTable`,
    `RtlGrowFunctionTable` and `RtlDeleteGrowableFunctionTable`. Up to 64 tables are
    registered at once (`function_tables.rs`, a spin-locked array copied out before a search,
    so a program's callback never runs under the lock).
  - **The search.** `frames::lookup` looks in the program's exception directory first, then
    in the registered tables whose code range holds the address: a table's entries are
    searched as `.pdata` is (`unwinder::lookup_in`, the table and the code in separate
    `Image`s, so the table may lie anywhere, even below its base); a callback is asked for the
    one entry. `lookup` now answers with the image the function's addresses are relative to,
    and each `Frame` carries that base (`Frame::image_base`), which the dispatcher context,
    `RtlLookupFunctionEntry` and `RtlVirtualUnwind` use.
  - **The code's extent.** The bytes the unwinder may read run from the table's base to the end
    of the run of pages that holds the end of the code: the given range for growable tables
    and callbacks, the base's own run for `RtlAddFunctionTable`, which gives no length.
- **Not yet.** `RtlPcToFileHeader` for generated code (it answers 0, as for any address outside
  an image); a language handler of generated code that reads its data through the image
  (`__C_specific_handler`, `__CxxFrameHandler*`) is given the table's base, as on Windows, but
  the layer's own copies of those handlers still read the program's image.

## D345 msvcp140: `std::system_category()`'s Windows messages and `std::notify_all_at_thread_exit` (batch part 12's rest, D230's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the documented behaviour of MSVC's standard library)

- **Decision.**
  - `_Winerror_map` maps a Windows error to the `std::errc` value it stands for (0 when none
    does), so `std::system_category().default_error_condition` compares equal to the generic
    conditions programs test for (`ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` to `no_such_file_or_directory`,
    `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` to `permission_denied`, the Winsock errors to their socket
    conditions; 78 entries, `cpp_errors::errc_of_windows_error`, binary searched).
  - `_Winerror_message`, `__std_system_error_allocate_message` and
    `__std_system_error_deallocate_message` give `std::system_category().message` Windows'
    own wording, from the same table `FormatMessageW` answers from (`errors::message`).
  - `_Cnd_register_at_thread_exit`, `_Cnd_unregister_at_thread_exit` and
    `_Cnd_do_broadcast_at_thread_exit`: what a thread registered (up to 64 at once, in a
    spin-locked table) is done as it ends: the flag set to 1, the mutex unlocked and the
    condition broadcast, in that order.
- **Not yet.** iostreams and the rest of msvcp140's out-of-line parts.

## D346 Windows: a stack overflow is `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW`, with signal stacks and a stack reserve the layer manages (batch part 12's rest, D230's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented guard-page behaviour)

- **Context.** A thread that overflowed its stack faulted with no room for the kernel to
  deliver the signal, so the process died with no Windows exception, while on Windows the
  program's `__try`/`__except` and vectored handlers see `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW` and may
  recover with `_resetstkoflw`.
- **Decision.**
  - **Signal stacks.** Every thread the layer runs gets a 64 KiB signal stack (with a guard page)
    when it starts (`fault_handler::give_thread_signal_stack`; the main thread at install,
    `CreateThread`'s threads in `thread_main`), unmapped when the thread ends. The fault
    signals are handled with `SA_ONSTACK` (`linux::handle_signal_on_signal_stack`).
  - **The dispatch stays on the thread's stack.** A fault's signal frame on the signal stack
    is copied below the faulting stack pointer and its red zone (`frame_on_thread_stack`,
    x86_64's `fpstate` pointer moved with it, `relocate_signal_frame`) and the dispatch
    enters below the copy, so the walk, the handlers and the unwinds run on the program's
    stack as before, and a later signal cannot overwrite the frame first.
  - **The reserve.** `CreateThread` maps a hard guard page, then a 64 KiB reserve, both
    inaccessible, under the stack; the TEB's `StackLimit` is the reserve's top and its
    `DeallocationStack` (0x1478) the mapping's bottom. A fault in the closed reserve opens it
    (read-write, `StackLimit` lowered to its bottom) and is dispatched as
    `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW` with the access and the address (`fault::stack_fault`,
    `thread::stack_fault_opening_reserve`); a fault in the hard guard, or in the open reserve's
    guard again, ends the process with `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW`, as Windows does for an
    overflow with no room left.
  - `_resetstkoflw` closes the reserve again once the stack is back above it, and answers
    nonzero when the reserve is closed.
- **Not yet.** The main thread runs on the Linux process stack, which the kernel grows: its
  overflow still ends the process (as an access violation report). `SetThreadStackGuarantee`
  and `GetThreadStackLimits` over the reserve.

## D347 Windows: collided unwinds (batch part 12's rest, D230's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented `EXCEPTION_COLLIDED_UNWIND` behaviour)

- **Context.** A termination handler (a `__finally` block, a C++ destructor) can start an unwind
  of its own (a `return` or `goto` out of a `__finally`, a `longjmp`). That unwind walks out
  of the handler into the frame whose handlers the first unwind was running. Before, it went
  on from that frame's caller, so the frame's handlers the first unwind had not reached yet
  never ran.
- **Decision.** As on Windows, the second unwind collides with the first:
  - Each call of a language handler to unwind a frame (`dispatch::unwind_frame`) goes through
    a bridge that remembers the frame and that call's dispatcher context
    (`Bridge::collided`, `frames::Collided`).
  - A walk for termination handlers that crosses such a bridge reports it
    (`Event::Bridge(Some(collided))`), and the unwind calls the frame's handler again with
    `EXCEPTION_COLLIDED_UNWIND` (0x40) and the earlier call's scope index, so
    `__C_specific_handler` runs only the `__finally` blocks the first unwind had not reached
    (it sets the index past each block before calling it). The walk then goes on from the
    frame's caller; when the frame is the second unwind's target, the unwind ends there.
- **Not yet.** The layer's C++ frame handlers (`__CxxFrameHandler3` and `4`) ignore the flag:
  a destructor that starts an unwind from inside an unwinding C++ frame may see that frame's
  earlier destructors run again.

## D348 Windows: `WSAAsyncSelect`, a socket's network events as window messages (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Winsock's documented behaviour)

- **Decision.**
  - `WSAAsyncSelect(socket, window, message, events)` makes the socket non-blocking and
    registers it (up to 64 sockets, `async_select.rs`); no window or no events forgets it,
    and `closesocket` does too.
  - **Watching.** The thread that sleeps on the window server's descriptor (`gui::sleep`) also
    watches each registered socket for the events still armed (`linux::wait_for_events`, a
    general `ppoll` over up to 72 descriptors), and every thread checks them, without
    waiting, whenever it looks for a message (`async_select::post_ready`), so a program that
    only peeks for messages gets them too.
  - **The messages.** Each event is posted to the window once, with the socket as `wParam` and
    `WSAMAKESELECTREPLY(event, error)` as `lParam`: `FD_CONNECT` when a connect finishes
    (`WSAECONNREFUSED` when it failed), `FD_WRITE` when the socket can take data, `FD_READ`
    when bytes wait, `FD_CLOSE` when the peer closed (`WSAECONNRESET` when it reset), told
    apart from data by a peek of one byte.
  - **Re-enabling**, as on Windows: `recv` re-enables `FD_READ` and `FD_OOB`, a `send` that
    would have blocked re-enables `FD_WRITE`; `FD_CONNECT` and `FD_CLOSE` come once.
- **Not yet.** `FD_ACCEPT` (the layer's Winsock has no `listen` and `accept` yet), `FD_OOB` as
  its own event (urgent data reads as `FD_READ`), `WSAEventSelect` and
  `WSAEnumNetworkEvents`.

## D349 Windows: hooks over the process's own messages and input (`SetWindowsHookEx`) (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented hook behaviour)

- **Context.** `SetWindowsHookExW` failed, so programs that rely on hooks did not run: MFC
  attaches its window objects in a `WH_CBT` hook, toolkits filter keys with `WH_KEYBOARD` and
  `WH_GETMESSAGE`, and remote-control and accessibility tools watch input with the low-level
  hooks.
- **Decision.** `SetWindowsHookExW` and `A` install a hook for one thread or, with thread 0,
  for every thread of the process (up to 32, `hooks.rs`); `UnhookWindowsHookEx` removes it and
  `CallNextHookEx` calls the next older hook of the same kind for the calling thread, 0 at the
  chain's end. The layer calls the newest hook of a kind:
  - `WH_GETMESSAGE`, then `WH_KEYBOARD` or `WH_MOUSE` (with a `MOUSEHOOKSTRUCT`), as
    `GetMessage` and `PeekMessage` return a message (`HC_ACTION`, or `HC_NOREMOVE` for a peek
    that leaves it); a nonzero answer from the keyboard or mouse hook discards the message and
    the call takes the next.
  - `WH_CALLWNDPROC` and `WH_CALLWNDPROCRET` around every sent message (`CWPSTRUCT`,
    `CWPRETSTRUCT`); the send path checks one counter when no hook is installed.
  - `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` and `WH_MOUSE_LL` for the window server's input to the process before it
    is routed (`KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT`, `MSLLHOOKSTRUCT`); a nonzero answer swallows it.
  - `WH_CBT`'s `HCBT_CREATEWND` before a program window's `WM_NCCREATE` (a nonzero answer
    refuses the window) and `HCBT_DESTROYWND` before each `WM_DESTROY`.
  - Hooks of the other kinds are kept and chained but never called.
- **Not yet.** Hooks into other processes (EggOS gives an app no way into another's input);
  `WH_CBT`'s other codes (activation, focus, moves); low-level hooks called on the installing
  thread's message loop, as Windows does (the layer calls them on the thread that reads the
  input); the injected-input flags.

## D350 Windows controls: multi-line edits follow the controls design's section 13 (amends D341; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (the design, docs/ux/windows-controls-v0.3.md section 13)

- **Context.** D341 was written before reading the design's section 13, which already specifies
  `ES_MULTILINE`. Where they differed, the design wins.
- **Decision.**
  - Lines start 2 pixels down and are 16 apart; `R = (h - 4) / 16` whole lines show, and the
    partial line below them is drawn, clipped (D341 started them 4 pixels down).
  - Page Up and Page Down move `R - 1` lines (D341: `R`).
  - A lone `\r`, like a lone `\n` or `\r\n`, ends a line, as `WM_SETTEXT` may set it.
  - A selected line end fills one extra cell after the line's last glyph.
  - `EM_GETMODIFY` and `EM_SETMODIFY`: the flag is set by any change of the text by typing or
    `EM_REPLACESEL`, cleared by `WM_SETTEXT` (`Edit::modified`).
- **Still not yet** (D341's list stands): word wrap without `ES_AUTOHSCROLL`, which the
  design wants with part 1's greedy rule, and the edit's own scroll bars inside its border.

## D351 Windows controls: multi-line edits wrap without `ES_AUTOHSCROLL` and draw their own scroll bars (D341's and D350's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (the design, docs/ux/windows-controls-v0.3.md sections 13 and 14)

- **Decision.**
  - **Wrapping.** A multi-line edit without `ES_AUTOHSCROLL` wraps each line at the text's
    width with the greedy rule: a display line ends after the last space that fits, or at the
    width when no space does (`Edit::row`). Its lines (`EM_GETLINECOUNT`, `EM_LINEINDEX`,
    `EM_LINEFROMCHAR`, `EM_LINELENGTH`, `EM_GETLINE`, Up, Down, Home and End) are the display
    lines, as on Windows; a caret at a wrap point stands at the start of the next line, and
    the view never scrolls sideways. With `ES_AUTOHSCROLL` the lines run on as in D341.
  - **The width** the lines wrap at is the view the control last gave the edit
    (`Edit::fit`), which every input, message and paint gives it.
  - **Scroll bars.** `WS_VSCROLL` and `WS_HSCROLL` on a multi-line edit draw the design's bars
    inside its border (the horizontal one only without wrapping), always shown and disabled
    while nothing scrolls, fed by (lines, visible lines, the first one shown) and (the widest
    line, visible cells, the column offset); the text's view is that much smaller
    (`Edit::inner`), the corner square the track's colour. A press on an arrow scrolls a line,
    on the track a page, without moving the caret (`Edit::press_bar`).
- **Not yet.** Dragging the edit's thumb and the arrows' repeat while held; `ES_AUTOVSCROLL`
  without a bar is the default behaviour already (the view follows the caret).

## D352 Windows: HTTPS in WinINet (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, reusing EggOS's TLS 1.3 client, D159)

- **Decision.** `InternetOpenUrlW` fetches `https://` URLs over EggOS's own TLS 1.3 client
  (`eggos-tls`, now a dependency of the Windows layer), the same way `fetch` does:
  - A request's connection is a `Link`: plain TCP, or a TLS session over it whose buffers live
    in their own heap block (freed when the link closes, after the session that borrows them).
    The request is written and the head and body read through the link, so redirects, chunked
    bodies and `InternetReadFile` are unchanged; a relative redirect keeps the scheme.
  - The handshake checks the server's certificate against the machine's roots
    (`/etc/ssl/roots.pem`, else `/media/host/roots.pem`, as `fetch` reads them) at the wall
    clock's time, with randomness from `getrandom`. A refused certificate is
    `ERROR_INTERNET_INVALID_CA`, any other handshake failure
    `ERROR_INTERNET_SECURE_CHANNEL_ERROR`; closing the handle sends TLS's close notice.
- **Not yet.** `INTERNET_FLAG_IGNORE_CERT_*` and the security flags of `InternetSetOption`,
  client certificates, and TLS 1.2 servers (the client speaks 1.3 only, D159).

## D353 Windows common controls: custom draw for list views (`NM_CUSTOMDRAW`) (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from comctl32's documented custom-draw protocol)

- **Context.** Programs colour rows (errors in red, alternating backgrounds) or draw rows
  themselves through `NM_CUSTOMDRAW`; without it they show the plain list.
- **Decision.** A list view's paint runs custom draw around the layer's own drawing, outside
  the GUI lock, with the paint's device context in each `NMLVCUSTOMDRAW`:
  - `CDDS_PREPAINT` for the whole control; with `CDRF_NOTIFYITEMDRAW`, `CDDS_ITEMPREPAINT`
    for each row shown (up to 64), with its index, rectangle, selected and focused states and
    `lParam`, and `CLR_DEFAULT` in `clrText` and `clrTextBk`.
  - The colours the parent wrote replace the list's for that row (the text of an unselected
    row, the row's background), and `CDRF_SKIPDEFAULT` leaves the row to the program
    (`list_view::RowDraw`, `paint_custom`).
  - After the paint, `CDDS_ITEMPOSTPAINT` for the rows that asked with
    `CDRF_NOTIFYPOSTPAINT`, then `CDDS_POSTPAINT` when the first answer asked.
  - `notify_parent_keeping` sends a notification and gives back the structure the parent
    filled.
- **Not yet.** Per-subitem custom draw (`CDRF_NOTIFYSUBITEMDRAW`), `CDRF_NEWFONT`, and custom
  draw for tree views, toolbars, headers and trackbars.

## D354 Windows common controls: editing a list view item's label (`LVS_EDITLABELS`) (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from comctl32's documented label editing; the editor is the design's `EDIT`, section 3)

- **Decision.**
  - `LVM_EDITLABELW`, and F2 on the focused item of a list view with `LVS_EDITLABELS`, ask the
    parent with `LVN_BEGINLABELEDITW` (a nonzero answer refuses); then an `EDIT` child
    (`ES_AUTOHSCROLL`, id 1) is made over the item's first column with its text, focused with
    the text selected. `LVM_GETEDITCONTROL` answers it.
  - **Ending.** Enter, or the focus leaving the edit, ends the edit keeping its text; Escape
    and `LVM_CANCELEDITLABEL` cancel it. The parent gets `LVN_ENDLABELEDITW` with the text
    (null when cancelled) and its nonzero answer to a kept edit sets the label. The edit is
    destroyed and the focus goes back to the list when the edit had it.
  - The edit's procedure hands Enter and Escape to its list (`label_editor_key`) and its
    focus loss (`label_editor_left`); `IsDialogMessageW` lets the label edit have Enter and
    Escape instead of the dialog's default and cancel buttons.
- **Not yet.** Starting an edit by a slow second click on the selected item, tree views'
  label editing (`TVM_EDITLABEL`), and the edit growing as the text gets longer.

## D355 Windows common controls: tooltips (`tooltips_class32`) (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md, sections 1 to 7) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Design.** Claude Fable designed Windows tooltips and the notification area
  (`docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md`): a white tile with a grey border in the Light
  palette, `w = 8n + 16`, 24 tall for a line, one line until `TTM_SETMAXTIPWIDTH`, a title
  row with an `i`, `!` or `x` circle for `TTM_SETTITLEW`, balloons as rounded titled tips
  without a stem, placed 20 px under the pointer (above when it does not fit), centred on the
  tool for `TTF_CENTERTIP` and balloons, Win32's 500, 100 and 5000 ms delays. (The design's
  table gives 88 px for two 8-cell lines; its own formula gives 80, which the code follows.)
- **Decision.**
  - `eggos_windows_gui::controls::tooltip`: the lines, the size, the placement and the
    painting, with host tests of the design's sizes.
  - `CreateWindowExW` of `tooltips_class32` (a `WS_POPUP`) makes a hidden child of its owner
    (or of the active window when it has none) with no rect, so it lives in its owner's tree
    and dies with it; its state holds up to 64 tools.
  - **Messages**: `TTM_ADDTOOLW`, `TTM_DELTOOLW`, `TTM_NEWTOOLRECTW`, `TTM_UPDATETIPTEXTW`,
    `TTM_SETTOOLINFOW`, `TTM_GETTOOLINFOW`, `TTM_GETTEXTW`, `TTM_GETTOOLCOUNT`,
    `TTM_ACTIVATE`, `TTM_SETDELAYTIME` (with `TTDT_AUTOMATIC`'s ratios) and
    `TTM_GETDELAYTIME`, `TTM_SETMAXTIPWIDTH` and `TTM_GETMAXTIPWIDTH`, `TTM_SETTITLEW`,
    `TTM_POP`, `TTM_POPUP`, `TTM_UPDATE`, `TTM_TRACKACTIVATE`, `TTM_TRACKPOSITION`;
    `TTM_RELAYEVENT` is accepted and changes nothing (the layer tracks the pointer itself).
  - **Showing.** The pointer's moves (`tooltip::pointer_moved`, from the input routing) pick
    the newest tool under it; after the initial delay (the reshow delay right after another
    tip hid) the tip shows: a callback tool is asked with `TTN_GETDISPINFOW`
    (`TTF_DI_SETITEM` keeps the answer), `TTN_SHOW` goes to the owner, and the tip is painted
    over the top-level window's buffer at each commit (`tooltip::paint_shown`, after open
    drop-downs and combo lists). It hides after the autopop delay (`TTN_POP`), when the
    pointer leaves the tool, and on any press or key (`tooltip::dismiss`), the tool then spent
    until the pointer leaves it; the window repaints under it. Tracking tools show only by
    `TTM_TRACKACTIVATE`, at `TTM_TRACKPOSITION`'s point (exactly there with `TTF_ABSOLUTE`).
  - `TTS_NOPREFIX` clear strips mnemonic ampersands. The tooltip is a `tooltip` element in
    agents' tree.
- **Not yet.** Tools other controls register (toolbars' `TBSTYLE_TOOLTIPS`, list views' info
  tips, tree views' `TVS_INFOTIP`, design section 8), `TTM_HITTESTW`, `TTM_ENUMTOOLSW`,
  `TTM_GETCURRENTTOOLW`, `TTM_GETBUBBLESIZE`, `TTM_ADJUSTRECT`, resource-id texts (shown as
  callbacks), touch's long-press, and `TTS_ALWAYSTIP`'s inactive-window rule. The tray
  (design sections 11 to 19) is its own decision.

## D356 Windows common controls: toolbars' tooltips (`TBSTYLE_TOOLTIPS`) (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md section 8) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A toolbar made with `TBSTYLE_TOOLTIPS` makes its own tooltip control (D355)
  on `WM_CREATE`; `TB_GETTOOLTIPS` answers it and `TB_SETTOOLTIPS` replaces it
  (`Toolbar::tooltips`). Before each paint the toolbar keeps one callback tool per shown
  button in it, its rect the button's and its id the command id (`tooltip::replace_tools`).
  When a tip is due, the tooltip's `TTN_GETDISPINFOW` reaches the toolbar, which tries, in
  the design's order: `TBN_GETINFOTIPW` to its parent (an 80-unit buffer, the command id, the
  button's data), then the same `TTN_GETDISPINFOW` passed on to its parent (`idFrom` the
  command id, as Win32 sends it there), then the button's own string when the toolbar draws
  no text (`TB_SETMAXTEXTROWS 0`).
- **Not yet.** `TBSTYLE_EX_MIXEDBUTTONS`' rule for buttons without `BTNS_SHOWTEXT`, list
  views' and tree views' info tips, tab controls' `TCS_TOOLTIPS`.

## D357 Windows programs' notification-area icons in the bar (`Shell_NotifyIconW`) (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15, M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md sections 11 to 13) and the code-only session (engineering, the protocol)

- **Decision.**
  - **Protocol.** `SET_TRAY_ICON` (request 51, 32 bytes: window, the client's key for the icon,
    flags hidden and remove, the tip's length and address, the pixels' address) adds,
    changes or removes an icon of one of the caller's windows; the kernel reads the tip
    (UTF-8, at most 384 bytes) and the 16x16 ARGB pixels from the program's memory. A press
    comes back as a `Tray` record (event 17: the Windows message, the key, the screen point).
    `docs/windows.md` lists both.
  - **The server** (`drivers/src/desktop/tray.rs`) keeps up to 16 icons; they sit in the
    bar's indicator run directly left of the keyboard and network indicators (28 px targets
    on the top bar with the icon at (6, 6), 40 px items on the taskbar with the icon at
    (12, 12), the run 8 px left of its neighbour there), the first added rightmost, at most
    four shown and, past that, the leftmost cell an overflow button (`Hidden icons`). The
    Agent and Updates chips and the taskbar's items move left of the run. An icon without
    pixels is the generic tile with its window title's first letter. Its tooltip is its tip
    (else its window's title), in the bar's own tooltip. A left, right or middle press sends
    the window that button's down and up messages at once; the icons of a destroyed window
    go with it.
  - **The layer** (`shell_desktop.rs`): `Shell_NotifyIconW` with `NIM_ADD`, `NIM_MODIFY`,
    `NIM_DELETE`, `NIM_SETVERSION` (0, 3 or 4) and `NIM_SETFOCUS` (accepted), `NIF_MESSAGE`,
    `NIF_ICON` (rendered to 16x16: scaled down or centred, alpha under half or the mask's set
    pixels transparent), `NIF_TIP` (64 or 128 units by the structure's size) and `NIF_STATE`'s
    `NIS_HIDDEN`. A `Tray` record posts the callback message to the icon's window, packed by
    its version: `uID` and the message for 0 and 3 (3 adds `NIN_SELECT` after a left up),
    the point and `MAKELONG(message, uID)` for 4, which adds `NIN_SELECT` after a left up
    and `WM_CONTEXTMENU` after a right up.
- **Not yet.** The overflow popup (its button shows, a press does nothing), the hover and
  tooltip messages of version 4 (`NIN_POPUPOPEN`, `WM_MOUSEMOVE`), double clicks, keyboard
  selection and `NIN_KEYSELECT`, `NIF_INFO` balloons as notices, the program's context menu
  in the server's chrome (section 14), the phone and tablet shade's `Programs` row,
  `Shell_NotifyIconGetRect`, 2x pixels.

## D358 Windows: layered windows (`WS_EX_LAYERED`, `SetLayeredWindowAttributes`) (batch part 13's rest, D231's "Not yet"; M15, M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented behaviour)

- **Decision.**
  - **The server** keeps each window's content opacity (255 by default) and colour key
    (`Window::opacity`, `colour_key`). `SET_LAYERED` (request 52, 16 bytes: window, alpha,
    key `0x00RRGGBB`, flags 1 alpha and 2 key) sets them for one of the caller's windows. The
    compositor blends such a window's content over what it already drew under it
    (`blend_row`: per channel, rounded; in 64-pixel chunks so the kernel stack holds the
    pixels underneath), and leaves what is under it where the content is exactly the key.
    The window frame and the fill outside the buffer stay opaque. Nothing in the server culls
    what a window covers, so a translucent window shows what is under it.
  - **The layer.** `SetLayeredWindowAttributes` on a top-level `WS_EX_LAYERED` window sends
    `LWA_ALPHA`'s alpha and `LWA_COLORKEY`'s key (COLORREF turned into the server's RGB);
    `GetLayeredWindowAttributes` answers what was set (a table of 16 windows).
- **Not yet.** `UpdateLayeredWindow` and per-pixel alpha (`ULW_ALPHA` with `AC_SRC_ALPHA`),
  child layered windows, and the frame fading with the content.

## D359 macOS Foundation: NSDictionary's hash index (batch part 14's rest, D232's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Context.** Every lookup compared the wanted key with each key in turn (`isEqual:`), so a
  dictionary of `n` keys cost `n` message sends per lookup, which large plists and caches
  make slow.
- **Decision.** The dictionaries the layer builds (immutable or mutable; not clang's constant
  literals, which keep their layout) carry an open-addressing index next to their keys
  (`MutableDictionaryObject::index`): once a dictionary holds 8 keys, a power-of-two table at
  least twice the count holds each key's position plus one, placed by the key's `hash` and
  probed linearly. A lookup probes it and compares by identity, then `isEqual:`, only the
  keys of its probe run; smaller and constant dictionaries still compare every key. Adding a
  key inserts it while the table stays at most half full and rebuilds it otherwise; removing
  one rebuilds it (the positions move); `dealloc` frees it. Keys are copied when stored, so
  their hashes do not change, and equal keys hash alike by Foundation's contract.
- **Not yet.** The `nsdictionary_lookup` benchmark, and an index for NSSet and NSCountedSet.

## D360 macOS Foundation: NSCoder and NSKeyedUnarchiver (batch part 14's rest, D232's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the keyed archive format: a property list with `$archiver`, `$top`, `$objects` and UIDs)

- **Decision.** `NSCoder` (`allowsKeyedCoding`) and its subclass `NSKeyedUnarchiver`
  (`keyed_unarchiver.rs`):
  - **Reading.** The archive is a binary or XML property list (`eggos-plist`) whose
    `$archiver` is `NSKeyedArchiver`; `$top`'s `root` names the root object. Objects are
    decoded by UID once each and kept in a cache the unarchiver owns, so shared objects stay
    shared. `$null` (object 0) is nil; plain strings, integers, reals, booleans and data are
    NSString, NSNumber (`new_integer`, `new_double`), the boolean objects and NSData. A
    dictionary names its class by `$class` (`{$classname, $classes}`): NSString and
    NSMutableString (`NS.string`), NSArray, NSMutableArray, NSSet and NSMutableSet
    (`NS.objects`), NSDictionary and NSMutableDictionary (`NS.keys`, `NS.objects`), NSData
    (`NS.data`), NSDate (`NS.time`) and NSNull decode natively; any other class is allocated
    and sent `initWithCoder:` with the unarchiver, whose `decode...ForKey:` then read that
    object's keys (the decoding object is a stack, so nested `initWithCoder:` calls read
    their own).
  - **Untrusted input.** Every UID is checked against `$objects`, at most 2^20 objects; a
    cycle through natively decoded objects decodes as nil instead of recursing.
  - **API.** `unarchiveObjectWithData:`, `unarchiveObjectWithFile:`,
    `unarchivedObjectOfClass:fromData:error:`, `unarchivedObjectOfClasses:fromData:error:`,
    `unarchiveTopLevelObjectWithData:error:`, `initForReadingWithData:`,
    `initForReadingFromData:error:` (secure coding on); `decodeObjectForKey:`,
    `decodeObjectOfClass(es):forKey:`, `decodeInteger`, `Int`, `Int32`, `Int64`, `Bool`,
    `Double` and `FloatForKey:`, `containsValueForKey:`, `requiresSecureCoding` and its
    setter, `finishDecoding`.
- **Not yet.** `NSKeyedArchiver` (writing), `NSError`s for a damaged archive (the error is
  nil and the result nil), the allowed-classes check of secure coding, `NSURL` and `NSUUID`
  archives, `decodeBytesForKey:returnedLength:`, and an object referring to itself through
  `initWithCoder:` (it gets nil, where macOS gives the object being decoded).

## D361 Windows common controls: tree views' custom draw and label editing (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, as D353 and D354 do for list views)

- **Decision.**
  - **Custom draw.** A tree view's paint runs `NM_CUSTOMDRAW` around its own drawing as a list
    view's does (D353), with `NMTVCUSTOMDRAW`: `CDDS_PREPAINT`, then `CDDS_ITEMPREPAINT` for
    each shown item (up to 64) with its `HTREEITEM`, row, selected state, `lParam` and level;

    background, `CDRF_SKIPDEFAULT` leaves the item to the program, and the post-paint stages
    follow (`tree_view::paint_custom`, sharing `list_view::RowDraw`).
  - **Label editing.** `TVM_EDITLABELW`, and F2 on the selected item with `TVS_EDITLABELS`,
    ask `TVN_BEGINLABELEDITW` and put an `EDIT` over the item's label (at least 8 cells wide),
    as a list view does (D354); Enter or the focus leaving keeps the text, Escape and
    `TVM_ENDEDITLABELNOW` with `TRUE` cancel, `TVN_ENDLABELEDITW` reports it and the parent's
    nonzero answer sets the label. `TVM_GETEDITCONTROL` answers the edit. The edit's key and
    focus hooks (`common_controls::label_editor_key`, `label_editor_left`,
    `is_label_editor`) now serve both views.
- **Not yet.** Starting an edit by a slow second click; custom draw for toolbars, headers and
  trackbars; `CDRF_NEWFONT`.

- **Decision.** Setting `LVS_EX_INFOTIP` makes the list view's own tooltip control (D355),

## D363 Windows common controls: tree views' info tips (`TVS_INFOTIP`) (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md section 8) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A tree view made with `TVS_INFOTIP` makes its own tooltip control (D355) on

## D364 Windows notification-area balloons as the shell's notice (`NIF_INFO`) (batch part 13's rest, D357's "Not yet"; M15, M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md section 15) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `Shell_NotifyIconW` with `NIF_INFO` joins `szInfoTitle`, `: ` and `szInfo`
  (the one that is set when only one is) and sends it with `SET_TRAY_ICON`'s new `BALLOON`
  flag (4), the tip field carrying the text. The server shows it in the shell's notice (a
  line feed as a space, cut at 36 glyphs with `...`, closed after 3000 ms like any notice;
  `Notice::balloon`, its text kept by the tray) and the icon's window gets `NIN_BALLOONSHOW`;
  a press on the notice is consumed and sends `NIN_BALLOONUSERCLICK`. An empty `szInfo`
  closes the icon's balloon when it is the one showing. A later balloon replaces the earlier

## D365 macOS Foundation: NSKeyedArchiver, keyed archives written as XML property lists (batch part 14's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the keyed archive format D360 reads)

- **Decision.** `NSKeyedArchiver` (a subclass of NSCoder, `keyed_archiver.rs`) writes the
  layout `NSKeyedUnarchiver` reads: `$archiver` `NSKeyedArchiver`, `$version` 100000, `$top`
  with `root`'s UID, and `$objects` with `$null` first. Each object is written once, found by
  identity, and referred to by its UID: strings, integers, reals, booleans and data plainly;
  arrays and sets (`NS.objects`), dictionaries (`NS.keys`, `NS.objects`), dates (`NS.time`)
  and NSNull as dictionaries naming their class (the mutable classes by their mutable
  names); any other object by the keys its `encodeWithCoder:` writes through
  `encodeObject:forKey:`, `encodeConditionalObject:forKey:`, `encodeInteger`, `Int64`, `Int`,
  `Int32`, `Bool`, `Double` and `Float:forKey:`. Each class is written once,
  `{$classname, $classes: [name, NSObject]}`. Reals are written with 17 significant digits,
  so they read back exactly (`number::exact_decimal`), and data in Base64.
- **API.** `+archivedDataWithRootObject:`,
  `+archivedDataWithRootObject:requiringSecureCoding:error:`, `+archiveRootObject:toFile:`;
  `-init`, `-initRequiringSecureCoding:`, `encodeObject:forKey:` of `root` for the archive's
  root, `-encodedData`, `-finishEncoding`, `-setOutputFormat:` (accepted; always XML).
- **Not yet.** The binary property list format (macOS's default output; readers accept
  XML), the class hierarchy in `$classes` past the class itself, mutable strings as
  `NSMutableString` (they are written as plain strings), and errors for unencodable objects.

## D366 Windows: `UpdateLayeredWindow` (batch part 13's rest, D358's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented behaviour)

- **Decision.** `UpdateLayeredWindow` on a top-level `WS_EX_LAYERED` window moves it to
  `pptDst`, sizes it to `psize`, copies `hdcSrc`'s pixels from `pptSrc` into its client area
  (`BitBlt` with `SRCCOPY` through the window's device context, which commits them), and then
  blends it as `SetLayeredWindowAttributes` does (D358): `ULW_ALPHA` with
  `BLENDFUNCTION.SourceConstantAlpha`, `ULW_COLORKEY` with `crKey`, `ULW_OPAQUE` opaque. Its
  ninth argument is on the stack on ARM64, so the export copies the caller's stack words.
- **Not yet.** Per-pixel alpha (`AC_SRC_ALPHA`): the source's alpha channel is not used,
  only the constant alpha; `UpdateLayeredWindowIndirect` and `prcDirty`.

## D367 Windows common controls: custom draw for toolbars (`NM_CUSTOMDRAW`) (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, as D353 does for list views)

- **Decision.** A toolbar's paint runs custom draw around its own drawing with

## D368 Windows common controls: custom draw for headers (`NM_CUSTOMDRAW`) (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from comctl32's documented custom draw for headers)

- **Decision.** A header control's paint runs custom draw with a plain `NMCUSTOMDRAW`
  (headers have no colour fields): `CDDS_PREPAINT`, then, with `CDRF_NOTIFYITEMDRAW`,
  `CDDS_ITEMPREPAINT` for each item (up to 64) with its index and rectangle. An answer with
  `CDRF_NEWFONT` takes the text colour the program set on the paint's device context with

## D369 Windows: per-pixel alpha in `UpdateLayeredWindow` (`AC_SRC_ALPHA`) (batch part 13's rest, D366's "Not yet"; M15, M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Windows' documented `BLENDFUNCTION`)

- **Decision.**
  - **The server.** `SET_LAYERED` gains the flag 4, `PIXEL_ALPHA`: the window's content
    carries each pixel's alpha in its top byte, its colour already multiplied by it, as
    Windows' 32-bit premultiplied bitmaps do (`Window::pixel_alpha`). The compositor scales
    such a pixel and its alpha by the window's constant opacity and adds it to what is under
    it times one minus that alpha (`mix_premultiplied`), rounded per channel and clamped; the
    colour key still wins where the colour matches. One `Blend` value (opacity, key, pixel
    alpha) now says how a window's row is drawn, so the opaque path stays a plain copy.
  - **The layer.** `UpdateLayeredWindow` with `ULW_ALPHA` and `BLENDFUNCTION.AlphaFormat`
    `AC_SRC_ALPHA` copies the source with its top byte kept (`gdi::copy_with_alpha`; every
    other GDI copy keeps clearing it, as `BitBlt` does) and sets the server's `PIXEL_ALPHA`;
    `SetLayeredWindowAttributes` turns it off again, as switching a window back to constant
    alpha does on Windows.
- **Why premultiplied.** `AC_SRC_ALPHA` is documented to take premultiplied pixels, so the
  server adds the colour as it is instead of multiplying it, one multiply per channel fewer.
- **Not yet.** `UpdateLayeredWindowIndirect` and `prcDirty`; GDI drawing that writes alpha
  (`AlphaBlend` into a layered window); child layered windows.

## D370 The tray's overflow popup (batch part 13's rest, D357's "Not yet"; M15, M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md section 11) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A press on the bar's overflow button (`Hidden icons`, from the fifth icon)
  opens the overflow popup: the power menu's chrome, 256 wide, one 32-pixel row per icon the
  button stands for, in the order they were added; the icon at the row's (8, 8), its name
  (the tip, or the window's title) at x + 32, cut with `...` at 26 glyphs; the hovered or
  keyboard row in `MENU_HOVER`. It is anchored as the keyboard layout menu: under the top bar
  with its right edge at the button's, or 4 pixels above the taskbar. A left, right or middle
  press on a row closes the popup first and then is the same press on that icon in the bar
  (its window gets the button's messages); a press on the button again, or anywhere else,
  closes it, and a press elsewhere goes on to what is under it. Up and Down move the
  highlight, Enter and Space are a left click, Shift+F10 and the Menu key a right click, Esc
  closes. While it is open the button is drawn pressed, the bar's tooltips wait and keys do
  not reach the terminal. Removing an icon, or its window going away, closes it.
- **Not yet.** The program's context menu as a shell menu (section 14), `NIN_POPUPOPEN`,
  double clicks, `NIN_KEYSELECT`, `Shell_NotifyIconGetRect`.

## D371 Tray programs' context menus as shell menus (batch part 13's rest, D357's "Not yet"; M15, M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/windows-tooltips-tray-v0.5.md section 14) and the code-only session (engineering, the protocol)

- **Decision.**
  - **When.** `TrackPopupMenu(Ex)` whose top-level window is hidden or minimised, or whose
    point lies outside that window's content, is a shell menu: a tray program's menu, opened
    at the pointer on the bar for a window usually never shown. Inside the content nothing
    changes (the menu is drawn in the window's buffer).
  - **Protocol.** `SHOW_SHELL_MENU` (request 53, 16 bytes: window, length, address) carries
    the entries, each a flags byte (1 grayed, 2 checked, 4 radio, 8 separator), a length byte
    and the label in UTF-8: at most 32 entries of 64 bytes; the kernel reads them from the
    program's memory. When the menu closes the window gets a `SHELL_MENU` event (18): the
    chosen entry's index plus 1, or 0 for none. A new shell menu dismisses an open one (it
    answers 0), and the window going away forgets it.
  - **Server.** The menu is anchored to the tray icon the same client pressed last (its
    place, or the overflow button's when it is hidden there), otherwise under the pointer;
    the power menu's chrome, width `max(160, 8 * widest + 48)`, rows of 32 and separators of
    8, the label at x + 24, grayed labels `TEXT_DIM`, a tick for a checked entry and a 6-pixel
    dot for a radio one; under the top bar with its right edge at the icon's, or 4 above the
    taskbar, clipped to the screen. The icon is drawn pressed while it is open. A click on an
    entry that can be chosen chooses it; a click on a grayed entry or a separator does
    nothing; a click elsewhere answers 0 and goes on to what is under it, except on the
    icon itself. Up and Down skip what cannot be chosen, Enter and Space choose, Esc answers 0.
  - **Layer.** The labels lose their `&` marks (`&&` stays one `&`) and the tab before an
    accelerator becomes two spaces. An item that opens a submenu is sent grayed (submenus in
    shell menus are not in this version, as section 14 says). The call runs the thread's
    messages until the answer comes, then posts `WM_COMMAND` or returns the id with
    `TPM_RETURNCMD`, as before.
- **Not yet.** Submenus and owner-drawn items in shell menus, `TPM_*` alignment (the anchor
  is the icon), keyboard access to tray icons (`NIN_KEYSELECT`, `NIM_SETFOCUS`).

## D372 AppKit's NSScrollView, NSClipView and NSScroller (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 10) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Geometry** lives in `eggos-macos-gui`'s `scroll_view` (host-tested): the border's four
    lines, the clip view and `contentSize` with the scrollers shown (8 pixels, autohiding when
    asked), the thumb (`track * view / document`, at least 24), the offset's clamp, the wheel
    (72 per notch), paging (`view - 24`), a track press, a thumb drag and the least scroll that
    reveals a rect. Offsets count from the document's top, so every document shows its top
    first; `bounds_y` turns one into AppKit's bounds origin (from the bottom for a document
    that is not flipped).
  - **The classes.** `NSScrollView` makes its `NSClipView` as its one subview; the clip view
    holds the document view as its one subview and keeps the offset. The scroll view lays the
    clip view out (`tile`) whenever its scrollers, border or document change and before it
    draws, and draws the border (`button.border`), the tracks (`progress.track`), the thumbs
    (`bar.pressed`, `button.inactive` while dragged, r4) and the corner. The clip view fills
    its background (`field.bg` or its `backgroundColor`) when it draws one.
  - **The view tree.** A clip view's bounds origin shifts its subviews in `draw_tree`,
    `hit_test` and `origin_in_window` (so `convertPoint:` and `setNeedsDisplay:` follow the
    scroll); the clip view's frame clips the document's drawing and hit-testing.
  - **Input.** NSView's `scrollWheel:` and `keyDown:` now pass the event to the superview,
    as AppKit's responder chain does, so the innermost scroll view that can scroll takes the
    wheel (Shift or the sideways wheel scroll across), and Page Up, Page Down, Home and End
    reach the scroll view when its document leaves them unhandled. Presses on a scroller page
    or grab the thumb; drags follow the grab.
  - **API.** `contentView`, `documentView`, the scroller, border, background and autohide
    properties, `contentSize`, `documentVisibleRect`, `tile`, `reflectScrolledClipView:`,
    `scrollToPoint:`, `scrollPoint:`, `scrollRectToVisible:`, `enclosingScrollView`, and
    `NSScroller`'s `floatValue`, `knobProportion` and `scrollerWidth`; rulers, magnification,
    elasticity and knob styles are accepted and ignored.
- **Not yet.** Hover colours on the scroller, the element tree for agents (section 17), a
    table's fixed header beside the scroller (section 11), the render-hash tests of section
    10.4 that need the runtime, re-tiling on `setFrame:` before the next draw.

## D373 AppKit's NSTableView, NSTableColumn and a single-index NSIndexSet (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 11) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Geometry** in `eggos-macos-gui`'s `table_view` (host-tested): the header's place, the
    columns' left edges, the 7-pixel resize handles on the separators, a row's rect under
    the offset, the rows shown, the row under a point, the alternate rows, a resize's clamp
    (at least the toolkit's 40), how Up, Down, Home, End and the page keys move the
    selection, and the least scroll that shows a row whole.
  - **The table is the scroll view's document** (D372), sized to the clip view's width (or
    its columns' when wider) and `28 + 24 x rows` tall. It draws its header at the top of
    the visible part of itself, so the header stays put while the rows scroll under it and
    the scroll range is the rows' height less the body's, as the design's worked example
    says (222 for 20 rows in a 286-pixel clip view). Header and rows scroll across together.
  - **Drawing** follows section 11: the surface (`field.bg` or the table's
    `backgroundColor`), odd rows `menu.bg` with alternation on, the selected row
    `selection` across the table with `>` in `accent` and, while the table is the first
    responder, the focus ring; the grid masks' lines in `menu.border`; each cell the data
    source's object's `description`, asked for every drawn cell at every paint, the first
    column's text at x + 24, right-aligned columns to their right padding; disabled tables
    draw their text dim and no mark.
  - **Input.** A press on a row makes the table the first responder, selects the row (the
    delegate's `tableView:shouldSelectRow:` may refuse) and sends `action`, or
    `doubleAction` for a second press on the row within 400 ms; a press below the rows
    deselects unless empty selection is refused. Keys move the selection and scroll it into
    view, Enter sends the double action, Left and Right scroll across by 48; other keys go
    up the responder chain. A press on a header handle of a user-resizable column drags its
    width live; release tells the delegate (`tableViewColumnDidResize:`), Esc restores it.
    The wheel reaches the scroll view through NSView's default (D372).
  - **Selection changes** by pointer, keys, `selectRowIndexes:byExtendingSelection:`,
    `deselectAll:` or `reloadData` send `tableViewSelectionDidChange:` to the delegate and
    post `NSTableViewSelectionDidChangeNotification`.
  - **NSTableColumn** keeps identifier, title, width (100), minimum (10), maximum (1000),
    resizing mask, alignment and hidden; its `headerCell` and `dataCell` answer the column
    itself, whose `stringValue` is the title, so `column.headerCell.stringValue = ...` works.
  - **NSIndexSet** holds at most one index (single selection): `indexSetWithIndex:`,
    `indexSet`, `firstIndex`, `count`, `containsIndex:`. It lives with AppKit for now, so a
    program that links Foundation alone does not find it.
- **Why the table answers `isFlipped` NO.** The layer draws every view with y growing upward
  (section 0); a table that said YES would make apps' rects for `scrollRectToVisible:` mean
  something the drawing does not. The scroll position from the top is the same either way.
- **Not yet.** Row hover (needs `mouseMoved:` for views), the resize pointer over handles,
  view-based tables (`tableView:viewForTableColumn:row:`), multiple selection and a full
  NSIndexSet in Foundation, sorting, per-row heights, the element tree for agents, the
  scroll view's scroller beside the body only, the render-hash tests that need the runtime.

## D374 AppKit's NSImage and NSImageView (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 12) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **NSImage** decodes PNG once with our own `eggos-png` row decoder into premultiplied
    `0xAARRGGBB` (at most 4096 a side and 16 M pixels, else nil; a damaged file is nil).
    `imageNamed:` looks in the bundle's resources for the name as given and with each of the
    design's extensions, keeps what it found under that name, and `setName:` registers an
    image; `initWithContentsOfFile:`, `initByReferencingFile:`, `initWithContentsOfURL:`
    (file URLs), `initWithData:` and `initWithSize:` (transparent) make one. Drawing from
    `drawRect:` blits at a point unscaled, or scales into a rect by nearest neighbour after
    cropping to a non-zero `fromRect`; `fraction` scales alpha and the premultiplied colour;
    `NSCompositingOperationCopy` writes without blending, every other operation blends
    source-over (`s + (d x (255 - a) + 127) / 255`).
  - **The toolkit canvas** gains `composite`, the premultiplied blit with that blend, at the
    canvas's scale, so 2x pixel-doubles like every bitmap.
  - **NSImageView** draws its frame style (a `menu.border` line for photo and groove, a
    `button.border` line around `button.bg` for bezel and button, the image area inset by
    2), then the image placed by `imageScaling` and `imageAlignment` as the design's tables
    say, clipped to the image area. The scaled pixels are kept until the image or the drawn
    size changes, so a repaint is a blit and a blend.
  - **Agents** see an image view as `graphic`, named by the image's name or its file's name
    without folder and extension, valued `<w>x<h>` or `none`.
  - **Geometry** (`eggos-macos-gui`'s `image_view`, host-tested): the limits, the image
    area, the drawn size under each scaling, the place under each alignment, nearest
    scaling, fading and premultiplying.
- **Not yet.** JPEG, GIF, TIFF, BMP, `.ico` and `.icns` decoding (the design's `eggos-image`;
    a name tried with those extensions finds nothing until they decode), the system images
    `NSImageName...`, `accessibilityLabel` as the element's name, `lockFocus`,
    `TIFFRepresentation`, `CGImage`, `representations`.

## D375 The About panel's icon image and credits (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md sections 15.1, 15.2, 15.5 and 15.6) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Icon.** The panel's 48x48 comes from the options' `ApplicationIcon` (an `NSImage`),
    then `setApplicationIconImage:`, then the installed `app.icon`, then the generic tile.
    An image is fitted once when the panel opens (`fit_icon`: proportional and centred, a
    larger image by area average, a smaller one by the largest whole factor) and blended
    over the panel as the installed icon is. `setApplicationIconImage:` repaints an open
    panel; `applicationIconImage` answers what was set (nil otherwise). Nothing else uses
    it. The tree's icon value gains `image`.
  - **Credits.** The options' `Credits` (`NSString`, or `NSAttributedString` through its
    `string`), else the bundle's `Credits.txt`, cut at 4096 bytes; RTF and HTML are not
    read. The text wraps at words to 232 pixels (newlines and empty lines kept, a word too
    wide broken at a glyph) in a 256x108 region below the body lines, bordered in
    `button.border` on `field.bg`; the panel grows to `T + 124`. When the lines overflow,
    an 8-pixel scroller shows (track 106); the wheel scrolls 60 per notch and a track press
    82, clamped. Agents see a `Credits` group valued `line <k> of <n>` and one label per
    line whose whole cell shows.
  - **Copyright fallback.** `CFBundleGetInfoString`'s first line when there is no
    `NSHumanReadableCopyright` and no `Copyright` option.
- **Not yet.** Dragging the credits' thumb, `set-text` on the credits group, an
  `applicationIconImage` made from `app.icon` when none was set; raising the panel instead of
  re-creating it and the panel in `NSApp.windows` (sections 15.3 and 15.4).

## D376 `RAISE_WINDOW`: an app raises its own window, and the About panel is raised, not re-created (batch part 15's rest; M15, M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 15.3) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Protocol.** `RAISE_WINDOW` (request 54, 4 bytes: the window) raises and focuses one
    of the caller's own windows as `ManageWindow Focus` does (restoring a minimised one),
    only while the caller owns the focused window or none is focused: `EPERM` for another
    client's window, `ENOENT` for none, `EBUSY` while another client has the focus, so an
    app in the background cannot take it (what `makeKeyAndOrderFront:` from a background
    app does on macOS too).
  - **AppKit.** `makeKeyAndOrderFront:` and `orderFront:` on a window already on the server
    send it instead of doing nothing. The About panel gathers its content again; when
    nothing changed (name, version, copyright, credits, icon) it is raised where the person
    left it, its credits' scroll kept; when the content changed it is destroyed and made
    again at its place, as before.
- **Not yet.** The About panel as an `NSPanel` in `NSApp.windows` (section 15.4).

## D377 NSAlert's element tree and agents' actions on it (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 16) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** While `runModal` runs, the dialog window answers `wm show` itself: element 1
  the window named by the app's name, then the message and informative lines as labels at
  their drawn cells (the informative one absent when empty), then the buttons left to right
  at their drawn rects, each `focusable`, `focused` on the ringed one while the dialog has
  the keyboard, `default` on the default button. `invoke` on a button answers `runModal`
  exactly as a click does and closes the dialog; `focus` moves the ring; `select` and
  `set-text`, and every action on the window or a label, are `NotSupported`; an id past the
  buttons is `NoSuchElement`. The parent windows still answer their trees and refuse actions
  (`Disabled`), as before. The toolkit's panel gains the accessors this needs (button count,
  titles, focus, default, line cells).

## D378 What agents see of scroll views and tables (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15, M14; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 17) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The window's element walk (`elements.rs`) becomes one walk that both writes
  the tree and finds an element by id, so the numbering of views and of the elements that
  are not views always agrees.
  - **Scroll view**: a `group` valued `<x>,<y>`, its offset in document pixels; the clip view
    has no element; the document view and its subviews are its children, their bounds
    clipped to the clip view, and one wholly outside gets its width and height 0 at the clip
    view's top or bottom edge (the Windows layer's rule). `set-text "<x>,<y>"` scrolls there,
    clamped; other text is `NotSupported`.
  - **Table**: a `table` valued `row <n> of <rows>`, `no row of <rows>` or `0 rows`,
    `focusable`, `focused`, `disabled`; `set-text "<n>"` selects row n (from 1) as a click
    does, scrolled into view, its action sent and the delegate told (`Done` with no change
    out of range); `focus` makes it the first responder. Its children are the header cells
    (`columnheader`, named by the title; `set-text "<width>"` resizes as a drag, clamped,
    `NotSupported` when the column refuses resizing) and then the **shown** rows only (`row`,
    named by the first cell, valued every cell joined by tabs, `selected`; `select` as a
    click, `invoke` as a double click).
  - Checkboxes, radios and toggle buttons were already described and acted on (D233); image
    views as D374 says.
- **Not yet.** `accessibilityLabel` as a name, rows beyond the tree's size, the element tree
  checks of `mac-views.app` (section 18).

## D379 The views test app `mac-views.app` (batch part 15's rest, D233's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/macos-gui-v0.3.md section 18) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `tests/macos-views/main.m` is our own Objective-C app, built on CI's macOS
  runner like `mac-paint` (`OBJC_PROGRAMS` gains it): one fixed 480x360 window with the
  checkbox, the two radios, the push-on-push-off `Bold`, an `NSImageView` subclass with a

  pasteboard and a result label, as section 18.1 lays them out; its main menu has `About
  mac-views` (opening the About panel with `ApplicationIcon` `egg` and section 15.7's
  `Credits`) and the Edit menu. `Info.plist` gives `mac-views`, version `0.3.0` and

  and `Contents/Resources/egg.png`, a 48x48 egg over transparency it draws itself
  (`encode_rgba_png`), and archives it as `mac-views.zip`.
- **Not yet.** Section 18.2's host renders (`mac_views.rs`) and 18.3's QEMU steps, and
  `NSImage` reading the bundle's `.icns` (D374's "Not yet").

## D380 C++ exceptions on macOS and the libc++abi basics (batch part 16's rest, D234's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from the Itanium C++ ABI's exception handling and RTTI layouts that macOS uses)

- **Decision.**
  - **One unwinder for both languages.** A C++ exception is the same record D175's unwinder
    already walks (`Raised`), placed in the 16-byte-rounded header in front of the object
    `__cxa_allocate_exception` returns, with the thrown `type_info`, the destructor, a count
    of the handlers holding it and the address the matching `catch` receives. `__cxa_throw`
    and `__cxa_rethrow` are register-capturing entries like `objc_exception_throw`; the
    search and cleanup phases, the LSDA reading and `_Unwind_Resume` are shared; the layer
    still reads every LSDA itself, so `__gxx_personality_v0` is only a symbol to bind.
  - **Matching** (`objc/cxx_types.rs`, host-tested): `catch (...)` takes everything; a type
    takes itself (same record, or same mangled name, the non-unique bit masked); a class
    takes a derived class through `__si_class_type_info` and the public bases of
    `__vmi_class_type_info` (virtual bases through the object's vtable), the handler getting
    the adjusted address; a pointer type takes a pointer whose qualifiers it has, of the same
    or a derived pointee, or `void`. An Objective-C `@catch` never takes a C++ exception, and
    a C++ `catch` of a type never takes an Objective-C one (`catch (...)` takes both).
  - **Handlers.** `__cxa_begin_catch` answers the adjusted object, `__cxa_end_catch` destroys
    the object and frees it when the last handler ends and it was not rethrown;
    `__cxa_get_exception_ptr`, `__cxa_current_exception_type`, `__cxa_free_exception`. AppKit's
    run-loop boundary destroys a C++ exception it takes. Uncaught, the program ends with
    libc++abi's line and the type's name.
  - **libc++abi basics** (`objc/cxx_abi.rs`): `operator new` and `delete` (plain, sized,
    aligned, `nothrow`; a failing `new` throws `std::bad_alloc`), static locals' guards,
    `__cxa_atexit` (run at `exit`, last first), pure and deleted virtual calls,
    `std::terminate`, `std::exception` and `std::bad_alloc` (vtables, type information,
    constructors, destructors, `what`), the five `type_info` vtables and the fundamental
    types' and `const char *`'s records.
- **Not yet.** `std::exception_ptr` and `std::rethrow_exception`, `dynamic_cast`
  (`__dynamic_cast`), the rest of libc++ (`std::runtime_error` and the other standard
  exceptions, strings, streams), foreign-exception interop with Swift, a C++ test program in
  CI's macOS programs, and UDCalc with its Sparkle framework.

## D381 Foundation's NSUserDefaults, and property-list objects written as XML (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Foundation's documented behaviour)

- **Decision.**
  - **Property lists** (`foundation/property_list.rs`): a parsed property list (XML or
    binary, our `eggos-plist`) is made into Foundation's immutable strings, numbers,
    booleans (`kCFBooleanTrue`/`False`), dates, data, arrays and dictionaries, 64 levels deep
    at most; those objects are written back as an XML property list (Apple's header and
    DTD, `&`, `<` and `>` escaped, data in base64, dates as UTC `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`,
    reals as their exact shortest decimal); anything else makes the write fail.
  - **NSUserDefaults** keeps the app's settings in
    `~/Library/Preferences/<CFBundleIdentifier>.plist` (the program's name without a bundle
    identifier), read once when `standardUserDefaults` is first asked for and written back,
    folder made, atomically, after every change; `registerDefaults:` values answer for keys
    never set and are never written. `objectForKey:`, the typed getters (`integerForKey:`,
    `boolForKey:`, `doubleForKey:`, `floatForKey:` reading numbers or strings;
    `stringForKey:`, `arrayForKey:`, `dictionaryForKey:`, `dataForKey:` answering nil for
    another type), the setters, `removeObjectForKey:`, `synchronize`,
    `dictionaryRepresentation`; `init` answers the standard defaults.
- **Not yet.** Suites (`initWithSuiteName:`), the global and argument domains, key-value
    observing of defaults, `NSUserDefaultsDidChangeNotification`, `URLForKey:`.

## D382 AppKit's NSScreen and NSTrackingArea (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from AppKit's documented behaviour)

- **Decision.**
  - **NSScreen**: one screen. `visibleFrame` is the server's work area in AppKit's
    bottom-left coordinates; `frame` runs from the screen's origin to the work area's far
    edges (the server tells clients the work area, not the panels outside it, so a bar on
    the far side is not counted); `backingScaleFactor` 1; `mainScreen`, `deepestScreen` and
    `screens` answer it.
  - **NSTrackingArea** (`initWithRect:options:owner:userInfo:`, `rect`, `options`, `owner`,
    `userInfo`) and NSView's `addTrackingArea:`, `removeTrackingArea:`, `trackingAreas`,
    `updateTrackingAreas`. The layer keeps the added areas in one table; on each pointer move
    in a window the areas of its views (their rect, or the view's bounds with
    `NSTrackingInVisibleRect`) send their owner `mouseEntered:` and `mouseExited:` as the
    pointer crosses their edge (`NSTrackingMouseEnteredAndExited`) and `mouseMoved:` inside
    (`NSTrackingMouseMoved`); the pointer leaving the window exits them. A view being freed
    takes its areas with it. The activity options (`ActiveAlways`, `ActiveInKeyWindow`, ...)
    are accepted; areas act while their window takes the pointer.
- **Not yet.** Cursor updates through areas (`NSTrackingCursorUpdate`), enter and exit
    while dragging, `NSEvent`'s `trackingArea` and `userData`, more than one screen.

## D383 AppKit's NSSound from WAV data, silent until EggOS has an audio device (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, researched: EggOS has no audio driver or audio API yet, and no roadmap item names one)
