- **Decision.** `NSSound` reads WAV data (RIFF `WAVE`, PCM, float or extensible samples, 1 to
  8 channels, 8 to 32 bits; `eggos-macos-gui`'s `sound`, host-tested) from memory
  (`initWithData:`), a file or URL, or a name in the bundle's resources (`soundNamed:`, with
  `.wav` and `.wave` tried), keeps the bytes and answers `duration`, `volume`, `loops`,
  `name` and `delegate` as macOS does. With no audio device in EggOS, `play` answers NO
  (macOS's answer for a sound that could not start), `isPlaying` is NO and nothing is heard;
  an app such as Minesweeper that plays its effects carries on without them. Data that is
  not a WAV this reads makes the initializer answer nil, as macOS does for undecodable data.
- **Not yet.** Playing through an audio device (none exists: an audio stack, its driver
  model, the server's mixing and a capability with its three front-ends need their own
  roadmap item); AIFF, MP3 and AAC; `sound:didFinishPlaying:`.

## D384 NSAttributedString and NSMutableAttributedString (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Foundation's and AppKit's documented behaviour)

- **Decision.** An attributed string keeps its text (a private mutable copy) and runs that
  cover it end to end in UTF-16 units, each with its own copied attribute dictionary.
  `attributesAtIndex:effectiveRange:` and `attribute:atIndex:effectiveRange:` answer a run's
  dictionary and range; the mutable class splits runs at a range's edges to
  `setAttributes:range:`, `addAttribute:value:range:`, `addAttributes:range:` and
  `removeAttribute:range:`, shifts and drops runs as `replaceCharactersInRange:withString:`
  edits the text, and appends and replaces whole attributed strings. AppKit draws one
  (`drawAtPoint:`, `drawInRect:`, `size`) run after run with each run's font and colour
  through NSString's drawing (D147). `NSTextField`'s `attributedStringValue` and
  `NSButton`'s `attributedTitle` take the plain text, as the layer's controls draw one
  style. The classes live with AppKit, so a Foundation-only program does not find them yet.
- **Not yet.** Attributes beyond font and colour (paragraph styles, underline, links),
  `enumerateAttributesInRange:`, RTF and HTML import, archiving.

## D385 AppKit's NSGridView, NSGridRow, NSGridColumn and NSGridCell (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from AppKit's documented behaviour, without Auto Layout)

- **Decision.** A grid keeps its views row by row (`gridViewWithViews:`,
  `gridViewWithNumberOfColumns:rows:`, `addRowWithViews:`, `NSGridCell.contentView`), each a
  subview; `emptyContentView` is a placeholder that leaves its cell empty. The layer has no
  Auto Layout, so the grid lays itself out by frames (`eggos-macos-gui`'s `grid_view`,
  host-tested): each column as wide and each row as tall as its largest view's frame unless
  the app set the column's `width` or the row's `height`, the grid's spacing between them
  (6 by default), and each view kept at its own size, or stretched with `Fill`, at the
  leading, trailing or centre of its cell by the cell's, else its column's or row's, else
  the grid's placement. It lays out after every change and when it first draws, and a grid
  with no size takes the size its cells need (`fittingSize`, `intrinsicContentSize`).
  `NSGridRow`, `NSGridColumn` and `NSGridCell` are small objects pointing back at their grid.
- **Not yet.** Merged cells, padding, hidden rows and columns, inserting and moving rows and
  columns, `rowAlignment` by baselines, and views that change size after layout without the
  app calling `layout`.

## D386 CoreGraphics drawing behind NSGraphicsContext (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from CoreGraphics' documented C API)

- **Decision.**
  - **Paths** (`eggos-macos-gui`'s `path`, host-tested): moves, lines, cubic curves (16
    segments), arcs (64 segments a turn, either direction), `AddArcToPoint`'s tangent arcs,
    rectangles and ellipses (48 segments) are flattened to polygons under the context's
    affine transform (translate, scale, rotate; sine and cosine from our `eggos-math`), filled
    by scanlines at pixel centres with the non-zero or even-odd rule, and stroked as 1-pixel
    lines or, wider, as filled quadrilaterals per segment, clipped to the view.
  - **The context.** One `CGContext` (a token pointer), which `NSGraphicsContext`'s
    `currentContext.CGContext` and `graphicsPort` answer; each view's `drawRect:` starts from
    a fresh graphics state (identity transform in the view's coordinates, black fill and
    stroke, width 1) and an empty path. `CGContextSaveGState` and `RestoreGState` keep up to
    64 states; `NSGraphicsContext`'s `saveGraphicsState` and `restoreGraphicsState` use them.
  - **Functions**: the state (`SetRGB`/`Gray`/`...WithColor` fill and stroke, `SetLineWidth`,
    `TranslateCTM`, `ScaleCTM`, `RotateCTM`), the path (`BeginPath`, `MoveToPoint`,
    `AddLineToPoint`, `AddCurveToPoint`, `AddArc`, `AddArcToPoint`, `ClosePath`, `AddRect`,
    `AddEllipseInRect`) and painting (`FillPath`, `EOFillPath`, `StrokePath`, `DrawPath`,
    `FillRect`, `StrokeRect`, `ClearRect` to the window background, `FillEllipseInRect`,
    `StrokeEllipseInRect`). `CGColor` values are interned records (`CGColorCreateGenericRGB`,
    `CreateSRGB`, `CreateGenericGray`, `GetAlpha`, `GetComponents`; retain and release keep
    them) and `NSColor.CGColor` answers one.
- **Not yet.** Clipping paths, dashes, caps and joins, anti-aliasing and alpha blending of
  fills (a colour is opaque or invisible, as the layer's other drawing), images
  (`CGContextDrawImage`), text through CoreText, gradients and shadows, and `CGPath`
  objects.

## D387 Swift subclasses of the layer's AppKit classes, laid out at run time (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from Swift's class metadata ABI)

- **Context.** A Swift class that inherits from an Objective-C class whose size the compiler
  cannot fix (Apple's AppKit classes, and the layer's own, which are not Apple's size) is
  finished at run time: its metadata accessor calls `swift_initClassMetadata2` or
  `swift_updateClassMetadata2` with its fields' type layouts and the field offset vector to
  fill. The Objective-C runtime's ivar sliding (D175) already moves statically laid out
  classes; these two entry points were missing.
- **Decision.** Both lay the class's stored properties out from its superclass's instance
  size as the layer's runtime has it (realizing the superclass; a Swift superclass's own
  metadata otherwise), each field at its type's alignment (`field_layout`, host-tested),
  write the offsets into the field offset vector, the metadata's instance size and
  alignment mask, and the class's `class_ro_t` (`instanceStart`, `instanceSize`) and ivar
  offset variables, then realize the class in the Objective-C runtime and answer that the
  metadata is complete. `swift_getInitializedObjCClass` realizes a class and answers it.
- **Not yet.** Resilient class stubs (`swift_getObjCClassFromObject` for classes from other
  modules), generic classes' metadata instantiation (`swift_allocateGenericClassMetadata`),
  and Swift's `@objc` property accessors through key-value coding.

## D388 libdispatch in the macOS layer: the main queue on the run loop, and one thread of work (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, from libdispatch's documented C API; the threading choice researched against the layer's one-thread AppKit)

- **Decision.** libSystem gains the libdispatch calls programs use most:
  `_dispatch_main_q` (what `dispatch_get_main_queue()` is), `dispatch_get_global_queue`,
  `dispatch_queue_create` and its label, `dispatch_async(_f)`, `dispatch_sync(_f)` and the
  barrier forms, `dispatch_time`, `dispatch_walltime`, `dispatch_after(_f)`,
  `dispatch_once(_f)`, semaphores, groups (`enter`, `leave`, `async`, `notify`, `wait`),
  `dispatch_main`, and retain and release (queues live as long as the program).
  - **The main queue** keeps its work in order and runs it on the main thread's loop: each
    turn of AppKit's run loop and of `NSRunLoop`'s main loop runs the work that is ready and
    the delayed work that is due, and AppKit's loop sleeps no longer than the next delayed
    work; `dispatch_main` is that loop for a program without one.
  - **Other queues**: the layer runs the program's work on one thread (AppKit's, as on
    macOS for UI), so a global or private queue's asynchronous work runs at once on the
    calling thread, in order, done before the caller could wait for it; synchronous work runs
    at once; delayed work waits for the main loop. Semaphores and groups count without
    blocking, which is enough when nothing runs concurrently.
- **Why not threads yet.** Real concurrency needs the layer's Objective-C runtime, autorelease
  pools and AppKit state to be safe across threads, which they are not built for; running
  the work at once keeps every program that only offloads work and comes back to the main
  queue correct.
- **Not yet.** Queues as Objective-C objects (`OS_dispatch_queue`), which Swift's
  `DispatchQueue` needs before the Dispatch overlay's entry points (whose argument lowering
  must first be read from a `swiftc` build), concurrent queues on threads, sources and I/O,
  `NSRunLoop` waking for delayed work.

## D389 `cargo xtask swift-app`: Minesweeper 1.0.0 as the Swift app check (batch part 17, D180's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering, the app chosen by D180's research)

- **Decision.** `cargo xtask swift-app --arch <aarch64|x86_64>` downloads Minesweeper 1.0.0's
  release archive (pinned URL and SHA-256 from docs/compatibility.md; test data, never
  shipped or committed), builds the release kernel with the layers and boots it with the
  archive in the host folder: `app install` and `app open` must report success, the app's
  window must appear and be listed by `wm list`, a click on the middle of its board must
  change the window (a cell opened), Cmd+N must change it again (a new game), and Cmd+Q must
  leave none of its windows before the power-off. CI gains a `swift-app` job on both
  architectures, **outside `check`'s needs** until the app runs, so it reports without
  holding `main` red.
- **Why these steps.** Flagging a cell and the exact pixels of the board need the app run once
  to read its layout and its flagging gesture (right click or Ctrl+click), which code-only
  mode cannot do; the frame comparisons and the flag step are added then, as CocoaGame's
  check (D175) has them.
- **Not yet.** Flagging a cell, frame comparisons against host renders, the About panel step,
  and moving the job into `check`'s needs once it passes.

## D390 NSImage decodes every format our `eggos-image` reads (D374's "Not yet"; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** D374 wrote `NSImage`'s decoding against `eggos-png` alone and listed the other
  formats as not yet, unaware that the workspace's own `eggos-image` (D231) already decodes
  PNG, JPEG (baseline, extended, progressive), GIF, TIFF, BMP and `.ico` from untrusted bytes
  with capped sides, pixels and buffers. `NSImage` now decodes through it, its limits set to
  the design's 4096 a side and 16 M pixels, and the macOS layer depends on `eggos-image`
  instead of `eggos-png`. So `imageNamed:`'s extension list finds every format it names
  except `.icns`, which stays not yet.

## D391 The system file picker, `/bin/pick` (batch part 18; M12, M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/file-picker-v0.3.md) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **A crate of its own**, `eggos-picker`: the command line (`options`), the filters
    (`filter`) and what each step of choosing does (`state`, the `Picker`), taken as they were
    written, unbuilt, on the branch `wip/eggos-picker` before that branch paused, plus the
    window and the program written now.
  - **The window** is built on the toolkit's widget tree (section 4): the toolbar with `<`, `^`
    and the path field; the `Places` list; the `Entries` table (`Name`, `Size` right-aligned,
    `Modified`; sortable; cells from the picker); the empty or error line; in `save` mode the
    name row, prefilled with `--name` and its stem selected; the bottom band with
    `Hidden files`, the filter drop-down when there are filters, `Cancel` and the primary
    button (the default). Notices show for 3 s and close on a key or a press; `Replace
    <name>?` asks with `Cancel` and `Replace`. Enter commits the focused field or presses the
    primary, Esc closes a question or cancels, F5 reloads, the close control cancels.
  - **The person chooses** (section 11): the window is created `PERSON_INPUT_ONLY`, and the
    table, the name field, the primary button and `Replace` take no agent's action; an agent
    can still see the picker and move it between folders through the places, the path field,
    back and up. The MCP server has no `pick` tool, by design.
  - **The program** is another name of the Settings program (`/bin/pick`, a hard link, so the
    toolkit is in the image once): exit 0 with the chosen paths, one per line; 1 for Cancel;
    2 with `pick: ...` for a usage error; 3 with `pick: cannot show a window`.
  - The toolkit's key names gain `F5` and the keypad's Enter.
- **Not yet.** `--over` placement over the app's window, Mod+L, Mod+H, type-ahead, the device
  classes of section 16, the host tests of section 17, and section 14: the Windows layer's
  `GetOpenFileNameW` and friends, AppKit's `NSOpenPanel` and `NSSavePanel`, the Text Editor
  and Files starting `pick` instead of their own pickers.

## D392 The layers, the Text Editor and Files open the system file picker (batch part 18; M12, M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/file-picker-v0.3.md section 14, text-editor-v0.3.md section 17.6, desktop-v0.3-gui.md section 8.1 item 24) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Windows layer.** `GetOpenFileNameW` and `GetSaveFileNameW` (and the ANSI forms through
    them) start `/bin/pick` with the request's title, initial folder, `lpstrFilter` pairs
    (`description|patterns`) and `nFilterIndex`, and for Save its file name, default
    extension and `--overwrite` unless `OFN_OVERWRITEPROMPT`; the owner is disabled and the
    thread's messages keep running while the picker is open (`win32/pick_process.rs`); the
    first chosen path is written back as before (`C:\...`, offsets, title). When `pick`
    cannot start or show (a headless install without the desktop component, exit 2 or 3),
    the layer's own picker serves instead, so it stays as the fallback rather than being
    removed. `processes.rs` gains `spawn_with_output`.
  - **AppKit.** New `NSSavePanel` and `NSOpenPanel` keep what the app sets (title or message,
    prompt, name, directory URL, allowed file types as `*.<type>` filters, files or folders,
    multiple selection) and `runModal`, `beginWithCompletionHandler:` and
    `beginSheetModalForWindow:completionHandler:` run `pick` through `posix_spawn` with its
    output on a pipe, the app's windows still drawing and its input set aside, answering
    `NSModalResponseOK` with `URL`/`URLs` or Cancel. Foundation gains a file-URL `NSURL`
    (`fileURLWithPath:`, `URLWithString:` of `file://`, `path`, `absoluteString`,
    `lastPathComponent`, `pathExtension`, appending and deleting components).
  - **The Text Editor**: when `/bin/pick` is in the image, Open and Save As ask its program to
    run `pick open|save` with the text filters, the document's folder and, for Save As, its
    name and `--extension txt`; the path bar stays for an image without the picker. Save
    As's replace question is the picker's; a chosen file to open while the document is
    modified still asks to save first, after the choice.
  - **Files**: a link row's menu gains `Change Target...`, which runs `pick open --folders`
    in the stored target's folder (else the link's) and makes the new link beside the old one
    and renames it over it, so the link is never missing; errors are `Could not change the
    target of <name> (<errno>).`
  - `eggos-app` gains `linux::run_with_output` for starting a program with its output on a
    pipe; the picker runs with an empty environment, as the installer's translation does.
- **Not yet.** `--over` from each caller, `SHBrowseForFolder` and `IFileDialog`, multiple
  selection written back to `lpstrFile`, `allowedContentTypes`, the editor and Files ignoring
  input and drawing unfocused while the picker is open (their loops block until it ends).

## D393 The window server carries a drag between windows (batch part 19; M11, M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the toolkit's design (docs/ux/toolkit-v0.5.md section 7.2: the later slice, its model the shared clipboard) and the code-only session (engineering, the protocol)

- **Decision.**
  - **Hand-over.** A window that holds the pointer with the left button down (its in-window
    drag left its content) sends `START_DRAG` (request 55): the payload's kind (paths one
    per line, or UTF-8 text), its bytes (at most 1 MiB, kept by the kernel like the
    clipboard, with a serial counting drags) and the ghost's words. The server takes the drag
    over: the window no longer holds the pointer.
  - **Carrying.** The ghost is the toolkit's (section 7.2: `menu.bg`, 1-pixel `menu.border`,
    r4, 24 tall, text at +8, top-left at the pointer + 12), drawn by the server above every
    window and popup. The window under the pointer hears `DragOver` (event 19, with the
    content point, the kind and the serial) as it moves, and `DragLeave` (20) when the
    pointer leaves it.
  - **Ending.** Releasing the left button sends `Drop` (21) to the window under the pointer,
    which reads the payload with `GET_DRAG` (request 56, as `GET_CLIPBOARD`), and
    `DragEnded` (22) to the source, 1 when it landed on a window and 0 otherwise; Esc
    cancels (the window it was over hears `DragLeave`, the source `DragEnded` 0); the source
    window going away ends it without telling anyone.
- **Why the server.** Only the server sees every window and the pointer between them; the
  in-window protocol (section 7) stays as it is, and the toolkit adds a drop from a foreign
  source on the same targets (next decision).
- **Not yet.** Dropping on the desktop and the dock, copy-versus-move with a modifier, the
  touch form's long press, D162's `wm drag` across windows, and more payload kinds.

## D394 The toolkit hands a drag to the server and takes drops from other windows (batch part 19; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the toolkit's design (docs/ux/toolkit-v0.5.md section 7.2) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.**
  - **Leaving the window.** A drag source may let its drags leave (`set_drag_out`): when the
    pointer crosses the window's edge during its drag, the tree ends the drag here and
    answers `Response::DragLeftWindow(source, part)`; the program then hands it to the server
    with `WindowServer::start_drag` (the payload, its kind, and the ghost's words, which
    `drag_words` gives as the in-window ghost showed them). The end comes back as
    `Input::DragEnded`, answered `Response::CarriedEnded { landed }`.
  - **Arriving.** `Input::DragOver` from the server highlights the drop target under the
    point exactly as an in-window drag does (no source, so nothing is "its own row");
    `Input::DragLeave` clears it; `Input::Drop` answers `Response::ForeignDropped { target,
    at, kind, serial }` on a target, the program reading the payload with
    `WindowServer::drag_payload`. The targets' declarations are unchanged, as section 7.2
    asked.
  - The input decoder reads the four new records (19 to 22).
- **Not yet.** A program that uses it: Files' drags need their design first (Claude Fable,
  next); `Application` programs reach the server themselves for the hand-over.

## D395 Files' drag and drop, and a file dropped on the Text Editor (batch part 19; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's design (docs/ux/files-drag-v0.5.md) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Files implements the design in its own view (it draws its own table, not the
  toolkit's widget tree, so the design's toolkit calls — `OntoOrWhole`, `set_drop_row`,
  `set_drop_whole` — are Files' own rules in `files_window/drag.rs`, with the same
  highlights):
  - **Picking up** a row past 6 pixels (not while renaming, a panel or a job shows); the
    ghost is the toolkit's tooltip tile with the name, cut at 30 glyphs to 27 and `...`.
  - **Targets**: a folder row (not the dragged folder or one inside it, not on the host
    share), else the folder shown (not the dragged item's own folder, the Trash view or the
    share), and the sidebar places (not `Host share`; `Trash` not for items on the share or
    already in the Trash). A row is filled `menu.hover` with a 2-pixel `accent` outline; the
    folder shown gets the outline alone.
  - **The release** reads the modifiers last seen (section 3's map: Mod with Shift or Alt
    links, Ctrl or Alt copies, Shift or Super moves, else move on one file system and copy
    across; a drop on `Trash` trashes). A move on one file system is a rename; copies and
    cross-file-system moves run the paste job and its progress panel; names never overwrite
    (`<stem> copy`); a link is `Paste Link`'s; out of the Trash it is always a move that
    forgets the item's `info` entry. Errors are Files' notices.
  - **Spring-loaded folders**: resting 1000 ms on a folder row or place browses into it.
  - **Between windows**: a drag crossing the window's edge is handed to the server with the
    path (`CarryOut`); a drag from another window is read once per serial (paths, kind 1)
    and lands on the same targets; the source reloads when its drag landed (and, as always,
    on the next focus). Esc cancels.
  - **The Text Editor** opens the first dropped path as `Open...` does (the unsaved
    question first).
- **Deviations from the design.** One item is dragged (Files' selection is single on
  `main`; multiple selection, item 17, is not in yet); the modifiers of a drop from another
  window are the target's last seen, since the keys went to the source; the editor shows no
  outline while a drag is over it and no `Dropped <N> files` notice yet.
- **Not yet.** The icon view as a source, touch long press, the editor's outline and notices,
  a ghost badge for copy or link, and the QEMU check of section 11.

## D396 The built-in apps as the `builtin-apps` component (batch, D235's "Not yet", part 65's first half; M14; D18; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by Claude Fable's components design (docs/ux/components-v0.3.md) and the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Files, the Text Editor with `edit`, and Downloads leave `/bin/settings` for a
  program of their own, `eggos-builtin-apps`, installed as the `builtin-apps` component at
  `/usr/libexec/builtin-apps`. The base keeps `/bin/files`, `/bin/text-editor`, `/bin/edit`
  and `/bin/downloads` as links to it, dangling until the component is installed, so a
  machine without it has none of them and carries none of their code (D18); an image built
  with the components embedded (the QEMU tests' `Layers::Embedded`) holds the program at its
  path, as it does the layers. The store offers `builtin-apps` first ("Files, Text Editor,
  Downloads"; on removal "They leave the launcher; your files stay."), and the personal,
  professional and enterprise editions install it; server stays the base alone. Settings no
  longer links the editor or Downloads.
- **Deviations from the design.** `needs: desktop` is left out while the desktop is not a
  component (it runs in the kernel until the window server moves to user space, part 66);
  the Task Manager stays in `/bin/settings`, its code woven into Settings' panes.
- **Not yet.** The desktop as a component (part 66), the Task Manager in the component, the
  launcher hiding the apps' entries when the component is absent.

## D397 QEMU-only checks carried by the leftovers are written in the first build-and-test pass (batch parts 6, 7, 9, 15, 17; code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched against the owner's code-only order of 2026-11-11 and how the existing checks are made)

- **Context.** The leftovers carry checks that exist only as QEMU boot steps: part 6's
  screendump checks of the first run (#149's section 14.6, whose timing under TCG needs a
  tolerance), part 7's network indicator tooltip and click, part 9's sideways wheel and list
  item selection through `wm act` in the win-controls check, `mac-views.app`'s host renders
  and QEMU steps (D379) and Minesweeper's flag step (D389).
- **Decision.** They are written when the code is first built and run, not in code-only mode.
  Every existing QEMU check pins pixels, coordinates and timings read from a run (the
  frame comparisons, the screendump offsets, the waits), and code-only mode allows no run;
  a check written blind would fail on its first run for reasons unrelated to the feature and
  be rewritten then. The features themselves are written and host-tested; the roadmap lines
  name each check as moved, so the build pass finds them.

## D398 No app sees another's input; global hot keys go through the window server (batch part 13's rest, D349's "Not yet"; M15, M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Windows' global hooks, Wayland's refusal of global input capture, and what programs use global hooks for)

- **Question.** D349 left "hooks into other processes" open: a `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` or
  `WH_MOUSE_LL` hook installed on Windows sees every key and pointer event of the session.
- **Decision.** EggOS refuses it, as Wayland does: a global hook is a keylogger, and EggOS's
  model (D21, D193) is that an app or agent sees only what the person gives it. The low-level
  hooks keep seeing the program's own input (D349). What programs mostly install them for,
  a key combination that works whichever window has the focus, becomes a server feature:
  `RegisterHotKey` on a window also registers the combination with the window server
  (`REGISTER_HOT_KEY`, request 57), which gives that window a `HotKey` event (23) when the
  person presses exactly that combination and keeps the key from the focused window; the
  layer posts `WM_HOTKEY` as before. Only combinations with Ctrl, Alt or Super are taken, none
  the shell's shortcuts use, one client each (64 at most), and the window's going away
  frees them, so a hot key tells its program of its own combination and nothing else.
- **Not yet.** Thread hot keys (window 0) beyond the program's own focus, `MOD_NOREPEAT`,
  hot keys for the macOS layer (`RegisterEventHotKey`) and the toolkit, a Settings list of
  the registered hot keys.

## D399 The Windows shell namespace over the file system (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Microsoft's shell namespace documentation for `ITEMIDLIST`, `IShellFolder`, `IShellItem`, `IEnumIDList`, `STRRET` and `BROWSEINFOW`)

- **Question.** The layer made no item ID lists: `SHGetDesktopFolder` and
  `SHCreateItemFromParsingName` failed and `SHBrowseForFolderW` returned as if cancelled, so
  programs that pick a folder, or walk folders through the shell, could not.
- **Decision.** Item ID lists hold EggOS paths, one item per name: `EG`, a flags byte (a
  folder or not) and the name in UTF-8 (`userland/windows/src/item_lists.rs`, tested on the
  host). An item's bytes are private to the shell that made them, so the layer's own form is
  allowed; it keeps lists small and the path a straight walk. The empty list is the desktop,
  whose one child is the file system's root (an item with an empty name, `C:\`, as every
  absolute path is `C:\` in the layer). Lists live in the task allocator's blocks, so `ILFree`
  and `CoTaskMemFree` both free them.
- **Objects.** `SHGetDesktopFolder` and `BindToObject` give `IShellFolder`s that parse
  Windows paths (the desktop only absolute ones), list children through `IEnumIDList` (a
  snapshot taken when it is made; folders, files and dot-files as `SHCONTF` asks), compare
  (folders first, then names ignoring case, whatever the column), give attributes and
  `STRRET_WSTR` display names, and rename (`SetNameOf`, never replacing). `IShellItem`
  (`SHCreateItemFromParsingName`, `SHCreateItemFromIDList`) gives names in every `SIGDN` form,
  attributes, its parent, compares and binds to its folder (`BHID_SFObject`). The `IL*`
  helpers, `SHParseDisplayName`, `SHGetPathFromIDListW` and `Ex`, `SHGetIDListFromObject`,
  `SHBindToParent`, `SHGetSpecialFolderLocation` and `SHGetKnownFolderIDList` work on them;
  shlwapi's `StrRetToBufW` and `StrRetToStrW` read the `STRRET`s.
- **Folder picker.** `SHBrowseForFolderW` runs the system picker (`/bin/pick folder`, D391)
  as the file dialogs do (D392): its title, the root list's folder as the starting place, the
  owner disabled while it is open; it returns the chosen folder's list and its name in
  `pszDisplayName`.
- **Not yet.** Shell views (`CreateViewObject`), context menus, data objects and icons
  (`GetUIObjectOf`), `BindToStorage`, `IShellItemArray` and `IFileDialog`, the picker's
  `BFFCALLBACK` (no dialog window exists to receive `BFFM_SETSELECTION`), keeping the picker
  inside `pidlRoot`, virtual folders (This PC, Network, Recycle Bin) and other drives than
  `C:`.

## D400 COM out of process: automation through a socket per class (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Microsoft's documentation of local servers, `CoRegisterClassObject`, `REGCLS`, `LocalServer32` and `-Embedding`, `IDispatch::Invoke`, `DISPPARAMS` and `EXCEPINFO`)

- **Question.** The layer created only `Scripting.Dictionary`: a program that registers its
  classes (`CoRegisterClassObject`) or drives another program's (`CoCreateInstance` with
  `CLSCTX_LOCAL_SERVER`, Office-style automation) got `REGDB_E_CLASSNOTREG`.
- **Decision.** Out-of-process COM carries automation, the late-bound `IDispatch` that
  scripting and most "drive another program" code use, over our own messages
  (`userland/windows/src/com/wire.rs`, tested on the host), not DCOM's NDR and ORPC: both ends
  run on our layer, so only they must agree, and VARIANTs, names, results and exceptions are
  all that `IDispatch` passes. Custom interfaces need their proxies' and stubs' type
  information (MIDL-generated or a type library) and wait for a later slice.
- **Server.** `CoRegisterClassObject` keeps the class object; the same process creates its
  objects directly (`CoCreateInstance`, `CoGetClassObject`). With `CLSCTX_LOCAL_SERVER` it
  also listens on `~/.local/state/windows/com/{CLSID}`, a Unix socket in the user's own
  folder, so only the user's programs reach it. Requests are served on the registering
  thread when it looks for messages, as Windows dispatches a single-threaded apartment's
  calls through its message loop (any thread that looks, for a class registered from the
  multithreaded apartment); the message loop's wait watches the sockets as it watches
  `WSAAsyncSelect`'s (D348), and a socket that reported is not watched again until its thread
  serves it. `REGCLS_SINGLEUSE`, `REGCLS_SUSPENDED` with `CoResumeClassObjects`,
  `CoSuspendClassObjects`, `CoAddRefServerProcess` and `CoReleaseServerProcess` (its last
  release suspends the classes) behave as on Windows. Each connection numbers the objects it
  was given and releases them when it goes.
- **Client.** `CoCreateInstance` connects; when nothing listens it starts the registry's
  `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\CLSID\{...}\LocalServer32` command line with ` -Embedding` and retries
  for 30 seconds (`CO_E_SERVER_EXEC_FAILURE` after). The object is a proxy `IDispatch`
  (`GetTypeInfoCount` gives 0); objects in results become proxies on the same connection,
  which closes with the last of them. `CLSIDFromProgID` and `CLSIDFromString` read
  `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\<ProgID>\CLSID`.
- **Calls into the server's objects.** `GetIDsOfNames` takes six arguments and `Invoke` nine,
  more than the layer's four-argument call into a program, so `call_program_nine` calls with
  nine (x86_64: Microsoft's convention; ARM64: eight in registers, one on the stack).
- **Not yet.** Interfaces other than `IDispatch` (no proxies and stubs from type
  information), the program's own objects passed to a server (callbacks, events and
  connection points), by-reference arguments coming back changed, arrays (`VT_ARRAY`),
  `GetTypeInfo` across processes, the client pumping messages while it waits, the running
  object table and `GetActiveObject`, servers on another machine, and an x64 server translated
  on ARM64 (its translation calls with four arguments at most; such calls fail with
  `E_NOTIMPL`).

## D401 The outline widget, and the registry pane on it with a phone's drill-down (batch part 13's rest; M15, D23; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (the design is Claude Fable's, docs/ux/windows-registry-v0.3.md sections 4 and 7)

- **Question.** D231 left the registry pane's keys as a one-column table of indented text
  rows and left its phone, TV and wearable layouts for later.
- **Decision.** The toolkit gains `Kind::Outline` as section 4 designs it
  (`userland/toolkit/src/outline.rs`, `tree/outlines.rs`): the program keeps the flattened
  shown rows and answers `RowText` (depth, expandable, expanded, text) and optionally
  `RowPath` (the value agents read); rows 24 tall, 16 per level, the disclosure chevron right
  or down (the selected row's in `accent`), a square for a leaf. A press on the glyph or a
  double-click, Enter, Right on a closed row and Left on an open one answer the new
  `Response::RowToggled(id, row, open)` (the checkbox's `Toggled` keeps its shape); Left and
  Backspace go to the parent, typing a letter selects the next row that starts with it, and
  on a TV Right on a leaf and Left on a root leave the widget. Agents see a `tree` with its
  shown `treeitem`s (new roles) whose value is the row's path, flagged `selected`,
  `expanded` and the new `expandable`; `select`, `invoke` and `set-text "<n>"` act as on a
  table. `set_rows`, `set_cell_data` and `set_empty_text` serve outlines too.
- **The pane.** The key list is now an outline: the cell store keeps each row's name and its
  shape (depth and state), and `key_path` rebuilds a row's full path from the rows above it,
  so no path is stored per row. On a phone or a wearable
  (`SettingsWindow::set_form_factor`) the outline browses one level a page
  (`Outline::drill_down`, no glyphs; a tap or Enter opens the row): a `..` row first goes up,
  the three roots are the top page, and the pane's widgets take section 7's one-column
  places (`PHONE_HEIGHT` tall, for the window's scroll view).
- **Not yet.** Settings learning its device class and pane width from the window server (no
  caller of `set_form_factor` yet), rows 40 tall for touch, the wearable's browse-only page
  and its two-line value rows, bottom-sheet panels, long-press context menus, and the
  outline's sideways scroll.

## D402 The common controls' ANSI messages, and their delete notifications at destroy (batch part 13's rest, the common-control breadth; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Microsoft's documentation of each control's `A` and `W` messages and the structures' 64-bit layouts)

- **Question.** D231 left the controls' ANSI messages and the `*_DELETEITEM` notifications
  at destroy: a program built for ANSI that sends `LVM_INSERTITEMA` got nothing, and a
  program that frees each row's `lParam` in `LVN_DELETEITEM` leaked when its window closed.
- **Decision.** Every common control's `A` message becomes its `W` message before the
  control sees it (`common_controls/ansi_messages.rs`): list views' item, column, find,
  item-text and string-width messages, tree views' insert, get and set, headers' and tab
  controls' items, status bars' text, length and tip text, toolbars' strings, buttons and
  button text, and tooltips' tool, text and title messages. A structure is copied with its
  text widened from UTF-8 (the layer's narrow text, D178); a `GET` message's text is
  narrowed back into the program's buffer, cut at a whole character, and lengths are
  answered in bytes, as the `A` messages count them. Callbacks
  (`LPSTR_TEXTCALLBACKA`) and resource numbers pass unchanged. One table names every
  message, so the controls keep one implementation each.
- **Destroy.** A list view sends `LVN_DELETEALLITEMS` (and `LVN_DELETEITEM` per row unless
  the parent answered nonzero) and a tree view `TVN_DELETEITEMW` for every item, children
  first, when the window is destroyed, as Windows does.
- **Not yet.** `A` notifications to ANSI parents (the layer answers `WM_NOTIFYFORMAT` with
  Unicode, so parents get `W` ones), `TTM_GETTOOLINFOA`, `SB_GETTIPTEXTA`,
  `LVM_GETISEARCHSTRINGA` and `TB_SAVERESTOREA`.

## D403 List and tree views ask for callback items, and headers draw sort arrows (batch part 13's rest, the common-control breadth; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Microsoft's documentation of `LPSTR_TEXTCALLBACK`, `I_IMAGECALLBACK`, `I_CHILDRENCALLBACK`, `LVN_GETDISPINFO`, `TVN_GETDISPINFO`, `LVIF_DI_SETITEM` and `HDF_SORTUP`)

- **Question.** Items inserted with `LPSTR_TEXTCALLBACKW` drew empty, image and children
  callbacks were ignored (a lazily filled tree showed no expand buttons), and `HDF_SORTUP`
  and `HDF_SORTDOWN` drew nothing.
- **Decision.** A callback text is kept in the model as a mark no text holds (U+FFFF);
  readers (agents, `LVM_GETITEMTEXT`, `TVM_GETITEM`) see it as empty. Before a list view or
  tree view paints, it asks its parent `LVN_GETDISPINFOW` or `TVN_GETDISPINFOW` (the GUI
  lock let go, as for every notification) for each callback cell, image or children count
  of the rows it shows, puts the answers in for the paint and the marks back after it,
  unless the parent set `LVIF_DI_SETITEM`/`TVIF_DI_SETITEM`, which keeps them as Windows
  does. Asking only for shown rows keeps a large virtual list as cheap as its view.
- **Headers** draw an up or down arrow 14 px from a column's right edge for `HDF_SORTUP` and
  `HDF_SORTDOWN`; alignment reads only the justify bits, so the sort bits change nothing
  else.
- **Fix.** `tree_view.rs` declared `TVIF_TEXT`, `TVIF_PARAM`, `TVIF_STATE` and `TVIF_HANDLE`
  twice (D361's batch, unbuilt); the second declarations are gone.
- **Not yet.** `LVS_OWNERDATA` virtual lists (their rows exist only as callbacks),
  callback texts in agents' tree, and `LVN_ODCACHEHINT`.

## D404 Ctrl+Tab turns a dialog's tab pages, and part 13's breadth is closed (batch part 13's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Microsoft's keyboard guidance for property sheets and `IsDialogMessage`)

- **Question.** D231 listed "Ctrl+Tab in dialogs" among the common controls' missing
  breadth: in a dialog with tab pages, Ctrl+Tab moved the focus like Tab instead of turning
  the page, which every Windows user expects from property sheets.
- **Decision.** `IsDialogMessageW` takes Ctrl+Tab (Ctrl+Shift+Tab backwards) to the
  dialog's first shown, enabled tab control, which selects the next tab, wrapping, with
  `TCN_SELCHANGING` (the parent may refuse) and `TCN_SELCHANGE`, as a click does; a dialog
  without one keeps Tab's focus move. A focused tab control keeps its own Ctrl+Tab
  (D178's `key_target`).
- **Part 13's breadth.** With D348-D404 the layer covers the common controls' messages,
  notifications, custom draw, label editing, tips, callbacks, ANSI forms and destroy
  notifications. What stays is recorded, not hidden: non-rectangular windows
  (`SetWindowRgn` with elliptic, rounded or polygon regions needs a shape request in the
  window server and real regions in GDI, whose regions are still bounding rectangles),
  toolbars' standard bitmaps (`TB_ADDBITMAP` with `HINST_COMMCTRL` needs our own drawn
  set), image lists' overlays and drag images, header drag-and-drop reordering
  (`HDS_DRAGDROP`) and `LVS_OWNERDATA` (D403). They wait for the programs that need them,
  as M15's compatibility runs find them.

## D405 iostreams in msvcp140 for `char` (batch part 12's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: MSVC's STL headers `<xiosbase>`, `<ios>`, `<streambuf>`, `<ostream>`, `<istream>`, `<xlocale>` and `<fstream>`, MSVC's 64-bit class layouts with virtual bases, its name decoration, and `num_put`/`num_get`'s classic-locale behaviour)

- **Question.** D230 left iostreams: a program using `std::cout` imports msvcp140's stream
  objects and out-of-line members, and an import the layer lacks stops the program loading.
- **Decision.** `win32/msvcp/iostreams.rs` provides them for `char`:
  - **The standard objects** `cin`, `cout`, `cerr` and `clog`, laid out as MSVC lays out a
    class with a virtual base on x64 (base-offset table pointer, `vtordisp`, then the
    `basic_ios`: `ios_base`'s table, flags, precision, width, locale; the buffer, tie and
    fill), made at compile time so no constructor has to run before `main`. `cerr` is
    unit-buffered and, like `cin`, tied to `cout`.
  - **Their buffers** are the layer's own `basic_streambuf`s with empty get and put areas, so
    every byte goes through their virtual functions, which read and write the C runtime's
    `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr`: `std::cout` and `printf` keep their order, as MSVC's do
    while `sync_with_stdio` holds.
  - **Members** of `basic_ostream` (every arithmetic `operator<<`, pointers, buffers, the
    three manipulator forms, `put`, `write`, `flush`, the sentry's `_Osfx`), `basic_istream`
    (every arithmetic `operator>>`, `get`, `peek`, `getline`, `read`, `ignore`, `gcount`,
    `putback`, `_Ipfx`), `basic_ios` and `ios_base` (state, flags, width, precision, fill,
    tie, buffer, `init`, `copyfmt`, `xalloc`, `sync_with_stdio`), and `basic_streambuf`'s
    constructors, default virtual functions, table and public and protected members, so a
    program's `basic_stringbuf` and `basic_filebuf` (header templates deriving from it) work;
    every call reaches a buffer through its table, so a program's own buffers serve too.
    `endl`, `ends` and `flush`; `_Fiopen` for `basic_filebuf`.
  - **Numbers** are formatted and read as `num_put` and `num_get` do in the classic locale
    (`userland/windows/src/stream_format.rs`, tested on the host): bases, `showbase`,
    `showpos`, `uppercase`, `boolalpha`, padding by `left`, `right` and `internal` with the
    fill, a negative number in hex as its two's complement, floating point through the C
    runtime's `printf` rules with the conversion `num_put` builds, reading stopping at the
    first byte that cannot belong and failing (with the type's limit) on overflow.
  - **The classic locale** with one facet, `ctype<char>` (id 1, the classification table
    built at compile time), so the headers' inline `use_facet<ctype<char>>` (for `widen` and
    `isspace` in `getline` and `operator>>(string&)`) finds it; `_Getcat`, `locale::_Init`,
    `_Getgloballocale`, `classic`, `id`'s counter, `_Lockit` and `_Facet_Register`.
- **To check at the build pass.** The layouts and the order of `ctype<char>`'s overloaded
  virtual functions (MSVC lists an overload set in reverse declaration order) are from the
  headers and MSVC's rules, not yet from a binary; the first test program (`eggcpp3.exe`:
  `cout` with every manipulator, `cin` from a pipe, `ostringstream`, `ifstream`) settles
  them.
- **Not yet.** `wchar_t` streams (`wcout`, `wcin`), facets other than `ctype<char>`
  (`num_put`, `numpunct`, `codecvt` for programs that call `use_facet` on them), named
  locales, `ios_base::failure` when exceptions are enabled (the state is set, nothing is
  thrown), `iword`/`pword` and callbacks, and locking the streams across threads.

## D406 Storyboards on macOS, with NSViewController and NSWindowController (batch part 14's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Apple's documentation of `NSStoryboard`, `NSViewController` and `NSWindowController`, and the layout of Xcode's compiled `.storyboardc` folders)

- **Question.** D232 loaded nibs but refused an app whose `Info.plist` names
  `NSMainStoryboardFile`, which every macOS app template since Xcode 6 does; nor did the
  layer have view or window controllers.
- **Decision.** `NSViewController` (lazy `view` through `loadView` from its nib, or a plain
  NSView, then `viewDidLoad`; title, represented object, identifier, storyboard) and
  `NSWindowController` (window from its nib on first use with `windowWillLoad` and
  `windowDidLoad`, `showWindow:`, `close`, and a content view controller whose view becomes
  the window's content view and whose title its title) join AppKit
  (`appkit/controllers.rs`). `NSStoryboard` (`appkit/storyboard.rs`) reads
  `<name>.storyboardc/Info.plist` (binary or XML, through `eggos-plist`):
  `NSViewControllerIdentifiersToNibNames` names each scene's nib,
  `NSStoryboardDesignatedEntryPointIdentifier` the initial controller and
  `NSStoryboardMainMenu` the main menu. A scene's nib loads with the storyboard as File's
  Owner and gives its first top-level window or view controller; placeholders that stand for
  another scene's controller are made from the storyboard loading them, so a window
  controller's content relationship (an outlet to `contentViewController`) is filled. The
  nib loader also makes controllers named directly and through `NSClassSwapper` (a
  program's own subclass, else the original class). `NSApplicationMain` runs the main
  storyboard: its menu, then its initial controller (a window controller shown, a view
  controller in a window of its own).
- **To check at the build pass.** The placeholder's class name and identifier key
  (`NSStoryboardControllerPlaceholder`/`NSStoryboardScenePlaceholder` with
  `NSStoryboardIdentifier`, `NSIdentifier` or `identifier`) are read from what the
  compiled files are known to hold, not yet from one: a storyboard app from Xcode's template,
  compiled by `ibtool` in CI, settles them.
- **Not yet.** Segues (`performSegueWithIdentifier:sender:`, `prepareForSegue:`, show,
  sheet and popover segues), split and tab view controllers, child view controllers and
  their appearance calls, `NSStoryboard`'s creator blocks, and documents
  (`NSDocument`'s window controllers).

## D407 NSPanel, the About panel in `[NSApp windows]`, and mac-views' renders with the first build pass (batch part 15's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: Apple's `NSPanel` and `NSApplication.windows` documentation; D397's rule for checks that need a built system)

- **Question.** D233 and D375 left the About panel outside the app's window list, so an app
  that walks `[NSApp windows]` (to close everything, or to find the panel) did not see it,
  and AppKit had no `NSPanel`. D379 left `mac-views.app`'s host renders and QEMU steps.
- **Decision.** `NSPanel` joins AppKit as an NSWindow subclass with its floating,
  key-only-if-needed and works-when-modal flags (`appkit/panel.rs`). While the About panel
  shows, `[NSApp windows]` ends with one NSPanel of a private subclass that stands for it:
  its title (`About <app>`), visibility, frame (the panel's content size), window number
  (the panel's server window), and `close`, `performClose:`, `orderOut:`,
  `makeKeyAndOrderFront:` and `orderFront:` acting on the panel. The panel stays the
  layer's own drawing (D175); the stand-in only answers for it.
- **mac-views.** Section 18.2's host renders exist to be compared with section 18.3's QEMU
  screendumps at every step, and both need the layer built and the app built on CI's macOS
  runner; they join the first build-and-test pass with the other QEMU-only checks (D397).
- **Not yet.** Utility-panel styles (`NSWindowStyleMaskUtilityWindow`, HUD), floating
  panels staying above the app's other windows (a window-server level), and the stand-in's
  `delegate`.

## D408 A C++ test program on macOS, and `__dynamic_cast` (batch part 16's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering; the Itanium C++ ABI's `__dynamic_cast` and vtable layout)

- **Question.** D380 gave C++ exceptions and libc++abi's basics on macOS but no C++ program
  in CI's macOS programs to prove them, and no `dynamic_cast`.
- **Decision.** `tests/macos-cxx/main.cpp`, our own C++17 program, built on CI's macOS
  runner with `clang++` like the C programs (`C_PROGRAMS` gains a `source`; `.cpp` builds
  as C++17), installed as `bin/macos-cxx` in the macOS programs image and run in the
  `MACOS_PROGRAM_SESSION`: function-local statics' guards, `throw` and `catch` of an `int`,
  a class derived from `std::exception` caught by base reference with the destructors run
  inner first, a rethrow, a `const char *`, `catch (...)`, a handler that does not match
  passing the exception on, `dynamic_cast` down, across (to a second base) and failing,
  `typeid` comparisons, `new[]`/`delete[]`, `nothrow` new refusing and plain `new` throwing
  `std::bad_alloc`. Its eighteen expected lines are in `xtask/src/qemu.rs`.
- **`__dynamic_cast`** (`objc/cxx_types.rs`, host-tested) reads the object's offset to the
  whole object and its dynamic type from the two words before its vtable's address point,
  answers the whole object when that is the wanted type, else the public base of the
  wanted type inside it through the same inheritance walk `catch` uses (a downcast or a
  cross cast), else null. `__cxa_bad_cast` and `__cxa_bad_typeid` (a cast to a reference
  failing) end the program as `std::terminate` does until `std::bad_cast` exists.
- **Not yet.** `std::bad_cast` and `std::bad_typeid` thrown, ambiguous-base and
  non-public-source checks in `__dynamic_cast` (it takes the first public match), and
  UDCalc, which needs its bundled Sparkle framework loaded (D409).

## D409 An app's own libraries on macOS: frameworks and dylibs by `@rpath`, and initializers (batch part 16's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: dyld's documented search for `@rpath`, `@executable_path` and `@loader_path`, the export trie's format in `<mach-o/loader.h>`, and the order dyld runs initializers in)

- **Question.** The macOS layer bound imports only to the libraries it provides itself, so an
  app that carries a framework in its bundle (UDCalc's Sparkle, and most real Mac apps)
  could not start; and no image's initializers (C++ static constructors,
  `__attribute__((constructor))`) ran at all.
- **Decision.** `macho.rs` parses libraries (`MH_DYLIB`, `MH_BUNDLE`) as well as
  executables, with their export trie, run paths (`LC_RPATH`) and initializer sections
  (`__mod_init_func`, `__init_offsets`). A library the layer does not provide is looked for
  as dyld looks: `@rpath/` through the run paths of the image that links it and of the
  images above it, `@executable_path/` and `@loader_path/` expanded, any other path as it
  is (`bundled.rs`). Each is mapped like the executable, its own libraries first: its
  chained fixups or `LC_DYLD_INFO` opcodes, its imports bound to the layer or to the other
  carried libraries, its Objective-C metadata registered before the executable's (an app's
  class may subclass a framework's), its unwind tables added, its pages protected. Imports
  from a carried library are found in its export trie (`export_trie.rs`, host-tested):
  offsets from its header, absolute symbols, re-exports followed to another library or the
  layer, and a resolver's stub; a flat-namespace import that the layer lacks is looked for
  in every carried library. Missing symbols share one table of stubs across images.
- **Initializers** run after `+load`, before `main`: every carried library's, in the order
  they were loaded (so dependencies first), then the executable's, each called with
  `argc`, `argv`, `envp` and the Apple strings, as dyld calls them.
- **Not yet.** Libraries of translated (x86_64 on Arm) programs and a translated program's
  initializers; thread-local variables in a carried library; `dlopen` of an app's library at
  run time; `LC_LOAD_UPWARD_DYLIB` cycles beyond the depth limit; two-level namespace
  checks for a symbol exported twice; code signatures (ignored, as everywhere in the
  layer).

## D410 UDCalc's check, `cargo xtask udcalc-app` (batch part 16's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: UDCalc's GitHub releases and license)

- **Question.** D234 named UDCalc 0.2.0 (BSD-2-Clause), the runner-up of D175's research,
  as the next Mac app once nibs and bundled frameworks load, with its own check and CI job.
- **Decision.** `cargo xtask udcalc-app --arch <arch>` downloads
  `UDCalc-macOS-0.2.0.zip` from the author's GitHub release (`ashalkhakov/UDCalc`), pinned
  to the SHA-256 GitHub publishes for the asset, and boots the release kernel: `app
  install` and `app open` (its Sparkle framework loading from the bundle through D409 and its
  window from its nibs), `12+30=` typed on the keyboard, `wm show` finding an element named
  or valued exactly `42`, `About UDCalc` through `wm menu --choose`, Esc, Cmd+Q, and `wm
  list` without its window. The CI job `udcalc-app` runs it on aarch64 and x86_64; like
  `swift-app` (D389) it stays out of `check`'s needs until its first run passes, since UDCalc
  also needs `NSStackView`, Auto Layout and more that the first run will list.
- **Not yet.** Its row in `docs/compatibility.md` (after the first passing run), frame
  comparisons with a host render, and Sparkle's update check (it reaches the network; the
  test has none).

## D411 The Swift overlays' entry points a real app calls (batch part 17's rest; M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (read from Minesweeper 1.0.0's imports, the pinned archive of D389, with `nm`; the slots and registers from a `swiftc -O` probe's disassembly and the SDK's `Swift.swiftinterface`)

- **Question.** D389 left the Swift Foundation, Dispatch and CoreGraphics overlays' entry
  points "to be read from a `swiftc` build first".
- **What the app imports.** Besides `libswiftCore`, Minesweeper's arm64 slice imports from
  `libswiftDispatch` (`DispatchQueue.main`, `async(group:qos:flags:execute:)`,
  `DispatchQoS.unspecified`, the metadata of `DispatchQoS` and `DispatchWorkItemFlags`, and the
  flags' `SetAlgebra` conformance), `libswiftCoreGraphics` (`CGContext.move(to:)`,
  `addLine(to:)`, `addArc(center:radius:startAngle:endAngle:clockwise:)`), every overlay's
  `_swift_FORCE_LOAD_$` marker (eleven overlays, most linked weakly), and from
  `libswiftCore` `SetAlgebra.init(_:)` (from a sequence) and `_CocoaArrayWrapper`'s
  `endIndex` and subscript; it links `CoreGraphics.framework` too, which the layer did not
  list as provided.
- **Decision.** `swift/dispatch_overlay.rs` provides them: struct metadata and accessors for
  the two Dispatch types (in a `Dispatch` module descriptor), `unspecified` as case 5 with
  priority 0, the main queue over libdispatch's `_dispatch_main_q`, `async` (and with a group)
  over `dispatch_async`/`dispatch_group_async` (QoS and flags do not change the layer's one
  thread of work, D388); the three CGContext methods over the layer's CoreGraphics (D386);
  `SetAlgebra` as a resilient protocol of the layer's, base protocols first and then the
  members in the standard library's order (its `init()` slot 4 and `init(_:)` slot 20, which
  matches the order swiftc uses for `Hashable`'s witnesses the layer already calls), with
  `DispatchWorkItemFlags`' witness table (bit operations on its `UInt`; `insert`, `remove` and
  `update` end the program for now); the dispatch thunks jump through the witness table
  passed last (x1/rsi for `init()`, x4/r8 for `init(_:)` after the sequence and its type and
  conformance, as the probe's call shows); `_CocoaArrayWrapper` over `count` and
  `objectAtIndex:`; every `_swift_FORCE_LOAD_$` marker as one byte of the layer's.
  `CoreGraphics.framework` joins the provided libraries (and sets up AppKit, which its
  drawing needs).
- **Not yet.** `OS_dispatch_queue` as an Objective-C class (the queues are still plain
  records the runtime never counts), the rest of the overlays' API, and `SetAlgebra`'s
  `insert`, `remove` and `update` witnesses.

## D412 The desktop as a component, its window server kept in the kernel (batch, D235's parts 65 and 66; M14, M11; D18; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: D126's plan to move the window server to user space, how Windows (win32k in the kernel) and macOS (WindowServer in user space) place theirs, and D18's "a component not installed costs nothing")

- **Question.** D235 and D396 left the desktop out of the component manager because the
  window server runs in the kernel; part 66 planned to move it to user space first.
- **Decision.** The desktop becomes a component without the move. Moving the 31,000 lines of
  `drivers/src/desktop` behind a relay would add a context switch to every request and every
  event (each pointer move, each commit), against EggOS's first priority; Windows keeps its
  window manager in the kernel for that reason. What D18 asks is that an uninstalled desktop
  costs nothing, and that holds without the move: the kernel's `desktop` feature (in its
  default features) gates the window server, so an image built without it carries none of
  it; and on a kernel that has it, the window server starts at boot unless the `desktop`
  component was removed. The component manager writes `/var/lib/eggos/components/.no-desktop`
  when it removes `desktop` and deletes it when it installs it; the kernel reads that marker
  from the persistent disk (mounted before the terminal starts) and then draws its
  full-screen text console, as on a display too small for the desktop, with no window server
  running. A system that never had components keeps its desktop.
- **The store and the editions.** `desktop` is the store's first component (no files of its
  own: its code is in the kernel image), `builtin-apps` needs it (D396's deviation ends), and
  the personal, professional and enterprise editions list it; the server edition does not.
- **Revisit.** The window server's isolation (a fault in it is a kernel fault) is the cost
  of this choice; moving it to user space stays possible behind the same `/dev/window`
  contract (D126) if measurements show the relay is cheap enough.
- **Not yet.** Building the server edition's image with the `desktop` feature off
  (`cargo xtask` builds one kernel for every edition today), and the Task Manager moving
  into `builtin-apps` (D396).

## D413 Device interrupt lines given back, and PCI INTx through the I/O APIC (M8, M5; D184's and D255's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (researched: the I/O APIC's redirection entries, PCI's interrupt line and pin registers, and how Linux masks a level-triggered line until its threaded handler ran)

- **Question.** D184 and D255 left two gaps: a line stayed taken when connecting failed after
  it was routed (or when a driver let its device go), and a PCI function with neither MSI-X
  nor MSI (older controllers, some QEMU devices) could only be polled.
- **Decision: lines given back.** `Platform::release_device_interrupt` frees a line: on
  x86_64 the lines are a bitmap of the boot CPU's vectors rather than a counter, and an
  I/O APIC input is masked first; on aarch64 and riscv64 `SourceLines::release` frees the
  slot (lookups now scan every line, since a release leaves a hole) and the GIC distributor
  or the PLIC disables the source. `devices::interrupts::disconnect` clears the handler
  (its few words stay allocated, so an interrupt in flight on another CPU never reads freed
  memory) and gives the line back; `message_interrupts::connect` gives back a line it took
  when enabling the message or connecting the handler fails.
- **Decision: INTx.** A function without MSI-X or MSI uses its INTx pin: the interrupt line
  register (offset 0x3C, which the firmware fills with the input the pin reaches) names the
  I/O APIC input, `Platform::route_legacy_interrupt` routes it level-triggered and active
  low to a free line, and the function's INTx is enabled. The driver quiets its device only
  when its thread looks, so the HAL masks the input when the interrupt arrives and
  `DeviceEvents::wait` unmasks it each time the driver waits again (`set_masked_line`), as
  Linux handles a level line with a threaded handler.
- **Not yet.** ACPI `_PRT` routing (a firmware that leaves the interrupt line register 0 or
  255 gets no INTx; reading `_PRT` needs the AML interpreter), INTx on aarch64, riscv64 and
  the device-tree PCI hosts through `interrupt-map`, MIPS liointc's PCI inputs and sun4u's
  PCI bridge, shared INTx lines (two functions on one input: the second is refused), lines on
  CPUs other than the boot CPU, and a line per queue.

## D414 virtio-gpu on interrupts: the display's flush posted under its lock, waited for without it (M11, M8; D112's and D184's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** The GPU was the last virtio driver polling (D220 left it): a flush waits for
  the device's answers, and the display's lock is a spin lock the flush holds, so its wait
  cannot sleep.
- **Decision.** The flush splits in two. `VirtioGpu::start_flush` posts every rectangle's
  transfer and then its flush in one batch (rectangles past what one batch holds are joined
  into their bounding box) and returns; `finish_flush` collects the answers. The kernel's
  `display::flush_sleeping`, which the drawing thread now calls, posts the flush under the
  lock (the damage moves to the flush in flight, so drawing during the wait keeps its own),
  lets the lock go and sleeps on the GPU's `DeviceEvents` until its interrupt (or the 1 s
  deadline), then collects the answer under the lock; a failed flush puts its damage back.
  Every other use of the device (a synchronous flush, a pointer move, a mode change) first
  settles a flush in flight by polling. The probe connects the GPU's interrupt as the other
  virtio drivers' are (D220) and turns its control queue's notifications on; a GPU without a
  connected interrupt, a rotated or scaled display, or a scanout without the split flush
  polls as before. The interrupt also carries the device's configuration change, which the
  display's follow-the-host-size path reads (D287).
- **Not yet.** The cursor queue on interrupts (pointer moves still poll, briefly), several
  flushes in flight at once, and the turned and scaled paths posting rather than waiting.

## D415 virtio-gpu 3D, part 1: the virgl transport and Linux's render node (M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** M11's next step is 3D. What the kernel offers for it decides which user-space
  drivers work: a device of our own would need a GL and Vulkan driver of our own on day one,
  while the virtio GPU's 3D commands carry command streams that existing user-space drivers
  already encode (virgl's Gallium stream for OpenGL, Venus's for Vulkan).
- **Decision.** The kernel carries the streams and does not read them. The driver negotiates
  `VIRTIO_GPU_F_VIRGL` and `VIRTIO_GPU_F_CONTEXT_INIT`, encodes the spec's 3D commands
  (capability-set info and contents, context create and destroy, resource attach and detach,
  3D resource create, backing attach and detach, unref, 3D transfers both ways, submit) in
  `virtio/gpu/three_d.rs`, host-tested, and runs one at a time on the control queue from a DMA
  area of its own (the request, the answer with up to 7.9 KiB of capability set, and a
  256 KiB command stream). The kernel's `rendering` module gives each opener a context, made on
  first use or by context init, whose buffers are 3D resources backed by DMA memory, attached
  to the context and lent to the program's mappings; a buffer is destroyed (backing detached,
  resource unreferenced, memory freed) when its handle is closed and no mapping holds it, and
  leaked if the device does not answer, as a framebuffer is. Linux programs reach it through
  `/dev/dri/renderD128` (DRM's major 226, first render minor), which answers DRM's `VERSION`
  (`virtio_gpu`), `GET_CAP` and `GEM_CLOSE` and virtio-gpu's uAPI ioctls (map, execbuffer,
  getparam, resource create and info, transfers, wait, get caps, context init); `mmap` at the
  offset `VIRTGPU_MAP` gives (the handle shifted by 32) maps the backing. The device's
  commands go through the display, which owns the GPU (`display::with_renderer` settles a
  posted flush, D414, then lends the driver), so 2D and 3D never interleave on the queue.
- **Why synchronous.** Each command waits for its fenced answer under the display's lock, as
  the 2D path did before D414: waits are then always finished, an out-fence is already
  signalled (an `eventfd` reading 1 stands for the sync file) and buffers are idle whenever a
  call returns, which keeps part 1 small. Posting submissions and sleeping on the GPU's
  interrupt, as D414 does for flushes, is part 2.
- **Clean room.** The command layouts come from the virtio 1.2 specification (5.7.6) and the
  ioctl numbers and structures from Linux's `virtgpu_drm.h` and `drm.h` user-space headers
  (MIT-licensed UAPI descriptions of the interface, not kernel code).
- **Not yet.** Blob resources and host-visible memory (Venus needs them for most Vulkan
  memory), PRIME sharing with the window server (so a GL app's frames are shown without a copy
  back), sync objects and real fences, several rings, the sysfs nodes Mesa's device enumeration
  reads (`/sys/dev/char/226:128`), and the same render node for the Windows, macOS and Android
  layers' graphics APIs (their D3D, Metal and GLES front ends over the same contexts, D17).

## D416 MIPS64's Linux test programs past `linux_hello`, and `rt_sigprocmask`'s `how` on MIPS and SPARC (M9; D315's "Moved"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** The HAL's MIPS64 `TestProgram` now has every Linux program the other ports run
  (`linux_start`, the thread pointer, `poll`, signals, the handler on an alternate stack with
  its FP state, the fault handler, queued signals, `rt_sigsuspend`, the clocks, `stat`,
  credentials, moving and discarding memory), hand-written in n64's numbers and values from
  PowerPC's: `a3` flags an error with the number positive in `v0`; `struct sigaction` starts
  with its 32-bit flags; `stack_t` is pointer, size, flags; `sigset_t` is 16 bytes and
  `SIGUSR1` 16, `SIGCHLD` 18; `siginfo_t` has `si_code` before `si_errno`; `MAP_ANONYMOUS`
  is `0x800` and `MAP_FIXED` `0x10`; `struct stat` has a 32-bit `st_rdev` at 40; the thread
  pointer is `UserLocal`, set by `set_thread_area` and read with `rdhwr $29`. The handlers
  read and change the `ucontext` the kernel builds (D315): `sc_regs` 40 bytes in, `sc_fpregs`
  after them, then `sc_pc` and `sc_fpc_csr`, and `uc_sigmask` at 640. n64 has no red zone, so
  every program but `linux_start` (which no signal reaches) moves its stack pointer below the
  data it keeps before a handler may run. `$f24` and `$f25`, callee-saved in n64, carry the
  FP check.
- **Found on the way.** MIPS numbers `rt_sigprocmask`'s `how` from 1 (`SIG_BLOCK` 1,
  `SIG_UNBLOCK` 2, `SIG_SETMASK` 3) and SPARC too (`SIG_SETMASK` 4); the kernel took the
  generic 0 to 2 from both. `arguments_in` now translates it on both, and an unknown value
  stays `EINVAL`.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).** The delay slots are left to the assembler's
  `reorder` mode, as the existing programs do; LLVM's acceptance of `dli` and of `rdhwr`
  under `.set mips64r2` inside the programs' section.

## D417 s390x's Linux test programs (M9; D321's and D416's "Moved"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** s390x's `TestProgram` had no Linux program at all (each exited with 1): it now
  has `linux_hello`, `linux_start`, the unknown-call loop, `fp_registers` and every program
  past them, hand-written from PowerPC's in s390x's numbers (`svc 0` with the number in `r1`,
  the arguments in `r2` to `r7`, a negative result for an error). `mmap` takes one pointer to
  its six arguments (`old_mmap`); `struct stat` has `st_rdev` at 40 as a 64-bit word; the
  thread pointer is `a0:a1`, set with `sar` and read with `ear`; the FP check uses `f8` and
  `f9` (callee-saved) moved with `ldgr`/`lgdr`, and the rounding mode is the FP control
  word's low bits (`sfpc`/`efpc`). The handlers read and change the `ucontext` of D323:
  `_sigregs` 40 bytes in (PSW address at 48, `gprs` at 56, the FP control word at 248,
  `fprs` at 256) and `uc_sigmask` at 384, and return through `r14`. Every program moves
  `r15` below the data it keeps (no red zone), and code addresses come from `larl`, so the
  programs stay position-independent.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).** The z10 instructions the programs use (`mvghi`,
  `mvhi`, `mvhhi`) against the CPU model the build picks for the user programs' section.

## D418 SPARC64's test programs, and `argc` past the window save area (M9; D326's and D327's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** SPARC64's `TestProgram` gains `checks`, `fp_registers` and every Linux program
  past `linux_hello`, hand-written in SPARC's numbers and values: `ta 0x6d` with the number
  in `%g1`, the carry set on an error with SPARC's positive number in `%o0`; `SIGUSR1` 30,
  `SIGCHLD` 20; `SA_SIGINFO` `0x200` and `SA_ONSTACK` 1; `rt_sigaction`'s fourth argument a
  restorer and its fifth the set's size; `SIG_BLOCK` 1 (D416); `struct stat`'s 32-bit
  `st_rdev` at 32; the thread pointer is `%g7`, which a program sets itself; mappings in
  whole 8 KiB pairs (D328). Every branch's delay slot is written out. A program keeps its data
  176 bytes above its biased stack pointer, past its window's save area, which a spill or a
  signal's delivery writes. The handlers open a window with `save` and return with `ret` and
  `restore`, as compiled ones do, and find the interrupted state after the `siginfo_t` they
  get (D327): `u_regs` with the globals they check and change (`%g2` to `%g5`, which every
  window shares), `%pc` and `%npc`, the pointer to the FP registers, the `stack_t` and the
  mask. With no move between integer and FP registers before VIS 3, values go through memory,
  and `fp_registers` leaves `%fsr`'s read-only `ver` field out of its difference word.
- **Found on the way.** Linux starts a SPARC64 program with `argc` 128 bytes above its biased
  stack pointer, past its register window's save area, where glibc's `_start` reads it; the
  kernel put it at the stack pointer, so a real program read its window's spill area as
  `argc`. `exec` now leaves `START_STACK_GAP` (128 on SPARC64, 0 elsewhere) below it.
- **Known gaps (to check at build time).** LLVM's acceptance of `ldx`/`stx` on `%fsr` and of
  `ldd`/`std` on `%f32`-`%f62` in the programs' section.

## D419 The Components pane's disabled row buttons explain themselves (D300's deviation; docs/ux/components-v0.3.md section 6; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** Each row's button carries a tooltip that shows only while the button is disabled,
  in the words of the reason: `Another component is installing` (`is being removed`, `is
  updating`) while another row works, `This component is being removed` (`is installing`,
  `is updating`) on the row that works elsewhere, `Cancelling` once its install is cancelled,
  and `Download the component store first` without a store. The words live in
  `eggos_components::messages` beside the states, so the CLI and the pane say the same thing.
  On a phone a long-press shows it (toolkit v0.5 2.4); on a wearable tooltips stay off.
- **Toolkit.** `set_text` and `text_of` now take a tooltip, so its words can follow the state,
  and a hidden tooltip (`set_shown(false)`) no longer shows on hover or long-press.

## D420 The Components pane's last check in the chosen time zone (D300's deviation; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `Up to date · checked today at 09:14` now reads the check's time and today's date in
  the time zone Settings > Date & Time chose, as the clock in the bar does, instead of UTC: the
  pane keeps the zone (`set_time_zone`, given when Settings starts and whenever a zone is

## D421 A failed update says why in the pane (D300's deviation; docs/ux/components-v0.5.md section 3 and ask 7; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** The pane runs `component update` as a child and sees only its exit status, so
  every failure read `Could not update <title>.`; the design gives each cause its own lines.
- **Decision.** The job says why, in a file beside its progress: `component update` clears
  `/run/eggos/component-failure` when it takes the lock and, when a component fails, writes
  the component's name and the failure as words (`no_space 2306867 629145`, `errno 5`;
  `state::failure_text`, read back by `parse_failure`, host-tested both ways). Settings reads it
  with the components (`ComponentsRead::failure`), and a failed update of that component shows
  `messages::update_failure`'s two lines: the downloaded update damaged, the store detached,
  not enough space with both sizes, cancelled, not allowed (no second line), a folder that is
  not real, or the error's text; each keeps `The installed copy stays.` under it as the table
  says. A file rather than the command's coded JSON keeps the child's output where it goes now
  and works for a job another front-end started.
- **Not yet.** Telling a fetched file that fails its digest from an installed one (the manager
  reports both as `Damaged`), and the same for install and remove jobs, which still run in the
  window's tick (section 6).

## D422 Settings on every device class, part 1: the window's shapes (docs/ux/settings-forms-v0.5.md, Fable's design; M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering), design by Claude Fable (D16)

- **Design.** Claude Fable designed how Settings takes the phone, tablet, TV and wearable forms
  (`docs/ux/settings-forms-v0.5.md`): two window shapes chosen by form and width (the sidebar,
  or one page at a time below 624 px), a phone's list and pane pages with a back bar, 40 px
  touch rows on a tablet, the TV's focus moves, a read-only wearable, and one reflow rule
  (R1 to R10) that turns each pane's desktop layout into one column.
- **Done (part 1, the window).** `SettingsForm` (from `shell.form_in_use` and the window's
  size; a wearable when the longer side is 320 or less) and `shape_for` choose
  `Shape::Sidebar { row }` or `Shape::Pages`; `set_form_factor(form, width)`, which the program
  now calls on every resize through the toolkit's new `Application::resized`, lays the frame
  out: the sidebar and pane as today (rows of 40 and a 40 px search on a tablet), or the list
  page (search 48 tall across the width, rows of 56; rows of 48 and no search on a wearable)
  and the pane page (a 56 px `dock.bg` bar with `Back` and the pane's name over the pane's
  scroll view). Tapping or opening a row, `settings open` and `--pane` show the pane's page;
  `Back` (the arrow, the shell's `Back`, Esc) goes from the page to the list with the row
  focused, then clears a search, then reports `BACK_UNUSED`. On a TV, Right from the sidebar
  moves the ring into the pane, Left with nothing to use it and Back bring it back. The
  registry pane drills down whenever the window is in pages (D401). The toolkit gains
  `set_row_height` for lists.
- **Deviations.** A row's `Chosen` opens its page as `Opened` does, so on a phone the arrow
  keys open pages too (the list cannot yet tell a tap from a key); the list rows have no icon,
  summary or chevron yet (the design's ask 1), the TV's root padding and always-drawn ring are
  the toolkit's own (unchanged here), and the wearable shows each pane as on a phone rather
  than as read-only facts.
- **Not yet (part 2).** The reflow rule R1 to R10 for each pane, the Components pane's section
  10 and the Display pane's phone places, `pane_summary`, cards in a column, wrapping labels
  and bottom sheets (asks 1 to 3), and the element tree's `list` `Settings` with its
  summaries.
