## D435 An accelerometer turns the screen while `display.rotation` is `auto` (M12's orientation sensor; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** `display.rotation`'s `auto` (D330) kept the screen upright: no sensor said
  which way up a tablet or a phone is held.
- **Decision.** The sensors that laptops, tablets and phones carry speak HID's sensor page
  (0x20, HID Usage Tables 1.4, chapter 22) over USB or I2C. `hid_report` decodes an
  accelerometer's data fields (usages 0x0453 to 0x0455, the acceleration along x, y and z)
  into absolute events with codes of their own (`ACCELERATION_X` to `_Z`, Linux's `ABS_RX` to
  `ABS_RZ`, which no pointer here reports). The kernel's input state hands each completed
  reading to `orientation::note`, which runs the drivers' `OrientationTracker` (host-tested):
  the axis in the screen's plane that leads by half again names the edge that is up, a flat
  or diagonal device keeps what it shows, and a new way up must hold for three readings. The
  desktop's loop then turns the screen to it while the setting is `auto`
  (`terminal::turn_screen`, the same path `SET_ROTATION` takes), and choosing `auto` turns to
  the way up already sensed. The other values still lock the picture.
- **Not yet.** Sensors that send nothing until their reporting state is set (HID sensor
  feature reports), I2C-HID and ACPI-described sensors (the kernel has no I2C controller
  driver yet), the sensor as a device in `devices` and in Settings' Display pane line, and
  apps that hold one orientation (their manifest asking portrait or landscape).

## D436 Apps that hold an orientation (M12; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** An app's manifest may say `orientation=portrait` or `orientation=landscape`
  (`eggos_app_manifest::orientation`, absent or anything else is any); the desktop's catalogue
  keeps it for each installed app and `Desktop::focused_orientation` answers for the focused
  window's app. While `display.rotation` is `auto` and the sensor took a new way up (D435), the
  screen turns to it only when the picture's shape there (portrait when its height exceeds its
  width after the turn, from the device's own mode) fits what the focused app holds; when it
  does not, the screen stays, and the way up the sensor took is looked at again at most twice a
  second, so the screen turns once the app loses the focus or the device comes round. A locked
  rotation always wins.
- **Not yet.** Apps of the foreign layers asking it through their own APIs (Android's
  `screenOrientation`, iOS's supported orientations), and a phone's shell turning a held app's
  window inside an unturned screen.

## D437 The Storage pane's format and install panels on narrow pages (settings-forms-v0.5.md section 2, R10; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** On a narrow page the format and install panels take the pane's full width from y
  64, their lines the column's width, their fields the column's width and 48 tall, and
  `Cancel` with `Format` (or `Install`) an equal pair on the last row; the desktop shape puts
  every place back. They stay in the pane rather than at the window's bottom: the pane's
  scroll view keeps the focused field in view, and a panel that belongs to the window's frame
  would need a toolkit sheet that the window lifts out of the pane (left for the build pass,
  with the Agents pane's grant panel, which keeps its desktop places).

## D438 virtio-gpu 3D, part 2a: command streams posted, waits that sleep on the GPU's interrupt (M11; D415's "Why synchronous"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The driver's 3D command splits as the flush did (D414): `start_three_d` posts
  and returns, `finish_three_d` collects the answer, `abandon_three_d` gives up on a wedged
  device, and `run_three_d` is the two with a poll between; while one is posted every 2D post
  is refused, so the queue never carries both. In the kernel an `EXECBUFFER` posts its stream
  and returns at once: the program encodes its next frame while the host GPU runs this one.
  `VIRTGPU_WAIT` (and the next submission, before it posts) sleeps on the GPU's interrupt with
  no lock held until the answer arrives (`display::settle_renderer_sleeping`, polling on a GPU
  without one); `VIRTGPU_WAIT_NOWAIT` answers `EBUSY` while it runs. Every other use of the
  device, 2D included, first settles a posted 3D command (`Display::settle`). Buffers are idle
  whenever no stream is posted, so a mapping read after a wait sees what the GPU wrote.
- **Not yet.** Several streams in flight at once and per-buffer fences (a wait waits for the
  last stream, whatever buffer it names), the out-fence still an already signalled stand-in,
  blob resources for Venus and PRIME sharing with the window server (part 2b).

## D439 virtio-gpu 3D, part 2b begun: guest-memory blob resources (M11; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** The driver negotiates `VIRTIO_GPU_F_RESOURCE_BLOB` and encodes
  `RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB` for a blob whose only copy is guest memory (`BLOB_MEM_GUEST`, one
  entry for its DMA backing, host-tested). `Context::create_guest_blob` makes one for a
  context; the render node answers `VIRTGPU_RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB` for it (handle and resource
  back, mapped like any buffer through `VIRTGPU_MAP`) and `VIRTGPU_PARAM_RESOURCE_BLOB` says
  whether the GPU takes them. A blob is destroyed by its unreference alone, then its memory is
  freed.
- **Not yet.** Host blobs (`BLOB_MEM_HOST3D`, which Venus uses for most Vulkan memory): they
  live in the device's shared memory window, which the virtio transports must map first
  (`VIRTIO_PCI_CAP_SHARED_MEMORY_CFG`), with `RESOURCE_MAP_BLOB` placing them in it; real
  fences; PRIME sharing.

## D440 virtio-gpu host blobs in the device's host-visible memory (M11 part 2b; Venus's memory; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** The virtio-pci transport lists a function's shared memory regions
  (`virtio_pci_cap64` with `cfg_type` 8; `shared_memory_regions`), and the probe of a virtio
  GPU records region 1, the host-visible memory, as the rendering module's window
  (`set_host_window`, its physical place in the BAR). The driver encodes a host blob's
  `RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB` (`BLOB_MEM_HOST3D`, a blob id, no entries), `RESOURCE_MAP_BLOB` (its
  answer `OK_MAP_INFO`) and `RESOURCE_UNMAP_BLOB`. `Context::create_host_blob` runs the
  command stream the call carries (which makes the blob on the host), creates the resource,
  takes a range of the window (first fit, freed ranges joined) and maps the blob there; the
  program maps it like any buffer, its frames the window's own. Its end unmaps and
  unreferences it and gives the range back. `VIRTGPU_RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB` takes both kinds
  and `VIRTGPU_PARAM_HOST_VISIBLE` says whether the window exists.
- **Not yet.** The map's cache type from `OK_MAP_INFO` (mappings are made as normal memory),
  the window on virtio-mmio and virtio-ccw, real fences, PRIME sharing with the window server.

## D441 GPU buffers as files: PRIME export and import (M11 part 2b; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `DRM_IOCTL_PRIME_HANDLE_TO_FD` hands a context's buffer out as a file
  (`FileKind::GpuBuffer`, Linux's `dma-buf`): it can be mapped (`MAP_SHARED`, from offset 0,
  the buffer's own frames), polled (always ready), `fstat`ed (a regular file the buffer's size)
  and passed to another program over a Unix socket like any descriptor. `PRIME_FD_TO_HANDLE`
  takes such a file back into a context: the handle the buffer already has there, or a new one
  with its resource attached to that context, so a compositor's context can sample what a
  client's context rendered. `GET_CAP(PRIME)` reports import and export. The buffer lives
  while any context, file or mapping holds it.
- **Not yet.** The window server taking a GPU buffer as a window's pixels (a request on
  `/dev/window` that shows the buffer after its transfer back from the host, or the
  `linux-dmabuf` Wayland protocol in `eggway`), and implicit fences on the shared buffer.

## D442 The window server shows a GPU buffer as a window's pixels (M11 part 2b, D441's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `/dev/window` takes `SHOW_GPU_BUFFER` (request 58): the caller's window, a
  `dma-buf` descriptor (D441), the picture's width, height, stride and starting byte. The
  kernel copies the rows from the buffer's guest memory into the window's pixels (as many as
  the window holds) and commits the whole window, so a GL or Vulkan program that rendered
  through the render node, and transferred its frame back from the host into the buffer,
  shows it with one call instead of copying it through its own mapping.
- **Not yet.** Zero copy (the window server compositing straight from the buffer's frames, or
  the host scanning the resource out), host blobs (their memory is the device's, outside the
  direct map), and `eggway` offering `linux-dmabuf` to Wayland clients on top of it.

## D443 Intel's display flips on the vertical-blank interrupt (M13, D268's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** The Intel display engine driver can have the lit pipe interrupt at each vertical
  blank (`interrupt_on_vblank`: the pipe's cause cleared, unmasked and enabled in the display
  engine's pipe interrupt registers, the display's master switch on with the pipe's bit, and on
  display 11 and later the graphics master's display bit too) and clears the cause when it
  looks (`acknowledge_vblank`: the master switch off, the cause written back, the switch on).
  The kernel connects the function's message interrupt (D255) to the scanout's events and
  takes the display's split flush (D414): `start_flush` copies the damage into the hidden
  buffer and flips, `finish_flush` answers once the plane's live surface is the new one, so
  the drawing thread sleeps until the blank instead of spinning on the register. Without a
  connected interrupt it polls as before.
- **Known gaps (to check on hardware).** The pipe interrupt registers' offsets and the
  display-11 master bit are from Intel's public programming references, unverified here;
  the device ids that mark display 11 and later are a short list.

## D444 Intel's display microcontroller firmware is loaded (M13, D268's and D265's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `gpu::intel_dmc::parse` reads a DMC file as Intel publishes them: the CSS header,
  the package header and its entries (one per stepping, or `*` for any), then the chosen
  firmware's header (its signature, version, program length and register writes; version 1
  loads at the program memory's start, later versions say where), host-tested on a built
  file. `DisplayEngine::load_dmc` writes the program word by word and then the writes that
  start it. Once the file systems are mounted a kernel thread waits for the device's file
  from the `display-firmware` component (`/usr/lib/firmware/i915`, the D265 component, which
  the store downloads on request: Tiger Lake, Alder Lake S and P, Raptor Lake P, Meteor Lake)
  and hands it to the display (`display::load_firmware`, a new `Scanout` method).
- **Known gaps (to check on hardware).** The header fields' offsets past version 1, the
  stepping (any is asked, as the kernel does not read the device's stepping yet), and the
  power wells and the DC-state enables that let the firmware save power, which come with mode
  setting.

## D445 Intel mode setting, part 1: EDID and the DisplayPort AUX channels (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `drivers::edid` reads a display's EDID base block (header and checksum, maker,
  product, name, and the first detailed timing as its preferred mode with its blanking, sync
  and refresh), host-tested on a 1920x1080 block. `gpu::intel_aux` drives each digital port's
  AUX channel (control and data registers, bytes packed most significant first, a 1.6 ms time
  out, deferrals retried): native DPCD reads, the receiver capabilities (revision, highest link
  rate, lanes), and the EDID over I2C on AUX at 0x50 in 16-byte reads. At probe the Intel
  display asks ports A to D and `/proc/driver/display` lists what answered: `port A AUO
  B140HAN preferred 1920x1080@60 dp 2.70 x4`.
- **Next (part 2).** The link training (clock recovery and channel equalisation with the
  sink's voltage swing and pre-emphasis requests), the port's PLL for the chosen rate, the
  transcoder's timings from the EDID and the pipe's source size: a mode the firmware did not
  set, and a second screen. HDMI's EDID over GMBUS with its TMDS PLL after that.

## D446 Intel mode setting, part 2: DisplayPort link training (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `drivers::display_port::train` is VESA's link training over one `Link` (the
  source port's patterns, drive and pauses, and the sink's DPCD): the rate and lane count
  written, training pattern 1 with scrambling off until every lane's clock recovers (raising
  the drive to the highest level any lane asks, at most five tries at one level), then pattern
  2 until every lane is equalised and symbol-locked and the lanes are aligned, then the
  pattern turned off. It is host-tested against a fake sink that needs a given swing, and one
  whose clock never recovers. The Intel display engine trains a port with it
  (`train_port`): `DDI_BUF_CTL` enabled for the lane count and the drive level, `DP_TP_CTL`
  sending the pattern, the DPCD through the port's AUX channel (native writes added).
- **Known gaps (to check on hardware).** The drive's buffer-translation index and the
  `DP_TP_CTL` pattern codes are the Skylake-era layout, unverified on later displays; the
  pauses spin on the deadline rather than timing microseconds.
- **Next (part 3).** The port's PLL for the trained rate, the transcoder's timings and the
  pipe's source size from the EDID's preferred mode, and the plane on the new pipe: a mode the
  firmware did not set, and a second screen.

## D447 Intel mode setting, part 3: the transcoder, M/N and the display-9 PLL (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `gpu::intel_modeset` computes, host-tested: a mode's transcoder timing registers
  from its EDID timing (totals, blanking, sync and the pipe's source size, each pair less one),
  the DisplayPort data and link M/N (the payload's share of the lanes, the pixel clock over the
  symbol clock, halved together until they fit 24 bits), the lanes' symbol clocks, and the
  display-9 PLL's link-rate codes. `DisplayEngine::set_mode` lights a pipe on port B, C or D:
  the ports' PLL set to the rate, enabled and locked, routed to the port; the transcoder's
  timings, M/N with a 64-symbol transfer unit, clock and DDI function (DP SST, lanes, sync
  polarities); the link trained (D446); then the pipe enabled and its plane given the size,
  stride, format and surface.
- **Not yet.** The kernel calling it (a second screen, or a mode other than the firmware's on
  the first), port A's eDP on its own PLL and transcoder, the combo and Type-C PHYs of
  display 11 and later, HDMI (GMBUS EDID, TMDS PLL, infoframes), and power wells.

## D448 AMD graphics, part 1: the video BIOS's ATOM tables (M13, D245's order; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** AMD's display engine (DCN) is set up from its video BIOS's tables and
  needs the DMCUB firmware to run; where to start without a board to test on.
- **Decision.** Start with what every later part needs and what can be checked on the host:
  `gpu::amd_atom` reads an ATOM BIOS image (the expansion ROM signature, the ATOM ROM header,
  the master list of data tables), the firmware table (revision, boot engine clock) and the
  display object table at 1.4 and 1.5 (each path's connector, encoder and device tag), from
  the layout AMD publishes in `atomfirmware.h` under the MIT licence; host-tested on a built
  image. A new `amd-display` driver (in the default kernel) takes AMD's PCI functions of the
  display class ahead of the class's other drivers, reads the card's expansion ROM through
  its ROM BAR (enabled for the copy, then off again) and keeps a line for
  `/proc/driver/display`: `amd 73bf firmware 00110022 engine 800 MHz DisplayPort HDMI`.
  The firmware's framebuffer (D236) stays the display.
- **Next.** The video BIOS from ACPI's `VFCT` when the ROM BAR is unassigned (UEFI shadows
  it there), running ATOM command tables (the interpreter AMD's design needs for the
  display's power-up), the DMCUB firmware from the component store (D265), then DCN's pipes,
  planes and flips.

## D449 NVIDIA graphics, part 1: the video BIOS's BIT and DCB (M13, D245's order; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `gpu::nvidia_bios` reads an NVIDIA video BIOS from the layouts NVIDIA publishes in
  `open-gpu-doc` (MIT): the BIOS Information Table found by its signature, its `i` token's
  BIOS version, and the Display Configuration Block 4.x pointed at from byte 0x36 (its
  signature checked, each entry's output type, skipped and end entries honoured); host-tested
  on a built image. The kernel's AMD driver (D448) becomes `vendor_gpus` (feature
  `vendor-gpus`, default), with an `nvidia-display` driver beside `amd-display` that reads the
  card's expansion ROM the same way and adds its line to `/proc/driver/display`:
  `nvidia 2484 bios 86042100 DisplayPort DVI/HDMI`.
- **Next.** The GSP firmware from the component store (the RISC-V core that runs modern NVIDIA
  GPUs, D246's firmware question settled by D265), its boot sequence and the display engine's
  methods, as NVIDIA's `open-gpu-kernel-modules` headers document them (MIT).

## D450 Android apps, part 1: reading an APK's manifest and DEX files (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** Android apps (D34, after Linux, Windows and macOS) ship as APKs: Dalvik
  bytecode in `classes*.dex`, native libraries per ABI, resources and a binary manifest. D17
  forbids interpreting their code, so the layer compiles the bytecode ahead of time, once, at
  install, and implements the Android framework natively. Where to start.
- **Decision.** With what install and the compiler both read, host-tested: a new
  `eggos-android-package` crate (`no_std`, no dependencies). `manifest` reads the binary XML of
  `AndroidManifest.xml` (its string pool in UTF-8 or UTF-16, its start and end elements and
  their typed attributes): the package, version name and code, lowest and target SDK, the
  permissions asked for, and the activity whose intent filter holds `MAIN` and `LAUNCHER`.
  `dex` reads a DEX file's header (magic and version 035 to 041, size, the little-endian tag)
  and its string, type, method and class-definition tables, with MUTF-8 strings after their
  ULEB128 lengths and the descriptors of the classes it defines. The APK itself is a zip,
  which `eggos_app::archive` (D148) already reads.
- **Next.** `app install` of an `.apk` (the Android layer as an optional component, D18): its
  manifest shown, its ABI's native libraries kept, its permissions asked through the agent
  permission model; the DEX code's method bodies and the ahead-of-time compiler to the CPU's
  own code; then the framework: `Activity`, views on the toolkit, and the intents and App
  Actions that make an app AI-usable (D21).

## D451 An `.apk` is named as an Android app when installing (M15, D450's next; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** An APK is a zip, so `app install`, Files' `Install` and the installer window took
  one for an archive and refused it as holding no program. The archive scan now stops at an
  `AndroidManifest.xml` entry and refuses with `NotRunnable::AndroidPackage`: `Could not install
  Notes: it is an Android app package (.apk), and installing Android apps is not built yet`,
  the same words in the CLI, the GUI and the `app_install` tool; host-tested.
- **Next.** Installing it: the Android layer's component, the manifest shown (D450), the
  ABI's native libraries kept, and the ahead-of-time compiler.

## D452 An `.ipa` is named as an iOS app when installing (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** An IPA is a zip whose `Payload/<name>.app/` holds an iOS app; the installer's scan
  now refuses it as `NotRunnable::IosPackage` (`it is an iOS app package (.ipa), and
  installing iOS apps is not built yet`) instead of failing on its flat bundle, in the CLI, the
  GUI and the tool alike; host-tested.
- **Next (iOS part 1 proper).** The bundle installed through the macOS layer's Mach-O loader
  (an iOS program is arm64 Mach-O with `LC_BUILD_VERSION` naming iOS), its `Info.plist`
  read, and UIKit's first classes (`UIApplicationMain`, `UIWindow`, `UIView`,
  `UIViewController`) over the toolkit, as AppKit's were (D17's iOS apps distributed outside
  the App Store).

## D453 `component install` reports as a job and stops when asked (components-v0.5.md section 6's backend, ask 1 for install; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** `manager::install_reporting` hands the file system to the copy's progress, as
  updates' already did (D299), and `install` keeps its old shape over it. `component install`
  now records each component's copy in `/run/eggos/component-job` (`installing`, its name,
  `copying`, bytes done of total), stops at its next piece when `component cancel` asked
  (the staged copy deleted, nothing installed: `Cancelled.`), and clears the job when each
  component ends; `component list` shows the row `installing 42 %` to any front-end, so an

- **Next.** The Components pane starting installs and removes as `/bin/component` children
  (`ComponentJob::Install` and `Remove`) instead of in its window's tick, its bar and
  `Cancel` read from the job file, and `Finishing...` while the copy is moved into place.

## D454 The Components pane installs through jobs, with live progress and `Cancel` (components-v0.5.md section 6; D300's deviation; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** An install the pane starts (one component, or each of a plan's in turn) is a

  inside the window's tick: the pane keeps drawing, reads the job file every 100 ms and moves

## D455 The Components pane's notes on a phone (components-v0.5.md section 10; D423's deviation; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

## D457 The Agents pane's grant panel on narrow pages (settings-forms-v0.5.md 2, R10; D430's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

## D458 The Components pane removes through jobs too (D454's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** Once a remove is confirmed, the pane runs `/bin/component remove <name> --yes` as
