## D459 `eggway` takes GPU buffers: `zwp_linux_dmabuf_v1` (M11, D442's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** Mesa's EGL and Vulkan presentation on Wayland hand the compositor each frame
  as a `dma-buf` through `zwp_linux_dmabuf_v1`; without it a GL program falls back to
  copying into `wl_shm` itself, or fails.
- **Decision.** `eggway` serves the global at version 3: it announces `XRGB8888` and
  `ARGB8888` with the linear modifier, takes one plane per params object (its `dma-buf`
  descriptor, offset and stride; other planes and modifiers refused with the protocol's
  errors) and makes the `wl_buffer` at `create_immed`. The buffer's pixels are the descriptor
  mapped (D441's files map from offset 0) as a pool of its own that goes when the buffer
  goes, so commits, damage, subsurfaces and the window's drawing are exactly the `wl_shm`
  path's. The asynchronous `create` answers `failed`, which clients handle by retrying with
  `create_immed`. The wire and dispatch tables gain the two interfaces; host tests check
  their signatures with the rest.
- **Not yet.** Zero copy (the window server compositing from the GPU's frames, D442's
  "Not yet"), feedback objects (version 4), and multi-plane formats.

## D460 Several command streams in flight, with real fences (M11, D438's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** D438 posted one command stream at a time and refused flushes while it ran, and
  an out-fence was an `eventfd` already signalled, so a GL program waited for each frame's
  stream before writing the next and the desktop's flushes waited behind a game's frames.
- **Decision.** The virtio-gpu driver gives command streams `STREAM_SLOTS` slots of their
  own (2 × 256 KiB, the 3D area growing from 264 KiB to 520 KiB), each with its own request and
  answer; `start_stream` posts one fenced and returns its fence. Answers are told apart by
  their chain's head, so streams finish in any order while flushes, 2D commands and the other
  3D commands run beside them (the device answers a fenced command only once it finished it).
  The kernel keeps the oldest fence still in flight: a fence passes once it is older. Each
  buffer keeps the fence of the last stream that named it in `EXECBUFFER`; `VIRTGPU_WAIT`,
  a copy back from the host and the buffer's release (detach and unref, then freeing its
  memory) wait for it. The out-fence is a sync file (`FileKind::GpuFence`), readable once its
  fence passed, with `SYNC_IOC_MERGE` and `SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO`; an in-fence must be one, and
  needs no wait, as all streams share one timeline the device runs in order.
- **Waits.** A fence wait sleeps on the console's input key, whose waiters the GPU's
  interrupt now also wakes, so any number of threads wait at once (a device's events keep one
  waiter); under the bucket's lock it only reads atomics: whether the fence passed or the
  interrupt was raised since the answers were last collected. Without an interrupt it polls,
  and `poll` looks again soon. After 5 s the streams are given up and the device is treated as
  wedged, as a flush that times out is.
- **Not yet.** Per-context timelines (`ring_idx`), sync objects, and zero-copy composition.

## D461 Zero-copy composition: a window shows a GPU buffer's frames (M11, D442's and D459's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** D442 copied each GPU frame into the window's pixels, and `eggway` (D459)
  copied a client's `dma-buf` into its window again, so a GL frame was copied twice before
  the compositor read it a third time.
- **Decision.** `SHOW_GPU_BUFFER` now makes the window show the GPU buffer's frame from then
  on (`GpuPicture`: the buffer, size, stride and first byte, checked to lie inside its guest
  memory): the compositor reads the rows straight from the buffer through the direct map, as
  it reads a window's own pixels (`WindowPixels`), and captures read them too. Each call
  first waits for the buffer's last command stream (D460) and commits the whole window; the
  next frame rendered into the same buffer is shown by calling it again. `NO_GPU_BUFFER`
  (`0xffffffff`), or a new buffer from `SET_SIZE`, shows the window's own pixels again.
  `eggway` shows a toplevel's `dma-buf` this way when nothing is composed over it (no
  subsurfaces, no viewport), holds that `wl_buffer` until another replaces it (releasing it
  at once would let the client draw into what is on screen), and goes back to copying, whole,
  when a `wl_shm` buffer or a composed frame comes.
- **Why not the host scanning the resource out.** `SET_SCANOUT` of a 3D resource would skip
  even the compositor's read, but only for one full-screen window, and the desktop draws its
  chrome, cursor and other windows over the frame; reading guest memory keeps every window
  and the desktop's drawing exactly as they are, at one read per composed pixel, which the
  window's own pixels cost anyway. Direct scanout of a full-screen window stays a later
  optimisation.
- **Not yet.** Host blobs (their memory is the device's, outside the direct map), direct
  scanout, and frames shown on the display's vertical blank instead of at the call.

## D462 Sensors behind I2C-HID: DesignWare I2C, HID over I2C and ACPI's I2C connections (M12, D435's and D256's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** Tablets and convertibles put their accelerometer (and their touchpad, touch
  screen and keyboard) on an I2C bus as a HID over I2C device that ACPI declares, not on USB;
  the kernel had no I2C controller, and the static ACPI walk (D252) read neither a device's
  I2C connection nor the HID descriptor's register, which firmware gives through methods.
- **Decision.** `eggos_drivers::i2c` has a bus trait and a polled DesignWare master (Intel's
  LPSS controllers on PCI and the ACPI-declared ones, such as AMD's): it keeps the firmware's
  clock counts, or works them out from the controller's input clock, and feeds `IC_DATA_CMD`
  as the FIFOs allow, a repeated start before the reads and a stop on the last word.
  `input::i2c_hid` reads the 30-byte HID descriptor (at the register `_DSM` names, else at
  0x0001, 0x0020 and 0x0000, the values most devices use), the report descriptor, powers the
  device on and polls each report carrying accelerometer axes with `GET_REPORT`, decoded as a
  USB HID sensor's (D435). The AML walk takes a device's connection from the first
  `I2cSerialBus` descriptor in its buffers or in its methods' bodies (firmware builds `_CRS`
  in a method more often than not) and the descriptor's register from the first constant its
  `_DSM` returns after the HID over I2C UUID; discovery then resolves the controller by the
  path the connection names: its own `_CRS` registers, or the root-bus PCI function its
  `_ADR` names. The kernel's `i2c-hid` driver (feature `i2c-hid`, on by default) shares one
  controller between the devices on its bus and installs each sensor as an input device
  polled every 100 ms, a few dozen bytes on the bus each time.
- **Why polling.** The devices' interrupt lines are GPIO pins (`GpioInt`), and the kernel has
  no GPIO controller drivers yet; a sensor's reading is a value, so asking for it ten times a
  second costs little and loses nothing. Touchpads, touch screens and keyboards send reports
  only when their interrupt says so, so they are refused until GPIO interrupts exist.
- **Not yet.** GPIO interrupts (Intel and AMD pin controllers) and the devices that need them;
  sensors whose readings must first be turned on through feature reports (reporting and power
  state); running `_DSM`, `_CRS` and `_STA` through an AML interpreter.

## D463 Panels lifted out of the pane as true bottom sheets (M12, D437's and D457's "left for the build pass"; settings-forms-v0.5.md R10; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Done.** The toolkit's `WidgetTree::set_sheet(container, height)` lifts a container out
  of its parent: while lifted it is laid out at the window's bottom, the window's full width
  and `height` tall, outside its parent's scrolling and clipping and out of its content size;
  it and its children are painted after every other widget (before popups, menus and
  tooltips), and a press that lands on it reaches only its own widgets. `None` puts it back
  in its parent's flow. On a narrow page the Storage pane's format and install panels and the
  Agents pane's grant panel are now sheets of their narrow height (D437's and D457's places
  inside them unchanged), and the desktop shape puts them back in the pane. `Back` first
  closes an open sheet, as its `Cancel` does (R10's "Back closes it"), before going back a
  page.
- **Not yet.** A dimmed scrim over the page behind a sheet and a tap above it closing it
  (the phone shell's own sheets do both); the Wi-Fi join note as a sheet (its rows keep their
  button, D434).

## D464 The kernel lights a second screen on Intel display 9: a mirror through the pipe scaler (M13, D447's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** D447 wrote Intel mode setting but nothing called it, so a monitor plugged
  into a laptop stayed dark. The kernel's display (D112) is one framebuffer the desktop draws;
  extending the desktop across two screens is the desktop's work (M12), lighting the screen
  is the driver's.
- **Decision.** At probe, the first sink on a port the firmware did not light that answers
  with DisplayPort link capabilities and an EDID preferred timing is lit, on display 9 only
  (the engine whose PLLs `set_mode` programs), on a free pipe, when the timing fits the link
  (24 bits a pixel within the lanes' 8b/10b payload). The new pipe mirrors the first screen:
  its source is the first screen's size, and the pipe scaler fits that picture to the
  monitor's timing, keeping its shape between bars; the pipe's plane shows the same buffer,
  and every flip writes the lit pipe's and its mirrors' planes, so both screens change at
  their vertical blanks. `/proc/driver/display` lists the mirror with the sinks.
- **Why a mirror first.** It needs no change above the driver: the desktop, the window server
  and the input's coordinates stay one screen's, and presenting a talk or a TV is what a
  second screen is plugged in for most often. Extending the desktop needs a second
  framebuffer and the desktop's screen arrangement.
- **Not yet.** Extending the desktop; the cursor on the mirror (the cursor plane is the
  first pipe's); display 11 and later (D465); HDMI sinks (D466); hot plug.

## D465 Intel display 11's combo PHY clocks, so Ice Lake lights a second screen too (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** On display 11 (Ice Lake, Jasper and Elkhart Lake) a combo port's DisplayPort
  clock comes from a combo PLL: `intel_combo_phy` works its settings out from the reference
  clock the straps name (24, 19.2 or 38.4 MHz, the last halved): the oscillator at 8.1 GHz as
  a whole and a 15-bit fractional multiple, and the P and K dividers that bring it to half the
  link rate (5 and 2 for 1.62 Gbps, 3 and 2 for 2.7, 3 and 1 for 5.4, 2 and 1 for 8.1).
  `set_mode` takes a combo PLL the firmware left off, powers it, writes its two configuration
  registers, enables it until it locks, routes it to the port and turns the port's clock on;
  the transcoder, M/N, link training and planes are display 9's (D447), which display 11
  keeps. The engine learns the device's display version at `take`, and the kernel lights a
  mirror (D464) on display 9 and 11.
- **Not yet.** Ice Lake's Type-C ports (the MG PHY and its PLLs, the FIA's lane assignment
  and Type-C cold), the combo PHY's drive tables (training keeps the drive the PHY was
  initialised with), and display 12 and later (Tiger Lake on: their clock routing moved).

## D466 HDMI on Intel display 9: EDID over GMBUS and the HDMI PLL (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A port whose AUX channel does not answer is asked over GMBUS, the display
  engine's own I2C controller, on its pin pair (B, C and D are 5, 4 and 6 on display 9): an
  index cycle at offset 0 and a 128-byte read at 0x50, four bytes a word, then a stop and the
  pins let go however it ended. A sink that answers is listed as `hdmi`. `set_mode_hdmi`
  lights it: the HDMI PLL's oscillator is five times the pixel clock times a divider, chosen
  (even dividers first) to lie within 1% above or 6% below 8.4, 9.0 or 9.6 GHz, closest to
  one; the divider splits into the PLL's P, Q and K dividers, and the oscillator is written
  as a whole and fractional multiple of the 24 MHz reference. A free PLL (2 or 3) in HDMI mode
  is locked and routed to the port, the transcoder takes the timing in HDMI mode at 8 bits a
  colour, the port's buffer turns on with no link to train, then the pipe and its plane. The
  kernel mirrors the first screen on it (D464) when no DisplayPort sink took the mirror.
- **Not yet.** HDMI 2.0's scrambling above 340 MHz, infoframes (AVI, audio), audio, deep
  colour, HDMI on display 11 and later, and the level shifter some boards put on the port.

## D467 AMD's ATOM command tables run by our own interpreter (M13, D448's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** An AMD board's video BIOS carries, besides its data tables (D448), command
  tables: byte-code for the steps that differ from board to board (pixel clocks, encoder and
  transmitter control, chip initialisation), which a display driver runs rather than
  reimplementing each board's wiring.
- **Decision.** `amd_atom_interpreter` runs them, from the layout AMD publishes for ATOM
  images: the ROM header's master command and data tables, each table's size, workspace and
  parameter-space bytes, then its code. Opcodes 1 to 134: move, and, or, xor, add, subtract,
  multiply and divide (16- and 32-bit, into the quotient and remainder slots), both shift
  forms, compare and test into the equal and above flags, the seven jumps, switch with its
  cases, clear and mask, delays, `CALL_TABLE` on the parameters past the caller's, the
  register block, data block and scratch base, and the no-ops; operands are registers,
  parameters, workspace slots and its special slots, scratch, constants in the image,
  immediates, and PLL and memory-controller registers, each read and written at the dword,
  word or byte the attribute byte names, keeping the rest of a register. The board is an
  `AtomCard` trait, so tables run on the host against fakes in tests. Limits stop a runaway
  table (a million steps) and deep calls (16). Only memory-mapped access is taken: a table
  that selects an I/O port stops. The AMD probe lists how many command tables the BIOS has.
- **Not yet.** Running a table on the hardware (the DCN display path, D468, is the first
  user), the I/O-port access modes, and the indirect PLL and memory-controller access a
  real card gives (the card's own registers).

## D468 AMD's IP discovery and the DMCUB firmware file (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** Since Navi an AMD GPU's display engine (DCN) differs by version in its
  register places, and its microcontroller (DMCUB) must run firmware before the engine is
  driven; both start from what the chip says about itself.
- **Decision.** `amd_discovery` reads the IP discovery binary AMD's published `discovery.h`
  lays out: its signature, the binary header's table list, the IP discovery table's dies
  (with 32- or 64-bit bases), and each die's blocks with their hardware id, instance,
  version and register bases; the display block (hardware id 271) is picked out. It also
  reads a DMCUB firmware file: the common header (IP version, firmware version, the array's
  offset) and the DMCUB header (instruction and data bytes), the instructions without the
  security processor's 256-byte header and footer. The AMD probe reads the last 64 KiB of the
  BAR 0 aperture, where the binary sits when the aperture spans video memory (resizable BAR),
  and lists the DCN version and the firmware file it needs, by the name the component store
  mirrors (`dcn_3_0_1_dmcub.bin`), as `display-firmware` (D265) carries.
- **Not yet.** Reading the binary when the aperture is smaller than video memory (through the
  memory index registers), loading DMCUB (its region windows and reset), and driving DCN's
  pipes (HUBP, DPP, OPP, OTG) at the register bases found: the roadmap's DCN item stays open
  until the per-version register places are written from AMD's published register headers.

## D469 NVIDIA's chip and its GSP firmware file (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** From Turing on, NVIDIA's display and the rest of the chip are driven through
  the GPU System Processor, a RISC-V core on the GPU running NVIDIA's GSP firmware, which
  NVIDIA publishes for open drivers. Driving the display starts with knowing the chip and
  finding its firmware's image and signature.
- **Decision.** `nvidia_gsp` names the chip from `PMC_BOOT_0` (BAR 0's first register: chip
  id, architecture, whether it runs GSP, its firmware folder name such as `tu104` and its
  signature family such as `tu10x`), and reads a GSP firmware file as the 64-bit ELF file it
  is: `.fwimage`, `.fwversion` and the `.fwsignature_<family>` section for the chip, each
  checked to lie inside the file. The NVIDIA probe reads `PMC_BOOT_0` and lists the chip and
  the firmware folder the component store mirrors (`nvidia/tu104/gsp`).
- **Not yet.** Booting GSP (the firmware's radix page tables, the booter and FWSEC handover,
  the message queues) and its display interface: the roadmap's GSP and display-engine item
  stays open until they are written.

## D470 `.apk` installs as an app the Android layer opens (M15, D451's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** An `.apk` (a `.zip` holding `AndroidManifest.xml`) now installs like any
  archive app (D148): the whole package is extracted into `/Applications/<name>/`, named after
  the `.apk` file, and its manifest says `source=android` and names `classes.dex` as what it
  runs (made executable). Opening it execs `classes.dex`, whose `dex\n` signature the kernel
  hands to the Android layer at `/usr/lib/eggos/android` on every architecture (the code is
  compiled ahead of time for the machine, D17), with the app's folder beside it: manifest,
  resources, assets and the native libraries of each ABI. `Source` gains `Android` (key
  `android`, label `Android`, badge `A`), whose layer is the `android-apps` component: without
  it the installer says which component to install, as for Windows and macOS programs. An
  `.apk` without `classes.dex` is refused as before.
- **Not yet.** The Android layer itself: compiling DEX ahead of time (D471) and the framework
  the code calls (D472); split APKs and app bundles; the manifest's label and icon as the
  app's name and icon.

## D471 DEX method bodies read and compiled ahead of time to x86_64, part 1 (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `android-package` reads a class's methods from its class data (direct, then
  virtual, with their access flags) and each method's code item (registers, arguments,
  outgoing words, `try` blocks, instructions), and `dalvik` decodes instructions by the
  formats AOSP publishes (all 26, from `10x` to `51l`), stepping over switch and array-data
  payloads. The new `dex-compiler` crate compiles a method ahead of time, never interpreting
  it (D17): a frame of 64-bit slots, one per virtual register, whose address the code gets in
  `rdi`; each instruction becomes loads into `eax`/`ecx`, the operation and a store, a wide
  value using its pair's first slot whole; branches are patched once every instruction's
  place is known, and those places are kept for mapping a code address back to its
  instruction. Part 1 compiles nop, moves, constants (int and wide), returns, `goto`, the
  twelve `if` forms, negation and not, int/long conversion, and int and long arithmetic,
  logic and shifts in their three-register, two-address and literal forms; anything else
  (division, which must throw on zero, objects, fields, arrays, invokes) is refused with its
  opcode and place.
- **Not yet.** The rest of the instruction set through calls into the runtime (D472), the
  aarch64 and riscv64 back ends, register allocation, and exception tables.

## D472 The Android layer, part 1: calls, objects and a first framework (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The compiler (D471) gets a real calling convention: a compiled method takes
  its argument words in `rdi` and the runtime's entry table in `rsi`, keeps the table in `r12`,
  builds its frame on the stack with `r13` at its first register (both survive calls), copies
  its arguments into its last registers, and returns in `rax` through an epilogue. Calls
  write their argument words at the frame's bottom and call through the table: `invoke-*`
  (both forms) to the method's entry, and `const-string`, `new-instance`, `iget`/`iput` and
  int/long division and remainder to the runtime's helpers, which come first in the table
  (`dex_compiler::helper`); `move-result` stores `rax`.
- **The layer.** `userland/android` (`/usr/lib/eggos/android`, the `android-apps` component,
  x86_64 for now) reads the app's manifest beside `classes.dex`, compiles every method it can,
  copies the code into memory it then makes executable, and fills the table: each method of
  the DEX file goes to its compiled code, or, looked up its class's superclasses, to an
  ancestor's compiled method or to a framework method the layer implements, or to a stop
  that names nothing found. Part 1's framework: `Object.<init>`; `Activity` and its AndroidX
  forms' constructors and lifecycle steps, and `setContentView`; `TextView.<init>` and
  `setText`. It creates the launcher activity, runs its `<init>` and `onCreate`, and shows the
  text view's text in a window, so an app whose first screen is a `TextView` runs natively.
  Objects are boxes kept for the app's life; a division by zero or a null field access stops
  the app with Java's exception name.
- **Not yet.** Virtual dispatch (calls go to the method the instruction names, up its
  superclasses), static fields, arrays, exceptions and switches in the compiler, layouts and
  resources (`R.layout`), more views and input, garbage collection, and the aarch64 and riscv64
  back ends.

## D473 iOS apps, part 1: `.ipa` install and UIKit on AppKit in the macOS layer (M15, D452's "Not yet"; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** An iOS app distributed outside the App Store is an arm64 Mach-O program in a
  bundle, so it runs natively through the macOS layer (D17, D120) on arm64 machines rather
  than through a layer of its own. The installer now takes an `.ipa`: it finds
  `Payload/<name>.app/Info.plist` (XML or binary), reads `CFBundleExecutable`, recognises that
  program, extracts the whole package and names the app after the bundle; the program runs
  as a macOS program, so on another CPU it is refused as one. The macOS layer provides UIKit
  (`/System/Library/Frameworks/UIKit.framework/UIKit`): its first classes are bound to AppKit's
  (`UIApplication`, `UIResponder`, `UIView`, `UIWindow`, `UIViewController`, `UILabel` as a
  text field, `UIButton`, `UIColor`, `UIFont`, `UIScreen`); a send that finds no method under a
  UIKit selector tries AppKit's (`setText:` is `setStringValue:`, `makeKeyAndVisible` is
  `makeKeyAndOrderFront:`, `rootViewController` is `contentViewController`, `bounds` is
  `frame`), and `-[UIWindow initWithFrame:]` makes a window of that frame.
  `UIApplicationMain` makes the shared application, makes the delegate of the class it names,
  sends it `application:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:` and runs the app.
- **Not yet.** Scenes (`UISceneDelegate`), touch events as `UITouch`, Auto Layout, storyboards
  for iOS, view controllers' presentation, the iOS bundle's own Info.plist keys in the layer,
  and x86_64 machines (iOS programs are arm64 only).

## D474 32-bit Arm and RV32, part 1: their page-table formats, and entries of either width (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** M9's 32-bit ports need the core free of its 64-bit assumptions; the first is
  the page-table code, which every architecture shares (D29) and which took every entry to be
  eight bytes in a 512-entry table.
- **Decision.** `Format` gains `ENTRY_BYTES` (8 by default), and the kernel's page-table code
  reads and writes each entry at that width, the value being a narrow entry's low half. Two
  formats join: `paging::arm::ArmLpae`, 32-bit Arm with the Large Physical Address
  Extension's long descriptors (Armv7-A from the Cortex-A7 and A15 on, and AArch32), which are
  AArch64's descriptors at three levels with a four-entry root, `TTBR0` alone translating the
  whole space and the kernel in the top gigabyte; and `paging::riscv32::Riscv32Sv32`, RV32's
  Sv32, two levels of 1,024 four-byte entries resolving 10 bits each, 4 KiB pages and 4 MiB
  megapages, a 22-bit physical page number (34-bit physical addresses), the kernel in the top
  gigabyte. Both are host-tested like the others.
- **Why LPAE, not the short descriptors.** Short descriptors cap physical addresses at 32 bits
  (or 40 only through supersections) and differ from every other format here; LPAE's are the
  64-bit format the core already builds, on every Armv7-A core with virtualisation support and
  QEMU's `virt` with a Cortex-A15, which is where 32-bit Arm runs Linux distributions today.
- **Not yet.** The HAL modules for `arm` and `riscv32` (boot, vectors, timers, context switch)
  and the rest of the core's assumptions (pointers kept in `u64`, the direct map's size, the
  Linux ABI's 32-bit system-call tables).

## D475 RV32, part 2: the boot path on QEMU `virt` (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `hal::arch::riscv32` boots under OpenSBI: `.bss` zeroed in words, the device
  tree and boot hart kept, one Sv32 root of 4 MiB megapages built (D474): the direct map, RAM
  from `0x8000_0000` at `0xc000_0000` on (896 MiB, Linux's "lowmem" split, the top gigabyte
  holding the kernel image, linked at `0xc040_0000` inside the direct map, so
  `KERNEL_VIRTUAL_OFFSET` and the direct map's offset are the same `0x4000_0000`), the image's
  megapage again at its physical address for the jump, and the UART's megapage at its
  physical address; translation on, the jump to the virtual address, the stack, and
  `early_main`, which reports on the console and stops the machine through SBI's system
  reset. The module also reads the 64-bit `time` counter as its two halves until the high one
  holds still, and asks SBI for timer interrupts with the deadline split across `a0` and `a1`.
- **Why the direct map holds the kernel.** A 32-bit address space has no room for a 64-bit
  kernel's separate top-2-GiB image (D33) beside a direct map: one gigabyte for the kernel
  means one mapping for both.
- **Not yet.** Exceptions and interrupts, threads, user mode, secondary harts and the rest of
  `Platform` (RV32 part 3), RAM beyond 896 MiB, and the core's remaining 64-bit assumptions.

## D476 32-bit Arm, part 2: the boot path on QEMU `virt` with a Cortex-A15 (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `hal::arch::arm` boots an ELF image QEMU loads at `0x4040_0000` (the device
  tree at RAM's start, where QEMU puts it for an ELF kernel) in SVC mode: interrupts masked,
  `.bss` zeroed, and the LPAE root (D474) given three 1 GiB blocks: RAM's first gigabyte at
  `0xc000_0000` (the direct map, holding the kernel image linked at `0xc040_0000`, so the
  image's offset and the direct map's are the same `0x8000_0000`, as on RV32, D475), the same
  gigabyte at its physical address for the jump, and the physical space's first gigabyte, QEMU
  `virt`'s devices, at its own address as execute-never device memory. `MAIR0` takes
  AArch64's attribute bytes, `TTBCR` turns LPAE on with `TTBR0` translating everything and
  write-back, inner-shareable walks, and `SCTLR` turns on the MMU and both caches; then the
  jump to the virtual address, the stack, and `early_main`, which writes to the PL011, reads
  the generic timer (`CNTVCT`, `CNTFRQ`) and powers off through PSCI's `SYSTEM_OFF`.
- **Not yet.** Exception vectors and modes (IRQ, abort, undefined, supervisor-call stacks),
  the GIC, threads, user mode, secondary CPUs, the rest of `Platform`, RAM beyond a gigabyte,
  and the core's remaining 64-bit assumptions.

## D477 RV32, part 3: traps and timer interrupts (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** RV32's boot sets `stvec` to a trap entry that saves `x1` to `x31` (with the
  stack pointer before the trap) and `sepc`, `sstatus`, `scause` and `stval` in a 144-byte
  `TrapFrame` on the kernel stack, calls the Rust handler with it, restores `sepc`, `sstatus`
  and the registers, and returns with `sret`. The supervisor timer interrupt counts a tick and
  asks SBI for the next one, a hundred a second; any other trap reports and stops. The boot
  path enables `sie.STIE` and `sstatus.SIE` and waits for three ticks before shutting down.
- **Not yet.** Traps from user mode (`sscratch` and a per-hart stack), external interrupts
  through the PLIC, threads, and the rest of `Platform`.

## D478 32-bit Arm, part 3: exception vectors, the GICv2 and the virtual timer (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `VBAR` points at an eight-entry vector table; IRQs enter through the usual
  Armv7 sequence (return address adjusted, `SRSDB` of the return state onto the SVC stack, a
  switch to SVC mode, the caller-saved registers pushed, the handler, then `RFEIA`), so no
  mode but SVC needs a stack of its own; every other exception sets a stack, reports and
  powers off. The handler acknowledges through the GICv2 CPU interface, re-arms the virtual
  timer (`CNTV_TVAL`, `CNTV_CTL`) on its interrupt (PPI 27) and ends the interrupt. The boot
  path gives PPI 27 a priority, enables it, the distributor and the CPU interface, arms the
  timer for a hundredth of a second, unmasks IRQs and waits for three ticks.
- **Not yet.** Data and prefetch aborts as page faults, undefined instructions, supervisor
  calls from user mode, the other modes' stacks for nesting, GICv3, threads and the rest of
  `Platform`.

## D479 The kernel thread switch on RV32 and 32-bit Arm (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Both ports get D35's switch: RV32's is RV64's with 32-bit words (`ra` and
  `s0` to `s11`, padded to 64 bytes so `sp` stays 16-byte aligned), and its trampoline calls
  `s1` with `s2`; 32-bit Arm's pushes `r3` (padding) to `r11` and `lr` in one `PUSH`, stores
  `sp`, loads the other thread's and pops, 40 bytes, and its trampoline calls `r5` with `r6`.
  Each module gives the initial frame its trampoline needs, written with
  `thread::write_initial_frame` like every other architecture's.
- **Not yet.** Wiring both into a `Platform` implementation with the rest of its methods.

## D480 RV32, part 4: user mode (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** RV32 keeps a program's registers in RV64's `Registers` layout (`hal::user`),
  each 32-bit register in the low half of its 64-bit slot, so everything the kernel does with a
  user context is shared between the two widths. `riscv32_enter_user` saves the kernel's
  callee-saved registers and `tp`, keeps its stack pointer in the context and the context in
  `sscratch`, points `stvec` at the user trap entry, clears `SPP`, sets `SPIE`, loads the
  program's registers (`a0` last) and `sret`s. The user trap entry swaps `a0` with
  `sscratch`, saves every register and `sepc`, takes the kernel's stack, puts the kernel's
  `stvec` back, clears `sscratch` and returns into `run_user`, which clears the slots' high
  halves and says why: a system call (`ecall` from U-mode, the program counter moved past it),
  an interrupt (handed to the timer's handler), or an exception decoded from `scause` and
  `stval`, kept for `last_exception`.
- **Not yet.** The Linux ABI for RV32 (its system-call table is the generic one, with 64-bit
  time calls), floating point state, the user test programs, and the `Platform` implementation
  that ties these together.

## D481 RV32, part 5: the `Platform` implementation and its user test program (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `Riscv32` implements `Platform`, so RV32 is `CurrentPlatform` and its boot calls
  the kernel's `kernel_main` after enabling the timer and wake-up interrupts. Most of it is
  RV64's at 32 bits: the console on the NS16550, the SBI timer and system reset, `wfi` and the
  interrupt window, the memory map, RAM and seeds from the device tree (the shared
  `boot_memory` code now covers RV32), Sv32 page tables through `satp`, `sstatus.SUM` for user
  access, `fence.i` and `sfence.vma`, page faults by `scause`, the thread switch (D479), user
  mode (D480), RV64's floating-point save and restore with 32-bit stores for `fcsr`, `tp` for
  the CPU-local block, SBI IPIs for wake-ups. Interrupts reach the kernel as RV64's do (the
  timer disarmed, then `Interrupt::Timer`; the software interrupt cleared, then `Wakeup`), and
  a kernel exception reaches `kernel_exception`. The user test program has the register
  check, floating point, null system calls, the spin, the illegal instruction and Linux's
  hello; the Linux programs not written for RV32 yet exit with status 1, so their self-tests
  fail plainly.
- **Not yet.** Secondary harts (`start_cpu` refuses), console input and device interrupts
  through the PLIC, Sstc, and the core's remaining 64-bit assumptions, first of them
  `AtomicU64`, which RV32's `A` extension does not have (the CPU-local 64-bit loads, clocks and
  counters).

## D482 32-bit Arm, part 4: user mode, FP and the `Platform` implementation (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A program's registers are `r0`-`r14` (user mode's banked `sp` and `lr`
  included), the program counter, `CPSR`, why it stopped, a fault's status and address, and
  its thread pointer (`TPIDRURO`), in `hal::user::arm`; system calls follow the EABI (`r7` the
  number, `r0`-`r5` the arguments, `r0` the result, `svc #0`, two bytes back in Thumb).
  `arm_enter_user` keeps the kernel's callee-saved registers and the context's address on the
  SVC stack, sets `TPIDRURO` and `SPSR` (user mode, the program's flags and Thumb bit, IRQs
  on), loads user mode's registers with `LDM ^` and enters with `MOVS PC, LR`. Every vector
  stacks its return address and `SPSR` on the SVC stack with `SRSDB` and switches to SVC
  mode; from user mode it saves the program through `STM ^` and returns into `run_user`
  with its cause (a system call; an IRQ, then handled; an undefined instruction; a prefetch
  or data abort, with `IFSR`/`IFAR` or `DFSR`/`DFAR`). In the kernel an IRQ is handled and
  resumed and anything else stops the machine. `Arm` implements `Platform` like RV32 (D481):
  LPAE tables through `TTBR0` and `TLBIALL`, the device tree at RAM's start, a direct map of
  768 MiB and a 2 MiB device window at `0xffc0_0000`, the virtual timer by compare value with
  its interrupt masked once taken, `TPIDRPRW` for the CPU-local block, data-cache cleaning to
  the point of unification and `ICIALLUIS` for new code, long-descriptor fault statuses
  (translation, access flag, permission) as page faults, VFPv3-D32 saved and restored with
  `FPEXC.EN` gating user use, and a user test program in the EABI (the Linux programs not
  written yet exit with status 1).
- **Not yet.** Secondary CPUs through PSCI `CPU_ON`, console input and device interrupts,
  ASIDs, PAN, the 32-bit Linux ABI's own system-call table, and the core's remaining 64-bit
  assumptions.

## D483 64-bit atomics on every target: `hal::atomic::AtomicU64` (M9, the core's 64-bit assumptions, part 1; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** The kernel and the HAL keep clocks, counters, generation numbers and per-CPU
  words in `core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64` (225 uses in 53 files); RV32's `A` extension has no
  64-bit atomic instructions, so `core` offers no `AtomicU64` there (32-bit Arm has `LDREXD`
  and keeps it).
- **Decision.** `hal::atomic::AtomicU64` is `core`'s where the target has 64-bit atomics, and on
  RV32 a word guarded by a spin lock with the same methods (`load`, `store`, `swap`, the
  compare-exchanges, the `fetch_*` operations, `get_mut`, `into_inner`), every operation
  sequentially consistent. The kernel takes interrupts only where it holds no lock (D37), so an
  interrupt handler never finds the lock held by the code it interrupted. Every user in the
  HAL and the kernel now imports it from there, so 64-bit targets compile to exactly what they
  did.
- **Not yet.** The pointer-width assumptions (addresses and lengths kept in `u64` and cast to
  `usize`, the direct map's size, user-space limits) and the 32-bit Linux ABIs.

## D484 RV32's Linux ABI (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `kernel/src/linux/abi/riscv32.rs` takes RV64's file whole (the generic table,
  `open` and `mmap` flags, `stat`, fault classification, signal-frame code and test support)
  and names the machine `riscv32`. RV32 Linux has only 64-bit time, so the generic numbers of
  the 32-bit-time calls name nothing and their `time64` numbers take their place
  (`clock_gettime64` 403 and its kin, `timerfd_*64`, `utimensat_time64`, `pselect6_time64`,
  `ppoll_time64`, `rt_sigtimedwait_time64`, `futex_time64`), the same arguments with 64-bit
  `timespec`s the kernel's handlers already read.
- **Not yet.** The 32-bit layouts the generic code reads at 64 bits (`iovec`, `msghdr`,
  `sigaction`, `stack_t`, `siginfo_t`, the auxiliary vector, RV32's 32-bit signal frame),
  `llseek`'s split offset, `mmap2`'s page offset, ELF32 programs in `exec`, and RV32's lack of
  `fstat` and `newfstatat` (programs use `statx`).

## D485 The Linux layer's word size, part 1: `abi::WORD_BYTES` and `iovec` (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `linux::abi` says how many bytes a C `long` and a pointer take in the
  architecture's user programs (`WORD_BYTES`: 4 on RV32 and 32-bit Arm, 8 elsewhere) and
  reads and writes such words (`word`, `put_word`). The generic structures move to it one at
  a time; `struct iovec` first, so `readv`, `writev`, `preadv` and every caller of `Iovecs`
  read a base and a length of the program's width. 64-bit architectures read exactly what
  they did.
- **Next in the audit.** `msghdr` and `cmsghdr`, `sigaction` and `stack_t`, the auxiliary
  vector and the argument and environment pointers `exec` writes, ELF32 programs,
  `siginfo_t`, the 32-bit signal frames, `llseek`, `mmap2` and 64-bit arguments in register
  pairs; then 32-bit Arm's own ABI file.

## D486 The Linux layer's word size, part 2: `msghdr` and `cmsghdr` (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `struct msghdr` is seven words of the program's width (the name pointer, its
  length, the `iovec` array and its count, the control buffer and its length, the flags) and
  `struct cmsghdr` a word of length and two `int`s, its messages aligned to a word: 56 and 16
  bytes on 64-bit programs as before, 28 and 12 on 32-bit ones. `sendmsg`, `recvmsg` on every
  socket kind, `SCM_RIGHTS` messages built and parsed, and the header fields written back
  (name length, control length, flags) all take their places from the word size.

## D487 The Linux layer's word size, part 3: `sigaction` and `stack_t` (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The kernel's `struct sigaction` is the handler, the flags and, where the
  architecture has one, the restorer, each a word of the program's width, then the 64-bit
  signal mask: 32 or 24 bytes on 64-bit programs as before, 20 on 32-bit Arm and 16 on RV32.
  MIPS keeps its own flags-first layout (D315). `stack_t` is three words, the flags an `int`
  at the second (padded on 64-bit), the size at the third, or the other way round on MIPS: 24
  bytes on 64-bit programs, 12 on 32-bit ones. `rt_sigaction`, `sigaltstack` and every signal
  frame's `uc_stack` take these sizes; the 32-bit frames themselves are D490's work.

## D488 The Linux layer's word size, part 4: ELF-32 programs and the initial stack (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The ELF reader takes images of the kernel's own class, as it already takes only
  its own byte order: ELF-64 on the 64-bit ports, ELF-32 on RV32 and 32-bit Arm (52-byte file
  header, 32-byte program headers whose flags come after the sizes). One table of field
  offsets serves both, addresses read at the class's width; an image of the other class is
  `ENOEXEC`, as Linux refuses a 64-bit program on a 32-bit kernel. `elf::build` writes the same
  class and native byte order, so the boot self-test's program is right on every port (it wrote
  little-endian before, wrong on the big-endian ones). On the initial stack `argc`, the `argv`
  and `envp` pointers and each auxiliary vector entry are words of the program's width, in
  native order; `execve` reads its pointer lists the same way and charges a word per string.
  32-bit Arm's `AT_PLATFORM` is `v7l`, as Linux gives on ARMv7 little-endian; `e_machine` 40.

## D489 The Linux layer's word size, part 5: `siginfo_t` (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `signals::info_offset` names where a `siginfo_t`'s fields are: the three `int`s
  first, then the union from the first word boundary after them, offset 16 on 64-bit programs
  and 12 on 32-bit ones, so a sender's ids, a child's status and times, `sigqueue`'s value and a
  fault's address move with the word size, its pointers and `clock_t`s a word wide. The kept
  record, the fault `siginfo_t`, `rt_sigqueueinfo`'s checks and the `signalfd_siginfo` built
  from it (whose own layout is the same on every architecture) all use them. `siginfo_t` stays
  128 bytes on both. The boot self-test that queues signals from kernel code keeps its 64-bit
  layout: the 32-bit test programs do not run it yet (D481).

## D490 The Linux layer's word size, part 6: RV32's signal frame (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The shared `ucontext_t` start follows the word size: `uc_flags` and `uc_link`
  a word each, then `stack_t` (D487), then the 64-bit mask, then the 128-byte `sigset_t` room,
  `uc_mcontext` 16-byte aligned after it: 304 bytes into the frame on 64-bit programs as before,
  288 on 32-bit ones. RISC-V's frame takes `sc_regs` as 32 words and `sc_fpregs` (the 528-byte
  union whose D state RV32 shares with RV64: `f0` to `f31` are 64-bit on both) right after
  them, so RV32's frame is 944 bytes and RV64's stays 1088. RV32 thus uses RV64's frame code
  as written, through D484's shared module. 32-bit Arm's frame (`sigcontext` of 21 words and
  the VFP record in `uc_regspace`) comes with its ABI file (D492).

## D491 The Linux layer's word size, part 7: calls that split 64-bit values (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** A 32-bit program passes a 64-bit file offset or length in two registers, so on
  the 32-bit ports `linux::wide_arguments` takes `_llseek` (high and low halves, the result
  written as a 64-bit `loff_t`), `mmap2` (the offset in 4096-byte units), `pread64`,
  `pwrite64`, `ftruncate64`, `fallocate`, `fadvise64_64`, and `statfs64`/`fstatfs64` (which
  take the structure's size and refuse any other with `EINVAL`), joins the halves (low first
  on a little-endian machine) and calls the same handlers the 64-bit ports do. The table sits
  where those calls have their generic numbers, so a port's number file names them once.
  32-bit Arm's EABI starts each pair at an even register (`abi::ALIGNED_REGISTER_PAIRS`) and
  its `arm_fadvise64_64` takes the advice second (`abi::FADVISE_ADVICE_SECOND`); RV32 packs
  them. The check is one constant-false branch on the 64-bit ports, so their system-call path
  is unchanged.
- `struct statfs64` is the type and block size a word each, the five counts 64-bit, then the
  name length, fragment size, flags and four spares a word each: 120 bytes on the 64-bit
  ports' `statfs` as before, 88 on RV32, 84 on 32-bit Arm (packed, `abi::STATFS_ALIGN`).
- `fcntl64`'s `F_GETLK64`, `F_SETLK64` and `F_SETLKW64` (12 to 14) are the record-lock
  commands on the 32-bit ports: `struct flock64` is the 64-bit ports' `struct flock`. The plain
  ones with a 32-bit `struct flock` are not answered (`EINVAL`); musl and 64-bit-offset glibc
  never use them.

## D492 32-bit Arm's Linux ABI (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** `kernel/src/linux/abi/arm.rs` is the EABI: its own table (the number in `r7`),
  with the 32-bit-uid calls (`setuid32` and the rest), the 64-bit-offset ones (`_llseek`,
  `mmap2`, `ftruncate64`, `fcntl64`, `statfs64`, `arm_fadvise64_64`, D491) and the 64-bit-time
  ones (`clock_gettime64`, `futex_time64`, `ppoll_time64`, ...) in the places of the generic
  names, the legacy calls (`open`, `pipe`, `dup2`, `fork`, ...) that musl still makes on Arm,
  and `renameat`. The calls that exist only with 32-bit time or the old `struct stat64`
  (`nanosleep`, `gettimeofday`, `settimeofday`, `getrlimit`, `setrlimit`, `stat64`,
  `fstat64`, `fstatat64`, `_newselect`) get numbers past the table and answer `ENOSYS`:
  64-bit-time C libraries (glibc 2.34 with `_TIME_BITS=64`, musl 1.2) use the `time64` calls,
  `prlimit64` and `statx` instead. The table check ignores those past-the-table names.
- `O_DIRECTORY` is `0o40000` and `O_NOFOLLOW` `0o100000`; `struct sigaction` has a restorer;
  `uname` says `armv7l` and `AT_PLATFORM` `v7l`; `epoll_event` is 16 bytes.
- **The signal frame** is Linux's `rt_sigframe`: the `siginfo_t`, `uc_flags`, `uc_link`,
  `uc_stack`, then `struct sigcontext` (`trap_no` 14 for an abort or 6 for an undefined
  instruction, `error_code` the fault status with the prefetch mark as Linux's `FSR_LNX_PF`,
  `oldmask`, `r0` to `r15`, `cpsr`, `fault_address`), then the mask and its 128-byte room,
  then `uc_regspace` (8-byte aligned) with the VFP record (`VFP_MAGIC`, 288 bytes: `d0` to
  `d31`, `FPSCR`, `FPEXC` with its enable bit) and a zero end word, then the 16 bytes of
  return code Linux keeps for handlers without a restorer, unused here: 888 bytes, 8-byte
  aligned. A handler at an odd address starts in Thumb state with the `IT` bits cleared;
  `rt_sigreturn` refuses a stack pointer that is not 8-byte aligned and a VFP record whose
  magic or size is wrong, as Linux does. The kernel's trampoline is `mov r7, #173; svc #0`.
- **Faults** read the long-descriptor fault status (LPAE, D474): alignment `SIGBUS`
  `BUS_ADRALN`, external aborts and parity errors `SIGBUS` `BUS_OBJERR`, debug events
  `SIGTRAP`, translation, access-flag and permission faults by the process's regions; an
  undefined instruction is `SIGILL`.
- **`set_tls`** (`0xf0005`, Arm's private range) sets `TPIDRURO` through the same code as
  MIPS's `set_thread_area`, answered on the past-the-table path so the hot path is unchanged.
  Arm's other private calls (`cacheflush`, `breakpoint`, `usr26`, `usr32`) and the kuser
  helper page are not given; ARMv7 C libraries read `TPIDRURO` directly.
- The HAL's `FpState` gives 32-bit Arm's `d0` to `d31` and `FPSCR` (`d`, `d_mut`, `fpscr`,
  `set_fpscr`). RV32's ABI file no longer re-exports RV64's host-test support, which only
  exists in host test builds.
- **Not yet word-sized**: `times`, `getrusage`, `wait4`'s `rusage`, `sysinfo` and the robust
  futex list, whose structures hold `long`s or pointers (D493).

## D493 The Linux layer's word size, part 8: `rusage`, `tms`, `sysinfo` and the robust list (M9, the 32-bit audit; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The last structures of `long`s and pointers the Linux layer writes or walks take
  the program's word: `struct rusage` is 18 words (144 or 72 bytes, `getrusage` and `wait4`),
  `struct tms` four `clock_t`s, `struct sysinfo` 112 or 64 bytes with its `long`s a word and
  its `mem_unit` a page when a 32-bit word cannot hold the memory's size in bytes, as Linux
  does; `struct robust_list_head` is three words (`set_robust_list` takes 24 or 12), its
  pointers read at the word's width and its offset sign-extended, the addresses cut to the
  word. 32-bit C libraries convert `rusage`'s 32-bit `timeval`s themselves (there is no
  `time64` `getrusage`).
- With D485 to D493 the 32-bit Linux layer's structures are those of RV32 and 32-bit Arm. What
  stays 64-bit is what 32-bit programs reach only through calls past the table (D492) or
  through `ioctl`s and `/proc` files whose layouts have no `long` in them.

## D494 RV32 and 32-bit Arm's build entries (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** xtask knows both ports by name only, like MIPS64, s390x and SPARC64 (D297):
  `riscv32` builds the kernel for `riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf` and its programs for
  `riscv32gc-unknown-linux-musl` (tier 3, so through the nightly `build-std` path, D324) and
  boots `qemu-system-riscv32 -machine virt -bios default`; `armv7` builds the kernel for
  `armv7a-none-eabi` (soft-float: the kernel touches VFP only in the HAL's save and restore,
  whose assembly names the FPU itself) and its programs for `armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf`,
  and boots `qemu-system-arm -machine virt,highmem=off,gic-version=2 -cpu cortex-a15`. Both use
  virtio-mmio devices, as AArch64 and RV64 on `virt` do. `.cargo/config.toml` gives the four
  targets their `eggos_kernel` and `eggos_user` flags. `all`, CI and the release matrix leave
  them out until they are tested.

## D495 The core on 32-bit kernels: offsets past a word (M9; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The core keeps addresses, sizes and offsets in `u64` and turns them into `usize`
  where they index memory. On RV32 and 32-bit Arm a `usize` is 32 bits while file offsets stay
  64-bit (D491), so a cast could cut an offset past 4 GiB to a small one and reach the wrong
  page. Memory files (`memfd`) and tmpfs files are therefore at most the pages a `usize` can
  count (16 TiB on a 32-bit kernel; Linux's largest offset elsewhere, as before): a write or
  truncation past it is `EFBIG`, and tmpfs counts a size's pages in `u64` before narrowing.
  The desktop protocol's drag payload offset is narrowed with a check. The other casts index
  memory that is already bounded by a length checked first (images, archives, user buffers,
  the direct map, which the 32-bit HALs cap to what their boot tables map: 896 MiB on RV32,
  768 MiB on 32-bit Arm), so they stay.
- With D474 to D495 every part of RV32 and 32-bit Arm on QEMU `virt` is written: page tables,
  boot, traps, threads, user mode, FP, `Platform`, atomics, the Linux ABIs and their build
  entries.

## D496 AMD's display engine at the firmware's mode, DCN 3.x (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** D468 left DCN's pipes undriven until per-version register places were written.
  Driving a pipe from scratch (DMCUB, clocks through the SMU, DIG encoders, link training, the
  pipe's HUBP, DPP, MPC, OPP and OTG) is a large driver; the firmware already lit one.
- **Decision.** As Intel's first step did (D268), the AMD driver takes the pipe the firmware lit
  at its mode. `amd_dcn` finds the hub (HUBP) whose viewport is the firmware framebuffer's
  size and whose surface is 32-bit ARGB, sets its flips to happen at the vertical update, flips
  by writing the surface address (high half first, the low half latching both) and waits for
  the hub's flip-pending bit; the cursor is the hub's 64x64 straight-alpha ARGB cursor, enabled
  in the paired DPP too, starting at the screen's edge with its hidden part skipped through the
  hot spot when it is off the top or left. The places are dwords from the display block's
  segment 2 base, which IP discovery gives (D468), in the register BAR (BAR 5), and are the same
  on every DCN 3.0 to 3.5 version for these registers.
- **Surfaces.** The two surfaces and the cursor are in video memory: the firmware's own
  framebuffer and the space right after it in the aperture (BAR 0), each 64 KiB aligned, written
  through one write-combining mapping. Their GPU addresses are the firmware surface's address
  plus their distance from it, since the aperture maps video memory in order, so no GART or
  page tables are needed. The kernel draws into a cached frame, copies the damage into the
  hidden surface, drains the writes and flips, as on Intel. A frame waits for the previous
  flip (no interrupts yet).
- **Sources.** The register places and fields are from AMD's published `dcn_*_offset.h` and
  `_sh_mask.h` headers, MIT-licensed separately from Linux; `drivers/src/gpu/AMD-NOTICE.md`
  carries their notice. No other code is used.
- The `Probe` trait gains `map_write_combining` and `boot_framebuffer`.
- **Not yet.** Loading DMCUB, setting modes and lighting more outputs (the firmware's mode is
  what the first screen shows), vertical-blank interrupts, DCN 2.x and older engines (DCE).

## D497 NVIDIA's GSP boot, part 1: the Falcon engines (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Question.** From Turing on, NVIDIA's display is driven through the GSP firmware (D469),
  which only starts after a chain of signed firmware runs on the GPU's Falcon microcontrollers:
  the video BIOS's FWSEC carves out the protected region (WPR2), SEC2 runs the booter that loads
  GSP's image into it, and GSP then answers the driver's remote calls. Every link needs to load
  and run code on a Falcon.
- **Decision.** `nvidia_falcon` drives one Falcon engine at its block in BAR 0 (GSP's at
  `0x110000`, SEC2's at `0x840000`): reset through its engine register, wait for the memory
  scrub, pick the Falcon core over the RISC-V one in the boot core register, let DMA run
  without a context, copy code into IMEM through the auto-incrementing port with one tag per
  256-byte block (the secure bit set for heavy-secure code) and data into DMEM, set the boot
  vector and the two mailboxes, start the core (through `CPUCTL_ALIAS` when the alias is
  enabled) and wait for it to halt, returning the mailboxes. It refuses code or data that does
  not fit the memories `HWCFG` reports. The NVIDIA probe reports GSP's IMEM and DMEM sizes.
- **Sources.** NVIDIA's published register manuals (MIT); `drivers/src/gpu/NVIDIA-NOTICE.md`
  carries their notice.
- **Not yet (part 2 on).** Extracting FWSEC from the video BIOS's Falcon ucode table and
  patching its DMEM command for the WPR2 region, running SEC2's booter with GSP's image and its
  WPR metadata, GSP's message queues and remote calls, and the display through them. Until
  then the firmware's framebuffer stays the display on NVIDIA boards (D236).

## D498 Intel display 12 and 13: mode setting on the combo ports (M13; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** Tiger, Rocket, Alder and Raptor Lake (display 12 and 13) light a second screen
  on their combo ports A and B as display 11 does (D465), with the registers that moved: the
  combo PLLs' configuration at `0x164284` (eight bytes a PLL), the transcoder's clock select
  field from bit 28, `TRANS_DDI_FUNC_CTL`'s port select from bit 27 holding the port plus one,
  and the link-training patterns in the transcoder's `DP_TP_CTL` (`0x60540` plus `0x1000` a
  transcoder) rather than the port's. `intel::Generation` names the engine (display 9, 11, or
  12 and 13) and gives each of these places, so `set_mode` and `train_port` (which now takes the
  pipe) stay one path. Register places are Intel's, from its public graphics programmer's
  reference manuals.
- **Not yet.** Type-C ports (their PHY ownership, lane assignment, the MG and Dekel PHYs and
  their PLLs), HDMI on display 11 and later, and display 14 (Meteor Lake's C10 and C20 PHYs);
  the firmware-lit screen on any of them is still taken (D268).

## D499 The Android layer, part 2: virtual dispatch, statics, arrays, switches and `throw` (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** The DEX compiler and the layer's runtime cover what ordinary app code uses
  beyond D472's slice:
  - **Virtual and interface calls** go through a dispatch helper: the call writes the method's
    index first and its own words after it; the helper takes the receiver's class, finds the
    first class up its superclasses that the framework implements the method for or that
    defines a compiled method of the same name and prototype (`Dex::method_prototype`; a file
    keeps each prototype once, so equal indexes are equal signatures), caches the answer per
    class and method, and calls it with the call's words. Direct, super and static calls stay
    direct.
  - **Static fields** are kept per field, and a class's `<clinit>` runs on its first static
    field access or new object (`Dex::field_class`), and for the launcher activity before it
    is created. Static calls do not trigger it yet.
  - **Arrays** are objects with elements: `new-array` (negative sizes stop with
    `NegativeArraySizeException`), `array-length`, `aget`/`aput` with Java's bounds check and
    each element narrowed to its type (`char` and `boolean` unsigned), and `fill-array-data`
    compiled into stores of its payload (at most 4096 elements).
  - **Switches**: `packed-switch` and `sparse-switch` become compare-and-jump runs read from
    their payloads at compile time. `cmp-long` compiles inline.
  - **Casts**: `check-cast` and `instance-of` follow the DEX file's superclasses; a class whose
    ancestry leaves the file (framework classes, interfaces) passes `check-cast` and is no
    instance, until the framework's class tree and interfaces are known.
  - **Exceptions**: `throw` stops the app naming the exception's class, as an uncaught
    exception ends an app; `move-exception` compiles (its handler is never reached yet) and
    `monitor-enter`/`monitor-exit` do nothing on the app's single thread.
- **Not yet.** Catching exceptions (`try` blocks and the unwinding through compiled frames),
  floating point, `filled-new-array`, method handles, interfaces in casts, garbage collection,
  and the framework's views, layouts and resources (D500 on).

## D500 The Android layer, part 3: layouts, resources, views and clicks (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** An app's first screens come from its compiled layouts:
  - `android-package::resources` reads `resources.arsc`: each package's type chunks (plain,
    sparse and 16-bit-offset entry tables), keeping every simple string value by resource id
    (`0xPPTTEEEE`), which holds string resources and the paths of layout files; the first
    configuration to give an entry a value wins (the default one, as the build tools write
    it). `android-package::layout` reads a compiled layout into a tree of views with their id,
    text or hint (literal or a string resource), `android:onClick` and orientation. The
    binary XML reading is the manifest's (D450), shared.
  - The framework (`userland/android`) gains `View`, `ViewGroup`, `Button`, `EditText` and
    `LinearLayout`, natives told apart by name and short signature
    (`Dex::method_shorty`): `setContentView(int)` inflates the layout the resource table
    names, `findViewById`, view constructors, `setOnClickListener`, `setText(int)`,
    `getText`, `getString`, `addView` and `setOrientation`. A layout element names its class
    as Android does (`Button` is `android.widget.Button`, a dotted name is whole).
  - The window shows the views as toolkit labels and buttons, linear layouts stacked down or
    across and other layouts stacked down; a click on a button calls the activity's
    `android:onClick` method, or its click listener's `onClick`, with the view, compiled code
    found up the class's superclasses, and the window then shows the texts the call changed.
- **Not yet.** Other resource types (drawables, dimensions, colours, styles), configurations
  beyond the default, `ConstraintLayout`'s constraints and other layouts' rules, text input
  in `EditText`, images, lists (`RecyclerView`), fragments, more activities and intents.

## D501 iOS apps, part 2: scenes, touches and target-action (M15; code written, unbuilt, untested: code-only mode) — Decided by the code-only session (engineering)

- **Decision.** UIKit in the macOS layer (D473) runs apps written for scenes and touches:
  - **Scenes.** The bundle's `Info.plist` is read from an iOS app's flat bundle too
    (`<name>.app/Info.plist` beside the program). When it names a scene delegate
    (`UIApplicationSceneManifest`, the first application-role configuration), after the app
    delegate's launch `UIApplicationMain` makes a window scene and its session, makes the
    delegate and sends it `scene:willConnectToSession:options:`, then
    `sceneWillEnterForeground:` and `sceneDidBecomeActive:` when it answers them.
    `-[UIWindow initWithWindowScene:]` makes a 390x844 window, the size of a current phone's
    screen in points, and `windowScene` answers the scene. Class names given as Swift's
    `Module.Class` (the app delegate's too) are found under their Objective-C names
    (`_TtC5MyApp13SceneDelegate`).
  - **Touches.** `UITouch` is a class of the layer's: its place in any view
    (`locationInView:` through `convertPoint:fromView:`), phase, view and window. A view's
    `mouseDown:`, `mouseDragged:` and `mouseUp:` that nothing overrides send
    `touchesBegan:withEvent:`, `touchesMoved:withEvent:` and `touchesEnded:withEvent:` with a
    set of one touch when the view's class answers them; AppKit apps' views do not, so nothing
    changes for them. `UIEvent` is the event.
  - **Controls.** `UIControl` stands on `NSControl` and `UIImageView` on `NSImageView`;
    `addTarget:action:forControlEvents:` for a touch up inside or a primary action sets the
    control's target and action, so a button's tap calls the app as AppKit's click does.
- **Not yet.** Several touches at once (multi-touch screens), gesture recognizers, Auto Layout,
  iOS storyboards and view controllers' presentation, safe areas, and the scene's own
  `UIScreen` and size classes.
